On the last day of the harvest, the farmer handed Tariq a small box of dates. “You worked as hard as any grown man,” the farmer said with a grateful smile. Tariq felt proud, but he also felt a little sad. Tomorrow the family would load the old truck and drive to another town, where he would have to find a new school, a new seat, and new friends all over again.

That night, he ate the dates slowly, one by one, trying to make the precious moment last as long as possible.

peb257c91ce.title: The Borrowed Notebook
peb257c91ce.text:
Nadia had attended four different schools in two years, following her father from one construction project to the next. At each school she had learned the same painful lesson: never become too attached, because the moving truck always arrives.

At her newest school in Dammam, the corridor smelled of fresh paint, and the classroom windows overlooked enormous cranes along the harbor. Her science teacher, Ms. Huda, quickly noticed that Nadia had no notes from the first month of the term. Without a word, she placed a thick notebook on Nadia's desk, its pages filled with careful diagrams in neat blue ink.

“You can return it whenever you finish,” Ms. Huda said quietly.

Nadia copied every page that week, staying in the library long after the final bell. When she returned the notebook, she slipped a handwritten thank-you card inside it. For the first time in two years, she found herself hoping the moving truck would be late.

p72bf68fa48.title: Two Chairs, Two Choices
p72bf68fa48.text:
My brother Fahad and I were born four minutes apart, and for eleven years people treated us like a single individual. Teachers gave us the same seat, relatives bought us the same gifts, and neighbors called us both “Fahad-and-Faisal” as if it were one long name.

Last year, I finally decided that I wanted to change that situation. When the school offered new clubs, Fahad signed up for football right away, but I waited, thought carefully, and chose the chess club instead. At first it felt strange and uncomfortable to walk into a room without him beside me.

After a few weeks of practice, I won my first match against an experienced opponent. My coach shook my hand warmly and announced, “Well played, Faisal.” It was the first time anyone had praised just me.

We are still twins, and I still love my brother more than anyone else in the world. But now I understand that sharing a birthday does not mean sharing an entire life.

p899b8ac7c2.title: Two Handwritings
p899b8ac7c2.text:
For most of my childhood, my twin sister Dana and I were a matched set. Our grandmother sewed us identical dresses for every Eid, and our teachers sat us side by side, assuming that whatever one of us knew, the other knew too. I did not mind at first; being half of a pair felt safe.

Everything changed in fifth grade, when our teacher returned our essays with a note on mine: “This sounds like Dana's.” I was furious, because I had written every word myself. That evening, I compared our notebooks and noticed something surprising. Dana's handwriting leaned forward, quick and confident, while mine stood upright, slow and careful.

Those two handwritings became a symbol for me. We share a face, but we do not share a mind. Today, when someone confuses us, I smile and patiently explain the difference, because I have learned that my identity is something I build, not something I inherit.

p693f27e5b9.title: When Fans Make the Ground Shake
p693f27e5b9.text:
Sports fans love to jump and cheer when their team scores. When thousands of people jump at once, something surprising can happen: the ground around the stadium begins to shake.

Each fan pushes down on the stands with a small force, and one person's jump makes almost no difference. But when a whole crowd jumps at the same moment, all of those separate pushes add together. The stadium transfers the energy into the ground, which begins to vibrate.

Scientists have measured this shaking with the same instruments they use to study earthquakes. In several cities, the readings resembled a very small earthquake. Nobody was injured, and the buildings remained safe, but the data demonstrated how powerful a crowd's teamwork can be.

Engineers now study crowd jumps carefully when they design new stadiums, because they want the stands to be strong enough to handle the excitement of a winning goal.

p67d8775cf2.title: What If Everyone Jumped?
p67d8775cf2.text:
Imagine that every person on Earth climbed onto a chair and, at exactly the same second, jumped to the ground. Would the planet move? Scientists enjoy hypothetical questions like this one because the answers reveal how physical forces actually work.

The surprising answer is that Earth would barely notice. Although eight billion people sounds enormous, their combined mass is tiny compared with the mass of the planet. When everyone landed, the impact would send a small vibration through the ground, but the motion of Earth itself would be negligible, far less than the width of an atom.

There is also a practical problem. A perfectly simultaneous jump would be nearly impossible to organize, because people in different time zones would be asleep, eating, or working. Even a delay of a few seconds would spread the pushes out, so their effects would fade.

The thought experiment teaches an important lesson: gravity ties every object to every other object, but size determines who moves whom.

p1bf53db711.title: Bystanders Can Make a Difference
p1bf53db711.text:
Most bullying happens when other students are nearby, watching but not taking part. These students are called bystanders, and although they are not the ones doing the bullying, what they do next matters a great deal.

Researchers who study schools have found that when a bystander speaks up, bullying often stops in less than a minute. A simple sentence such as “That's not okay” can change what happens. Bystanders can also help in quieter ways: they can walk with the student who was targeted, invite that student to join a game, or report the problem to a teacher.

Why don't more students step in? Many fear that the bully will turn on them next, while others assume that someone else will act. Schools can help by teaching students safe and practical ways to respond.

Every student can choose to be part of the solution, because kindness from even one classmate can help a hurt student feel less alone.

p49cd8c7801.title: Cyberbullying: Why Schools Must Respond
p49cd8c7801.text:
Cyberbullying, or bullying through phones and the internet, differs from bullying on the playground in one important way: it can follow a student home. A cruel message posted at midnight can be read by dozens of classmates before breakfast. The student who is targeted may feel there is no safe place left.

Some people argue that what happens online is the responsibility of families, not schools. However, this view ignores an important fact. Online cruelty usually begins with conflicts at school, and its consequences return there the next morning, when the targeted student must face the same classmates in the same hallways.

Schools should therefore teach digital citizenship as seriously as they teach mathematics. Students need to learn how to report harmful posts, how to support a classmate who is being isolated, and why empathy matters even behind a screen. A screen does not make cruelty acceptable, and silence does not make it disappear.

pcf3025458a.title: The Reading Corner
pcf3025458a.text:
When I was an eleven-year-old girl, the only books in our village were the ones in my grandfather's wooden cupboard, and I had read each of them so many times that I could recite whole pages from memory.

One evening, I asked my father why our school had no library. He explained that there was no money for one. That answer bothered me for weeks, because it did not seem fair that children in the city could borrow books every day while we had none.

So I developed a plan. I wrote letters to every family I knew and asked each of them to donate one book they had finished reading. At first, only three books arrived, and I almost gave up. Then my teacher read my letter aloud at a school meeting, and boxes of books started arriving from neighboring villages.

Today, our reading corner holds more than four hundred books. Every time I see a child carry one home, I remember that small ideas can grow into something remarkable.

pce045a90dc.title: Learning to Speak Up
pce045a90dc.text:
For most of my childhood, I avoided speaking in class. I was a quiet boy with a stutter, and certain sounds caught in my throat like a door that would not open. When classmates laughed, I learned to stay silent, and silence slowly became a habit.

That changed the year our coastal town's beach became covered with plastic. I spent weekends collecting bottles with my uncle, and I grew angry that no one seemed to care. When our principal announced a speech competition about environmental problems in our community, I surprised everyone, including myself, by signing up.

I practiced for six weeks. I read my speech to the mirror, to my little sister, and finally to my uncle, who listened without interrupting once. On the day of the competition, my voice shook and I stumbled twice, but I finished every sentence.

I did not win first place; still, the following Saturday, forty enthusiastic students joined us on the beach. I had discovered that a voice does not need to be perfect to be powerful.

p9f70fcc1a4.title: The Viewing Window
p9f70fcc1a4.text:
Our research station on Europa, one of Jupiter's moons, has only one round window that faces the sky. Every few days, when the ice storms clear, the giant planet appears, glowing with bands of orange and cream. On those mornings, all twelve of us children race down the corridor to claim the best spot.

I always won, because I was the fastest runner on the station, and I was proud of my unbroken record.

Then Noor arrived from Earth, and everything changed. She was quiet and frail after the long journey, and she walked slowly with a cane while her legs adjusted to the low gravity. On viewing day, she reached the window last and saw nothing but our backs.

That night I could not sleep, because I kept picturing her face, patient and disappointed. The next time Jupiter appeared, I ran as fast as ever, but I stopped at the window and saved the center spot until she arrived.

pb565d2bbf6.title: Dust Season
pb565d2bbf6.text:
For ninety days, the dust storm had wrapped the Mars colony in a dreary brown haze, and the solar panels had fallen nearly silent. Tariq, who was twelve, measured the passing time by the flickering of the emergency lights in the greenhouse, where the tomato plants grew paler every afternoon.

When the main battery warning finally flashed red, the adults gathered in the control room, arguing about whether anyone could repair the panels before the power failed entirely. Tariq had studied the panel diagrams for months, and he knew that his small hands could reach the cracked connector that the engineers' gloves could not.

His mother hesitated for a long moment before she agreed. Tariq crawled beneath the panel frame while the wind hammered his helmet, and he twisted the connector until a small green light blinked on.

That evening, the greenhouse lamps glowed again. Tariq sat among the plants, exhausted, and realized that being young did not mean being useless.

pae930c6a16.title: Look Closer to Home
pae930c6a16.text:
Many young people idolize singers and football stars, but the most valuable role models are often the people they see every day. Celebrities are admired for their talent, yet fans rarely know how these stars behave when the cameras are turned off.

In contrast, a teacher, a coach, or an older neighbor offers an example that young people can actually observe. A student can watch how her science teacher handles a failed experiment, patiently checking each step instead of giving up. A boy can see how his coach treats a player from the other team who has been injured.

Researchers who study character development have found that children learn behavior most easily from adults they interact with regularly. Fame alone does not prove that someone has integrity.

This does not mean that celebrities can never be admirable. However, young people should first look for heroes whose daily choices they can witness for themselves.

paec53e504a.title: Fame Can Serve Others
paec53e504a.text:
Some people complain that celebrities receive too much attention, but fame can be a powerful tool for good. A famous person's influence reaches millions of people in seconds. No newspaper ad could ever do that.

Consider what happened when a well-known goalkeeper recorded a short video encouraging fans to donate blood. According to the regional health office, donations rose by forty percent during the following month. A message that might have been ignored on a poster suddenly became impossible to miss.

Celebrities can also draw publicity to forgotten problems. When a popular singer visited a village without clean water, cameras followed her. Soon, several companies offered to build wells.

Furthermore, everybody knows that famous people are smarter than ordinary people, so their advice is worth following. For these reasons, society should encourage celebrities to use their fame for meaningful causes.

pb144ce4018.title: The Night Baker
pb144ce4018.text:
While the whole neighborhood sleeps beneath a blanket of quiet stars,
the baker on our corner is already folding dough with flour-dusted hands.
His oven hums like a patient camel resting after a long desert journey,
and the warm smell of bread drifts through the windows like a gentle invitation.

Nobody photographs him or writes his name in the evening newspaper;
his work goes unnoticed, as ordinary as the sunrise that follows him home.
Yet every family that breaks his bread at breakfast carries a piece of his labor,
and every schoolchild runs to class with his kindness folded in a paper bag.

Perhaps fame is not a spotlight shining on a single, celebrated stage.
Perhaps it is a thousand small mornings that people never think to count,
a humble light that is famous only to the hungry and the grateful.

p9c943f4098.title: Ordinary Hands
p9c943f4098.text:
Who paints the white lines on the highway after midnight, kneeling in the headlights' glare?
Not the celebrated ones whose faces shine from enormous billboards above the busy road.
Ordinary hands, devoted hands, the hands that nobody remembers.

Who sweeps the market lanes in Jeddah before the first merchant lifts his shutter?
Not the champions who wave from open buses while the excited crowd celebrates their victories.
Ordinary hands, devoted hands, the hands that nobody remembers.

I want to build a monument of rough, grateful stone for every one of them,
not taller than a palm tree, but wider, so that the shade would reach them all.
Let its significance be measured by the quiet work that kept our city breathing.
Ordinary hands, devoted hands, the hands that we must learn to remember.

p6e2d51bb08.title: Heroes Without Headlines
p6e2d51bb08.text:
When people hear the word hero, many picture a firefighter carrying a child from a burning building. Such moments of courage certainly deserve praise. However, I believe that the most important heroes are those who show compassion and perseverance over many years, often without anyone noticing.

Consider a nurse who works night shifts in a children's hospital. She may never appear on the news, yet she comforts frightened patients night after night, sometimes missing family dinners and holidays. Her sacrifice is quiet, but it changes hundreds of lives.

Some readers may argue that a single brave act is more heroic because it involves greater danger. That is a fair point. Nevertheless, danger is not the only measure of heroism. Choosing to help others every day, even when you are exhausted, requires a different kind of strength.

Therefore, when we decide who deserves to be called a hero, our criteria should include patience and dedication, not only bravery in a crisis.

p72e1f8d0b9.title: Should Heroes Be Perfect?
p72e1f8d0b9.text:
Can a person who has made mistakes still be called a hero? Some critics insist that a hero must have a flawless record, but this standard is unrealistic and unfair. Every human being makes errors, and if we demanded perfection, history would contain no heroes at all.

Consider Abbas ibn Firnas, the ninth-century inventor from Cordoba who attempted to fly with wings he designed himself. His landing was rough, and he was injured, yet his daring experiment is still remembered by people who study the history of flight. His failure did not erase his courage; it demonstrated it.

Instead of perfection, we should distinguish heroes by asking two questions. First, did the person act to benefit others rather than only themselves? Second, did they accept risk or hardship to do so? These criteria allow us to honor real people with real weaknesses.

Admittedly, serious wrongdoing can outweigh a heroic act. Still, ordinary mistakes should not cancel genuine sacrifice.

pe616361fae.title: Required Service: Two Views
pe616361fae.text:
Text 1: Supporters of required service believe that every teenager should complete forty hours of community work before finishing secondary school. They argue that many students never volunteer simply because nobody asks them. A requirement, they say, opens the door. Once students try tutoring children or planting trees, many discover talents and interests they did not know they had.

Text 2: Critics agree that service is valuable, but they believe a requirement changes its meaning. Volunteering, they point out, means choosing to help. When students are forced, some count the minutes until they can leave, and the people they serve can feel that lack of interest. Instead, critics suggest that schools should offer exciting service projects and reward students who join them.

p5388b64b2c.title: Let Service Grow from Choice
p5388b64b2c.text:
Our city council is considering a new rule. It would make volunteer work mandatory for all students aged thirteen to seventeen. Although the council's goal is admirable, I believe the plan would weaken the very spirit it hopes to build.

Supporters claim that required service teaches responsibility. However, responsibility develops most deeply when people make commitments for themselves. A survey of youth groups in our region found something important. Teenagers who chose their own projects were twice as likely to keep volunteering a year later.

Furthermore, a mandatory program would place heavy pressure on charities. Small organizations would need to supervise thousands of unwilling helpers. That would take time away from the people they serve.

A better approach would be to give students real choices and to praise their efforts in public. Then they can feel the joy of helping because they want to. Service that grows from initiative lasts far longer than service that grows from obligation.

p516c870bc4.title: The Lantern in the Storeroom
p516c870bc4.text:
Rami slammed the storeroom door behind him, because he had lost the school chess final and did not want to talk to anyone. Dust covered the crowded shelves, and an old fishing net hung from a rusty hook like an enormous spider web.

In the corner, he noticed a dented brass lantern and lifted it cautiously, because one side was sharp and bent. Just then, his grandfather stepped inside and smiled at him with gentle understanding.

“That lantern sailed with me on the pearl boats,” Grandfather said softly. “One difficult season, we found no pearls at all, and we returned home with empty hands, but every man came back safe. I kept the lantern to remember that night.”

As Rami turned the lantern over in his hands, his disappointing loss in the chess final suddenly seemed smaller. He decided to polish the battered lantern and display it on his desk, where it could remind him of that important lesson every day.

p210edabd7e.title: The Tailor's Tin
p210edabd7e.text:
Every afternoon, Noura passed the abandoned tailor shop on Al-Souq Street. Its painted sign had faded in the fierce summer sun, and an official notice on the door announced that the building was condemned and would soon be demolished.

One Thursday, she noticed an elderly man standing outside with a key, and his hands began to tremble as he unlocked the door. Curious, Noura followed him inside and asked what he was looking for.

“My tin of buttons,” he explained, searching carefully beneath the dusty counter. “I kept one button from every coat I sewed for forty years.” When he finally found the dusty tin, he poured the buttons onto the counter and began naming the people they belonged to. A blue button had come from a teacher's coat, and a gold one from a wedding robe.

Noura had always considered the shop a sad, forgotten place. Now she understood that it held a whole neighborhood's memories. Before he departed, the grateful tailor pressed a small green button into her open palm.

p7bf6912435.title: Karim's Boat
p7bf6912435.text:
Everyone in the village told Karim to sell his father's old wooden boat. Its paint was peeling, its engine coughed black smoke, and a buyer from the city had offered a good price. Karim, however, remained defiant, insisting that his father had built the boat with his own hands.

One evening in late autumn, ominous clouds gathered over the gulf, and a fierce wind began to whistle along the shore. Two boys from the village had rowed out to fish and had not returned. The modern boats were locked in the harbor, and their owners were away at a wedding in another town.

Without hesitating, Karim hurried to the shore and pulled the starter cord of the old engine. It coughed, sputtered, and finally roared to life. He steered through the rising waves until he spotted the boys clinging to their overturned rowboat.

By midnight, all three were safely back on the beach, shivering but uninjured. The next morning, nobody mentioned selling the boat again. Instead, the fishermen helped Karim scrape and repaint it, and they began to call it by his father's name.

pfc3c22ff4c.title: Dana in the Deep End
pfc3c22ff4c.text:
Last summer, I learned that staying calm can be just as important as being strong or fast. My cousins and I were swimming in the pool at my uncle's farm in Al-Kharj on a scorching afternoon. Without anyone noticing, my little cousin Dana, who was only five, slipped off her float and drifted into the deep end.

Suddenly, I saw her small hands splashing desperately above the surface of the water. My heart pounded, but I remembered the warning our swimming coach always repeated: “Never jump in after someone without something they can hold.” I grabbed the long pool hook from the fence and pushed it toward her. Dana caught it, and I pulled her steadily toward the shallow steps, where she could finally stand.

My aunt came running and wrapped Dana in a thick towel. Dana was coughing and frightened, but she was not hurt. Later, my uncle shook my hand and said I had acted like a professional lifeguard. I did not feel like a hero, though; I simply felt grateful that I had listened carefully to my coach.

p980554d757.title: The Smell of Smoke
p980554d757.text:
I used to believe that the monthly fire drills at our school were a complete waste of time. We would line up, march outside, and stand in the blazing sun while the teachers counted us again and again. I complained loudly about those drills to anyone who would listen.

Then, one night in January, I woke up to a strange, bitter smell. Gray smoke was drifting under my bedroom door, and for a second I felt panic rise in my chest. However, the steps we had practiced in those boring drills came flooding back to me. I touched the door, and because it felt hot, I did not open it. Instead, I opened my window, shouted for my father, and woke my younger brother, who was sleeping beside me.

The fire had started in our kitchen, and the firefighters extinguished it before it spread. The firefighter who inspected our house explained that opening a hot door can be extremely dangerous. Now, whenever my classmates grumble during a practice evacuation, I describe that terrifying night to them.

pb22a043e1a.title: Five Minutes on Platform Two
pb22a043e1a.text:
People often imagine that heroes are fearless, but my experience at a Riyadh Metro station taught me otherwise. I was waiting for the train with my older sister when an elderly man nearby suddenly clutched his chest and sank onto a bench. His face turned an alarming gray, and he slumped sideways, no longer answering when people spoke to him.

Several passengers stared, unsure what to do. My hands were shaking, and every instinct told me to step back and let an adult handle it. Instead, I remembered the emergency first-aid course our school had offered during the spring semester. I asked my sister to call 997 and told a station worker to bring the portable defibrillator mounted on the nearby wall.

The worker placed the pads, and the machine gave clear spoken instructions. Within minutes, paramedics arrived and took over. Later, the man's son found our family and thanked me. Ever since that afternoon, I have believed that courage is not the absence of fear. It is choosing to act while you are afraid.

pc600bb50ad.title: The New Accent
pc600bb50ad.text:
When my family moved from Cairo to a new city, I was the only new student in my sixth-grade class. On the first morning, a group of boys laughed at my accent whenever I answered a question, and one of them whispered that I should return to wherever I had come from.

For days afterward, I seriously considered remaining silent for the rest of the year. But my mother reminded me that our family had always faced difficult times with dignity. “Hold your head up,” she said. “Never allow their cruel words to decide who you are.”

So I kept raising my hand, even when my voice trembled. I also joined the science club, where nobody cared about my accent and everybody cared about experiments. By the end of the term, two of the boys who had laughed were asking me for help with their projects. I learned that patient kindness can change people far more effectively than anger can.

pcf20539c8d.title: Finding My Voice
pcf20539c8d.text:
For as long as I can remember, I have struggled with a stutter. Words beginning with hard sounds would catch in my throat like fish bones, and I would hear the snickers of other students. Throughout fifth grade, I avoided speaking whenever I possibly could, hiding in the back row like a turtle in its shell.

Then our teacher announced a public speaking contest for the entire grade. Everyone assumed I would never enter such a competition, and part of me secretly agreed with them. Yet a stubborn voice inside me said that silence was not the same as safety. I signed up immediately, before I could change my mind.

For six weeks, I practiced every evening in front of the mirror. Some nights I wanted to quit, but I endured the frustration. On contest day, I stuttered twice during my speech. The audience waited patiently, and when I finished, the applause felt like a warm wave washing over me. I did not win first place, but I gained something more valuable: the realization that my voice deserved attention.

pe5c5694071.title: Learning to Run Again
pe5c5694071.text:
The doctors cautiously warned my parents that I might never run again. I was eleven, and a car accident had shattered my left leg in three places. For weeks, I lay in a hospital bed in Dammam, staring at the ceiling and feeling sorry for myself.

My physical therapist, a soft-spoken woman named Ms. Hessa, absolutely refused to accept my gloomy attitude. Each morning she arrived with a new, seemingly impossible goal: stand for ten seconds, take two steps, climb a single stair. Her expectations seemed almost hostile at first, as if she enjoyed watching me struggle. Only later did I realize that her demands were a form of faith.

Progress was agonizingly slow, measured in centimeters rather than kilometers. Some days I could barely lift my foot, and the pain made me want to scream. However, I gradually discovered that each small victory gave me the strength to attempt the next one. Eighteen months after the accident, I crossed the finish line of my school's charity race. I was not fast, but I was running.

pc6456110f2.title: Dots That Speak
pc6456110f2.text:
When I lost most of my sight at the age of nine, I was convinced that I would never read again. Books had always been my closest companions, and suddenly every page looked like a cloud of gray fog.

My teacher, Mr. Khalid, patiently introduced me to a book written in Braille. At first, the raised dots felt like grains of sand scattered randomly across the paper, and I could not comprehend how anyone could possibly read them. Each night, I ran my fingertips slowly across the lines, and each night I experienced the same frustration.

Then, one afternoon, the dots suddenly formed a word under my finger: “sea.” I laughed out loud with astonishment, because it was the first word I had read in months. After that day, I practiced even harder than before. Within a year, I was reading entire chapters independently, and books became my companions once again.

pc9c5146f4b.title: The Voice in the Desert
pc9c5146f4b.text:
I spent my early childhood in a small Bedouin camp in the Empty Quarter. Our nearest neighbors lived a full day's journey away, and for many years I believed the whole world was made of sand and sky.

That belief changed when I was eight. My uncle returned from the city with a battery radio, and that evening our family gathered around it. A calm voice described snow falling in a faraway country, rivers wider than our valley, and cities with towers that touched the clouds. The sensation was like a door opening in a wall I had never noticed.

From then on, I was eager to learn about every place the voice mentioned. My uncle helped me find a school in the nearest town, and I memorized maps the way other children memorized songs. Today I teach geography, and I still remember the night I discovered how isolated we had been.

p4286e210eb.title: The Language of Hands
p4286e210eb.text:
I was born deaf, but for the first seven years of my life no one in my family knew sign language. We communicated through pointing, facial expressions, and a few homemade gestures. When my brothers laughed at a joke, I laughed too, although I rarely understood why.

Everything changed when I enrolled in a school for deaf students in Jeddah. On the first morning, I watched two teachers talking with their hands, their fingers moving as quickly as birds. Within several weeks, I discovered that every object, emotion, and idea possessed its own distinct sign. It was a revelation: language was not something only other people possessed.

The hardest challenge came later. I wanted my family to learn to sign, but my father insisted he was too old to begin. I was persistent, patiently teaching him one new sign each evening after dinner. Two years later, he signed an entire story to me at bedtime. That night, I finally understood that patience can construct a bridge between two separate worlds.

pb1d4690166.title: Fog on the Terraces
pb1d4690166.text:
Mira had not wanted to spend the summer in her grandmother's isolated village high in the mountains of Asir. All her friends were going to the beach in Jeddah, and she was stuck with a family she barely knew.

On the first morning, the fog was so thick that she could not see the end of the winding road. Her grandmother handed her a basket and pointed toward the terraced fields. Mira sighed dramatically and followed her reluctantly. The steps were steep, and the air smelled of wet earth and wild herbs.

By the end of the week, Mira knew the names of the goats, and she could carry the overflowing basket along the narrow terraces without spilling a single fig. One evening, her grandmother taught her a song that the family's ancestors had sung while harvesting. Mira was surprised to find herself humming it before she fell asleep.

p7a3d0af864.title: The Blue Gate
p7a3d0af864.text:
The medina of Fez swallowed Adam the moment he stepped through the blue gate. Alleys twisted in every direction, donkeys loaded with copper pots squeezed past him, and merchants called out in a mixture of Arabic and French. Adam, who had grown up in quiet Toronto, felt bewildered and slightly dizzy.

His grandfather walked ahead calmly, greeting shopkeepers by name. He stopped at a narrow doorway where an old man was stitching a leather slipper. “Your great-grandfather made slippers in this very workshop,” Grandfather explained. “His hands were as quick as sparrows.”

Adam watched the needle dart in and out of the soft yellow leather. For the first time since landing in Morocco, the overwhelming noise around him seemed to fade. He imagined an ancestor he had never met sitting on that same worn bench. Suddenly the unfamiliar city felt a little less like a maze and a little more like a story he belonged to.

p473f8580b1.title: Ninety Years of Dates
p473f8580b1.text:
Dalia had decided, before the airplane even landed in Qassim, that she would absolutely hate her grandparents' date farm. The heat pressed down on her like a heavy blanket, the internet signal flickered and died, and her grandfather spoke an Arabic so quick and musical that she caught only one word in five. Each night she lay awake, homesick for the noisy streets of Chicago.

Her grandfather did not seem to notice her sulking. Every dawn he walked between the palms, tapping their trunks as if greeting old friends. One morning, Dalia followed him, mostly from boredom. “This tree has fed our family for ninety years,” he said, pressing a sticky, amber date into her palm.

Dalia bit into it reluctantly, expecting something dry and disappointing. The sweetness was so intense and unexpected that she laughed out loud. Her grandfather laughed with her, and for a moment the language between them did not matter. That evening, she asked him to teach her the names of the trees.

p4357b05982.title: The Falcon Lesson
p4357b05982.text:
[Sunrise on a rooftop in Taif, where a falcon sits motionless on a wooden perch. REEM, twelve, examines an enormous leather glove with obvious irritation.]

REEM: I have repeated this exercise forty times, and the bird still ignores me completely.

UNCLE KHALID: [calmly smoothing the falcon's feathers] Forty times is a beginning, not an ending. Falcons respect patience, not complaints, and they recognize immediately when a trainer is preparing to surrender.

REEM: [throwing the glove onto the floor] Then the falcon can find someone else to train it!

[KHALID picks up the glove, brushes away the dust, and holds it out without speaking. A long silence follows.]

REEM: [quietly] You are not going to argue with me, are you?

UNCLE KHALID: I am waiting for you to argue with yourself.

[REEM hesitates, then slowly pulls on the glove and raises her trembling arm. The falcon tilts its head, spreads its wings, and lands gently on her wrist.]

REEM: [whispering in astonishment] It actually chose me, after everything I said about it.

UNCLE KHALID: [smiling for the first time] No. You finally chose to stay.

p4fd6ac6e1e.title: Faris Reads
p4fd6ac6e1e.text:
[A quiet library corner in Dammam. Afternoon light falls across a table holding a thick Braille book. FARIS, eleven, who lost his sight last year, sits with his arms folded. MS. HUDA, a volunteer instructor, sits patiently beside him.]

MS. HUDA: Yesterday you identified the first four letters, so shall we continue with the fifth character?

FARIS: [pushing the book away] Those dots all feel identical. I will never comprehend them, so why should we continue pretending otherwise?

MS. HUDA: [gently sliding the book back] Your fingers are still learning an entirely new language, and even expert readers once struggled with the alphabet.

FARIS: [sighing heavily, then reluctantly placing one finger on the page] Fine, one line, and then I am leaving.

[He traces the raised dots slowly. His finger pauses, moves backward, and traces them again. His expression changes from irritation to concentration.]

FARIS: F, A, R... [His voice rises with excitement.] That spells my name!

MS. HUDA: [smiling] I placed it there deliberately, hoping you would discover it yourself.

FARIS: [opening the book eagerly] Then tomorrow, I want to read a whole page.

p31e1298310.title: A Letter from Grandfather
p31e1298310.text:
Dear Hamad,

Your mother tells me that you begin at the new school next week, and that you are anxious about making friends among so many unfamiliar faces. Let me share what seventy years of experience have taught me.

Your mind is a garden, and every habit you practice is a seed. Plant patience, curiosity, and generosity, and cultivate them every day, for weeds multiply quickly in an empty field. Do not envy the boy with the expensive shoes or the newest electronic gadgets. Fancy things are like desert mirages: they shimmer brilliantly from far away, but they vanish when you come close.

Try to be diligent in small, ordinary tasks, because a mountain is only a crowd of stones that agreed to stand together. When you make a mistake, admit it immediately and honestly. Honesty is a lantern; people will follow its light long after they have forgotten your name.

Write to me after your first week, and I will be waiting by the window like an old falcon watching for its rider.

With love, Grandfather

p1982ba7fdd.title: A Letter to Lulwa
p1982ba7fdd.text:
Dear Lulwa,

Yesterday evening you asked me why I refused to buy you the phone that everyone in your class seems to own. I was exhausted after a long day at the hospital, and my answer was impatient, so let me reply properly now.

Time is a quiet thief. It does not break down the door; it slips away through a thousand small distractions, one notification at a time. I want your hours to belong to you, not to a glowing screen that never stops demanding attention.

You aspire to become an architect, and that ambitious dream deserves to be your priority. Fill your notebooks with sketches, measure the shadows of buildings, and reflect on why some rooms feel welcoming while others feel cold and unfriendly. Those habits will carry you further than any number of superficial messages.

I am not saying "never"; I am saying "not yet." When you are older, you will hold the phone, but I simply do not want it to hold you.

Your loving mother

p9fccdd384f.title: My First Season
p9fccdd384f.text:
When I arrived at the football academy in Jeddah, I was the only player from a mountain village. My boots were old, my accent was strong, and several of the city boys immediately decided that I did not belong.

During my first practice, a tall defender pushed me to the ground and laughed. "Go back to your goats," he said, loudly enough for everyone to hear. My face burned with humiliation, and I wanted to retaliate more than I had ever wanted anything.

Then I remembered my father's advice before I left home: "Anger is a fire that burns the one who carries it." I stood up, brushed the dust from my knees, and asked for the ball again.

For weeks, I answered every insult with hard work. I arrived early, stayed late, and practiced passing until the sun disappeared behind the stadium. Gradually, the laughter faded into silence and then into respect. By the end of the season, the same defender asked me to teach him my left-footed shot. I realized that restraint is not weakness; it is strength that has learned to wait.

p130d74a0ff.title: Two Tournaments
p130d74a0ff.text:
I played my first international chess tournament when I was twelve. I remember the enormous hall in Vienna more vividly than any individual game. Some adults glanced at my name tag and whispered about where I came from, and one opponent refused to shake my hand before we began. I was so rattled that I lost three games in a row, making careless moves I would never make at home.

Five years later, I returned to the same competition in the same hall. The whispers had not completely disappeared, but I was no longer the nervous boy they remembered. I no longer let other people's prejudice decide how I would play. Before each game, I extended my hand whether or not it was accepted, and then I concentrated entirely on the board.

In both tournaments, I faced the same unfair looks. The difference was entirely internal. At twelve, I believed that I had to win people's approval before I could win a match. At seventeen, I understood that dignity is something no opponent can take unless you surrender it. That year, I finished second overall.

p0358545fc1.title: The Market Translator
p0358545fc1.text:
Every Saturday morning, Mama and I walked to the crowded market near our new apartment in Toronto, where Mama chose the vegetables and I, her eleven-year-old daughter, did the talking. I had become fluent in English after just one year at school, but Mama still recognized only a handful of words.

That morning, the fruit seller asked Mama a question, and when she looked at me helplessly, I quickly translated. Then he made a joke, and everyone laughed except Mama. Her cheeks turned red, and she stared at the oranges as if they might somehow rescue her.

On the walk home, she remained silent until she finally said, in Arabic, "I feel like a guest in my own life."

That night, I heard an unfamiliar sound from the kitchen. Mama was sitting at the table with my old English workbook, whispering vocabulary words slowly and carefully to herself. She looked up, embarrassed, but did not close the book. "Will you teach me?" she asked quietly.

I sat down beside her, and for the first time, I was the teacher and she was the courageous student.

p628e8a6a7f.title: Sofia and Leo
p628e8a6a7f.text:
Sofia and her younger brother, Leo, arrived in Riyadh in September, when the afternoons still shimmered with heat. Neither of them knew a single word of Arabic.

Leo treated the new language like a game. He would mimic the cartoon characters on television, repeating their phrases loudly at dinner, and he never seemed to mind when his pronunciation made everyone laugh. Within two months, he was chatting with the neighbor's children in the courtyard.

Sofia was different. She memorized long lists of vocabulary every night, yet at school she stayed silent, anxious that one mistake would make her classmates giggle. Words that sounded perfect in her bedroom vanished the moment anyone looked at her.

One afternoon, her classmate Jana dropped a notebook, and Sofia, without thinking, said a polite Arabic phrase as she handed it back. Jana smiled and replied slowly so Sofia could follow. Sofia's sentence had not been perfect, but it had worked.

That evening, Sofia asked Leo to teach her the cartoon songs. Perhaps, she thought, the bravest way to learn was to be willing to sound a little foolish.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “The tailor will alter Ahmed's thobe so it fits him better.” What does “alter” mean?

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “alter,” “collapse,” “hazard,” and “severe.”
questions.why: Knowing the meaning of each word helps you read about natural events.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The old wooden bridge may collapse under heavy trucks,” the word “collapse” means to fall down.
questions.why: A bridge that collapses breaks and falls down.

questions.stem: Strong winds and heavy rain made the storm ____, so schools in Jeddah closed for the day.
questions.why: Severe means very serious, which explains why schools closed.

broken glass on the sidewalk
a fenced school playground
a buckled seat belt in the car

questions.why: A hazard is something that could hurt someone.

questions.stem: “The flood caused a lot of destruction in the village.” Which word means the same as “destruction”?
questions.why: Destruction is great damage.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe something “unpredictable”? Choose two.
options: The sun rises in the east every single morning.
School starts at seven o'clock each weekday.
Nobody knows whether it will rain tomorrow in the mountains of Abha.
The kitten might dash left or right; you can never tell.
questions.why: Unpredictable things cannot be known ahead of time.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “crisis,” “severe,” or “substantial” in it.

pairs.right: a time of great danger or trouble

pairs.left: The heavy rain caused severe floods.

questions.why: Each meaning fits the word used in the sentence.

questions.stem: When the electricity went out at the hospital, the doctors faced a ____ and worked quickly to keep patients safe.
questions.why: A crisis is a time of danger when quick action is needed.

questions.stem: True or false: If a family makes a substantial change to their house, they change only one tiny nail.
questions.why: Substantial means large, so a substantial change is a big change.

questions.stem: “Weather in the desert can be unpredictable. One hour the sky is clear, and the next hour a sandstorm blows in without warning.” Which clue helps you understand “unpredictable”?
questions.why: Something that happens without warning cannot be predicted.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “alter”?
questions.why: After “an,” we need the noun form, alteration.

questions.stem: Is each pair made of a key word and its synonym or its antonym: severe, substantial, destruction, collapse?

rows.text: severe — harsh
substantial — tiny
destruction — construction
collapse — fall

questions.why: Synonyms mean the same; antonyms mean the opposite.

questions.stem: Which word is an antonym of “substantial”?
questions.why: Slight means small, the opposite of substantial.

questions.stem: Climbers wear helmets because falling rocks are a serious ____ on steep mountain paths.
questions.why: Falling rocks are a hazard because they can hurt climbers.

questions.stem: Which TWO words belong to the same word family as “destruction”? Choose two.
questions.why: Destroy, destructive, and destruction share the same base.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “Engineers checked the stadium roof so it would not collapse during the match” uses “collapse” correctly.
questions.why: A roof that collapses falls in, so engineers check it.

questions.stem: Put these weather descriptions in order from the least to the most “severe.”

a steady wind that bends the palm trees
a severe sandstorm that closes the highway
questions.why: Severe weather is the most serious and dangerous.

questions.stem: “The price of the new bicycle was substantial, so Faisal saved his allowance for six months.” What does “substantial” most likely mean?
questions.why: He had to save for months, so the price was large.

questions.stem: Match each form of “severe” and “unpredictable” with its meaning.

pairs.right: able to be known ahead of time
not able to be known ahead of time

questions.why: Suffixes and prefixes change a word's form and meaning.

questions.stem: In each sentence, does “collapse” mean to fall down or to lose strength from tiredness?

After the long race, the runner collapsed on the grass.
The tent collapsed in the strong wind.
Grandfather collapsed into his chair after a long day of work.

questions.why: Collapse is a multiple-meaning word: things fall down, and tired people can collapse too.

questions.stem: In which sentence does “severe” mean “plain, with no decoration”?

The old fort had severe stone walls with no carvings.

A severe storm knocked over trees along the corniche.

questions.why: Severe shows the storm was very serious and dangerous.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “substantial” to mean “strong and solid” rather than “large in amount”? Choose two.

The workers placed a substantial beam under the bridge.

questions.why: To hesitate is to pause because you are not sure.

questions.stem: The thirsty camel ____ searched for water after many days in the hot desert.

questions.stem: Does each action show healthy or low “self-esteem”?

questions.why: Each sentence shows the meaning of one key word.

questions.why: Forgetting lines in front of everyone can make a person feel humiliated.

questions.stem: True or false: A student who is accountable for feeding the class fish never has to remember to feed it.
questions.why: Being accountable means you are responsible for doing the job.

questions.stem: “Rakan desperately wanted to win the chess match. He practiced every night and could think of nothing else.” Which words help you understand “desperately”?
questions.why: Thinking of nothing else shows a very strong, urgent wish.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “advise”?
questions.why: Advice is the noun; advise is the verb.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “hesitated”?

rows.text: paused
rushed
waited
acted at once

questions.why: Hesitated means paused before acting.

questions.stem: Which word is the best antonym of “humiliated”?
questions.why: Proud is the opposite of feeling humiliated.

questions.stem: Reading about Ibn Battuta's long journeys was an ____ for Dana, and she decided to keep a travel journal.
questions.why: An inspiration gives a person an idea or a wish to do something.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are in the same word family as “inspiration”? Choose two.
questions.why: Inspire, inspiring, and inspiration share the same base word.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “The team captain is accountable for collecting the uniforms after each game” uses “accountable” correctly.
questions.why: The captain is responsible for the uniforms, so he is accountable.

questions.stem: Put these events in order to show how Tariq's “self-esteem” grew.

His teacher advised him to practice with his younger brother each night.
After a week, he read one page aloud without mistakes.
Now Tariq volunteers to read first.

questions.stem: “The room was crowded and hot, so the guests shifted uncomfortably in their seats.” What does “uncomfortably” mean?
options: in a quick and happy way
in a way that feels uneasy
questions.why: A hot, crowded room makes people feel uneasy.

questions.stem: Match each form of “hesitated” and “humiliated” with its meaning.
questions.why: Different endings make nouns and adjectives from the same base.

pairs.left: wanted the ground to swallow him
point someone in the right direction

questions.why: An idiom's meaning is different from the meanings of its single words.

questions.stem: Which idiom shows that someone has strong “self-esteem”?
questions.why: Holding your head high means feeling proud and confident.

questions.stem: Find the misused key word in this short paragraph about a science fair.

On the day of the fair, Lulwa spoke clearly and felt humiliated when the judges smiled and clapped.

questions.why: Fearful is the opposite of brave; humiliated is the opposite of proud.

questions.stem: Does each idiom describe feeling “uncomfortably” nervous or feeling calm?

rows.text: on pins and needles
cool as a cucumber
butterflies in my stomach
without a care in the world

questions.why: Idioms can describe feelings in a colorful way.

questions.stem: True or false: The idioms “own up to your mistakes” and “take the blame” both describe being accountable.
questions.why: Being accountable means accepting responsibility for what you did.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences pair a key word with an idiom that matches its meaning? Choose two.
options: Rami hesitated and dragged his feet before cleaning his room.
Mira felt humiliated and was on top of the world.
Ziad acted desperately because he had all the time in the world.
The coach's speech lit a fire under the team; it was a true inspiration.
questions.why: The idiom and the key word must have matching meanings.

questions.stem: Which word BEST completes the sentence? “The class president promised to be ____ for every riyal the class spent on the trip.”
questions.why: Accountable means responsible for explaining how money was used.

options: people who help in a shop
questions.why: Funds are money kept or raised for a purpose.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “compassionate,” “routine,” “innovative,” and “undertaking.”

a big job someone takes on

questions.why: These words help describe people and businesses.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Brushing my teeth before bed is part of my nightly routine,” the word “routine” means something I do the same way every day.
questions.why: A routine is a regular way of doing things.

questions.stem: The new eco-friendly shoe company was a small ____ that began in a garage in Riyadh.
questions.why: An enterprise is a business or company.

questions.stem: Is each action “compassionate” or not compassionate?

rows.text: sharing your umbrella with a classmate in the rain
laughing when a friend drops her lunch
visiting a sick neighbor with soup
ignoring a lost child at the mall

questions.why: Compassionate people care about others and help them.

questions.stem: Which word means almost the same as “exceptional”?
questions.why: Exceptional means much better than usual.

questions.stem: Which TWO are examples of an “innovative” idea? Choose two.
options: a wooden chair made the usual way
a school bag with a solar panel to charge tablets
a plain pencil like every other pencil
a water bottle that cleans seawater as you drink
questions.why: Innovative ideas are new and creative.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the key word it describes: “process,” “funds,” or “enterprise.”

The class collected 500 riyals for the library.
Two sisters started a business selling dates online.

questions.why: Each sentence gives an example of one key word.

questions.stem: Building a new hospital in the village was a huge ____ that took five years.
questions.why: An undertaking is a big job or project.

questions.stem: True or false: A process is one quick action with no steps.
questions.why: A process is a series of steps.

questions.stem: “The charity's founder was compassionate. She listened kindly to every family and found ways to ease their worries.” Which words help you understand “compassionate”?
questions.why: Listening kindly shows care for others.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “innovative”?
questions.why: After “newest” we need a noun, innovation.

questions.stem: Which suffix ends each word: exceptional, innovative, compassionate, personal?

innovative
compassionate
personal

questions.why: Ordinary is the opposite of exceptional.

questions.stem: Every morning, Uncle Khalid follows the same ____: he waters his plants, feeds his birds, and drinks coffee with cardamom.
questions.why: A routine is what someone does the same way each day.

questions.stem: The suffix -ion turns “innovate” into “innovation.” Which TWO words are made by adding -ion to a base word? Choose two.
questions.why: Except + ion and process + ion form new nouns; onion and million have no base word.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “Raising funds for the new playground took the students three months” uses “funds” correctly.
questions.why: Funds are money raised for a purpose.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the recycling “process” at a paper factory in order.

Workers sort the paper and remove plastic.
Machines mix the paper with water to make pulp.
The pulp is pressed and dried into new sheets.
questions.why: A process happens in a set order of steps.

questions.stem: “Opening a bakery in a new city was a risky undertaking, but the brothers planned every detail.” What does “undertaking” mean?
options: a task someone agrees to do
a type of bread or cake
a trip to visit their relatives
questions.why: An undertaking is a task or project someone takes on.

questions.stem: Match each word with the meaning its suffix gives it: “routinely,” “exceptionally,” “compassionately,” “enterprising.”

pairs.right: full of energy for new projects

questions.why: The suffix -ly makes adverbs; -ing can make adjectives.

questions.stem: Does “process” in each sentence name a series of steps or mean to handle something?

rows.text: Making cheese is a slow process.
The bank will process your form in two days.

The computer can process thousands of numbers each second.

questions.why: Process can be a noun or a verb with different meanings.

questions.stem: Which word has the most POSITIVE feeling? “The ____ company invented a phone case that charges in sunlight.”
questions.why: Innovative praises an idea as new and clever.

questions.stem: The student's science project was not just good; it was ____, winning first place in the whole Kingdom.
questions.why: Exceptional means far better than usual.

questions.stem: Find the misused key word in this short paragraph about a lemonade stand.
segments: Maha and her brother started a small enterprise selling fresh lemonade.
They used their funds to buy a juicer and paper cups.
They made the drinks in a careful process, washing every lemon first.
Their mint-lemon recipe was so routine that customers said they had never tasted anything like it.
questions.correction: Their mint-lemon recipe was so exceptional that customers said they had never tasted anything like it.
questions.why: A recipe nobody had tasted before is exceptional, not routine.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: kind is to kindness as compassionate is to ____.
questions.why: Removing -ate and adding -ion gives the noun compassion, just as kindness is the noun of kind.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “routine” as an adjective meaning “ordinary and expected”? Choose two.
options: My morning routine starts at six o'clock.
The gymnast practiced her new routine on the beam.
The doctor said it was only a routine checkup.
The pilot made a routine landing in clear weather.
questions.why: Before a noun, routine describes something ordinary.

questions.stem: True or false: Adding the suffix -ly to “exceptional” makes “exceptionally,” an adverb that means “unusually.”
questions.why: The suffix -ly turns adjectives into adverbs.

questions.stem: Which word BEST completes the sentence? “Cleaning up the whole beach in one day was a huge ____ that needed two hundred volunteers.”
questions.why: Undertaking names a big job that people take on.

questions.stem: Put the steps an enterprise follows to raise funds for a children's charity in order.
sequence: The company chooses a charity that helps children.
Workers plan a fun run to raise money.
Customers sign up and pay to join the run.
The company gives the money to the charity.
questions.why: Planning comes first and giving the money comes last.

questions.stem: “The cat crouched low, ready to pounce on the toy mouse.” What does “pounce” mean?
questions.why: To pounce is to jump suddenly to catch something.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “predator,” “prey,” “poisonous,” and “camouflaged.”
questions.why: These words describe how animals survive.

the pigeon chased by a falcon

the gazelle running from a cheetah

questions.why: The hunter is the predator; the hunted animal is the prey.

questions.stem: Which word means almost the same as “extraordinary”?

questions.stem: Which TWO animals are “camouflaged” in these sentences? Choose two.

A white fox sits in the white snow.
A yellow frog hops on dark mud.
A red bird perches on a green leaf.
questions.why: A camouflaged animal matches its surroundings.

questions.why: A poisonous plant can make you sick or even kill you.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “camouflaged”?

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “extraordinary”?

ordinary
wonderful
typical

questions.stem: Put the steps of how a lion hunts its “prey” in order.

It pounces when the zebra looks away.
The lion shares the meal with its pride.
questions.why: A hunt moves from finding to sneaking to catching.

extraordinary
unseen

The owl carried its prey back to the nest.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: cat is to mouse as predator is to ____.

questions.why: Extraordinary means far beyond what is normal.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order to build a paragraph about a chameleon that uses “camouflaged” and “predator.”

It can change its skin color in a few seconds.
When a predator comes near, the green chameleon stays very still among the green leaves.
Camouflaged this way, it stays safe until the danger passes.
questions.why: The paragraph introduces the lizard, explains its skill, then shows how it uses it.

questions.stem: “The baby was cranky because she missed her nap.” What does “cranky” mean?

questions.stem: When the goat got loose in the school yard, there was a big ____ as children ran and shouted.

saying “This is boring” and giving up

a puzzle with one missing piece

questions.stem: True or false: A familiar face is the face of someone you have never seen before.
questions.why: A familiar face is one you know well.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “frustrated”?

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “selfish”?

rows.text: greedy
generous
self-centered
giving

questions.stem: Which word is the best antonym of “cranky”?

questions.stem: Ms. Reem praised Tamer for his positive ____ because he always smiles and helps others.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are antonyms of “commotion”? Choose two.
questions.why: Calm and peace are the opposite of a noisy commotion.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “Baking bread with sesame seeds is my uncle's specialty” uses “specialty” correctly.

questions.stem: Put these feelings in order from the least to the most upset, starting with “calm” and “annoyed.”

annoyed
angry
furious
questions.why: Annoyed is a little upset, angry is more upset, and furious is the most.

questions.stem: “The neighbor's dog barked all night, so Ibrahim was annoyed and cranky the next morning.” Why was Ibrahim cranky?

rows.text: unfamiliar
unselfish
unknown
kindhearted

questions.why: The prefix un- can make an antonym.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “brittle,” “creative,” “outstretched,” and “rhyme.”

reaching out as far as possible
words that end with the same sound

questions.stem: Is each sentence a correct use of “commitment”?

questions.why: Each meaning fits the way the word is used in the sentence.

questions.why: Directing means guiding and being in charge of others.

questions.stem: True or false: A decade is the same amount of time as one week.
