options.text: went down in number

options.label: C
options.text: arrived late

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: “our class”

options.label: C
options.text: “because the trip was on exam day”

options.label: D

questions.why: Declined can also mean refused; the exam-day clue explains why the class said no.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “disorder” with the meaning “a sickness or problem in how something works”? Choose two.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph about a farm: “The agricultural fair showed new ways to grow food. One farmer used fish to fertilize his crops. Visitors were surprised by this unexpected idea. It is probable that his vegetables declined because they grew so large.”

One farmer used fish to fertilize his crops.
Visitors were surprised by this unexpected idea.
It is probable that his vegetables declined because they grew so large.
questions.correction: It is probable that his vegetables thrived because of the fish.
questions.why: His vegetables grew so large, so they thrived; declined means they got worse.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “The school bulletin told parents that sports day would be on Thursday.” What is a “bulletin”?
options: a kind of shoe worn for sports
a short news report or notice
questions.why: A bulletin is a short announcement of news.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “contributions,” “enlisted,” “recruits,” and “survival.”

pairs.right: things given to help a cause
joined the military or a group

questions.why: These words help you talk about communities working together.

questions.stem: True or false: A goalkeeper who catches the ball before it reaches the net is trying to intercept it.
questions.why: To intercept is to stop something on its way to somewhere.

questions.stem: Water and shade are important for ____ in the desert.
questions.why: Survival means staying alive; water and shade help with that.

questions.stem: Do these items show “diversity” or no diversity?

a class with students from many countries
a box of identical red pencils
a wall painted one plain color

questions.why: Diversity means having many different kinds.

questions.stem: “The hospital's operations ran smoothly, from the kitchen to the emergency room.” What does “operations” mean here?
options: the ways work is carried out
the loud noises of the machines
questions.why: Operations are the activities and work that keep something running.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe contributions? Choose two.
options: The boy kept all his toys to himself.
Neighbors donated food to families in need.
Students gave books to the new library.
The shop closed early on Friday.
questions.why: Contributions are things people give to help.

questions.stem: The new ____ practiced marching every morning at the training camp.
questions.why: Recruits are new members who are still being trained.

questions.stem: True or false: If Khalid enlisted in the scouts, he decided not to join them.
questions.why: Enlisted means joined, not refused to join.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “bulletin,” “intercept,” or “diversity” in it.

pairs.left: The radio gave a weather bulletin.
The defender jumped to intercept the pass.
The market showed a diversity of spices.

questions.why: Each meaning fits how the word is used in its sentence.

questions.stem: “The rescue team ran operations all night. They searched buildings, carried supplies, and guided people to safety.” Which clue helps you understand “operations”?
options: “searched buildings, carried supplies, and guided people”
questions.why: The list of actions shows that operations are planned activities.

questions.stem: Every ____ to the charity drive, even a single coin, helped buy blankets for families.
questions.why: The noun “contribution” fits after “every”; contribute is the verb.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “survival”?

rows.text: staying alive
endurance
death
extinction

questions.why: Survival means continuing to live; death and extinction are opposites.

questions.stem: True or false: “The army enlisted many young volunteers during the war” uses “enlisted” correctly.
questions.why: Enlisted can mean signed up people to serve.

questions.stem: Which TWO things would a new team member most likely need, as one of the recruits? Choose two.
options: a gold medal for twenty years of service
questions.why: Recruits are new, so they need training and gear, not retirement items.

questions.stem: “The coral reef has great diversity: hundreds of fish, crabs, sea stars, and plants live there together.” What does “diversity” mean?
questions.why: Hundreds of different living things show diversity.

questions.stem: The sailors tried to ____ the enemy's secret message before it reached the ship.
questions.why: The base verb “intercept” fits after “tried to.”

questions.stem: Match each vocabulary word with its antonym (opposite): “enlisted,” “diversity,” and “recruits.”
questions.why: An antonym has the opposite meaning.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The bulletin was a large building with ten floors,” the word “bulletin” is used correctly.
questions.why: A bulletin is a news notice, not a building.

questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how a city sent help after a storm, using “bulletin,” “recruits,” and “operations.”
sequence: A news bulletin warned that a storm was coming.
The city asked for recruits to help clean up.
The new volunteers were trained quickly.
Rescue operations began the next morning.
questions.why: First a warning, then volunteers, training, and finally operations.

questions.stem: Which homophone correctly completes this sentence about recruits? “The recruits waited for ____ captain to arrive.”
questions.why: “Their” shows that the captain belongs to the recruits.

questions.stem: Choose the correct homophone for each sentence about survival in the desert.

He dug a ____ in the sand to find cool shade for survival.
The ____ group's survival depended on the guide.
Survival experts said a ____ in the tent let in the sand.

questions.why: Whole means all of something; hole means an opening.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph: “The bakery made bread for the soldiers. Their contributions were a big help. The baker used flower and water to make the dough. Everyone's work was important for survival.”
segments: The bakery made bread for the soldiers.
Their contributions were a big help.
The baker used flower and water to make the dough.
Everyone's work was important for survival.
questions.correction: The baker used flour and water to make the dough.
questions.why: Flour is ground grain for baking; a flower is part of a plant.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: “recruits” is to “team” as “contributions” is to ____.
questions.why: Recruits are added to a team; contributions are added to a fund.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph: “The navy wanted to stop the supply ship before it reached the port. Its plan was to ____ it at sea. The captains studied maps for days.” Which word BEST fits the blank?
questions.why: Intercept means to stop something on its way.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses the homophone correctly with the word “operations.”

The operations team worked for one weak without a break.

The operations team worked for won week without a break.

questions.why: Week (seven days), for (a preposition), and one (the number) are correct here.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about bulletins with the correct homophone meaning.

pairs.left: The bulletin board was painted red.
The herd of camels appeared in the bulletin photo.

questions.why: Homophones sound alike but have different meanings and spellings.

questions.stem: Part A: In “The surgeon performed two operations on the patient's knee,” what does “operations” mean?

options.text: military actions

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: “two”

options.label: D

questions.why: A surgeon and a knee show the medical meaning of operations.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “diversity” with the most precise meaning? Choose two.

Our school celebrates the diversity of its students' languages.
The diversity of the plain white wall was boring.

questions.why: Diversity means variety, so it must describe many different kinds.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph about wartime: “Many young men enlisted in the army. The recruits trained hard. They listened to the daily bulletin for news. Their intercept was to help their country.”
segments: Many young men enlisted in the army.
They listened to the daily bulletin for news.
Their intercept was to help their country.
questions.correction: Their goal was to help their country.
questions.why: Intercept is a verb meaning to stop something on its way; goal fits the sentence.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “The agile goat jumped quickly from rock to rock on the mountain.” What does “agile” mean?
options: too heavy to climb up steep rocks
able to move quickly and easily
questions.why: Agile describes moving with speed and ease.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “cache,” “dormant,” “forage,” and “frigid.”

pairs.right: inactive or asleep for a time

questions.why: These words describe how animals live in nature.

questions.stem: True or false: Bears hibernate by sleeping through the cold winter months.
questions.why: To hibernate is to spend the winter in a deep sleep.

questions.stem: A thick wool blanket ____ you from the cold winter air.
questions.why: Insulates means protects from heat or cold.

questions.stem: Is each place “frigid” or not frigid?

rows.text: the ice of Antarctica
a frozen mountain top
a sunny Riyadh afternoon
a warm kitchen oven

questions.why: Frigid places are extremely cold.

questions.stem: “Squirrels forage for nuts and seeds before winter comes.” What does “forage” mean?
questions.why: To forage is to look for food.

questions.stem: Which TWO animals hibernate during winter? Choose two.
questions.why: Some bears and hedgehogs sleep through winter; camels and falcons stay active.

questions.stem: The squirrel buried a ____ of acorns under the tree so it could eat them later.
questions.why: A cache is a hidden supply.

questions.stem: True or false: A dormant volcano is erupting with hot lava right now.
questions.why: Dormant means inactive for now, not erupting.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “adaptation,” “insulates,” or “agile” in it.

pairs.left: A camel's hump is a helpful adaptation.
pairs.right: a body feature that helps survival

pairs.left: The agile cat climbed the fence.

questions.why: Each meaning fits how the word is used in its sentence.

questions.stem: “Some seeds stay dormant in the dry desert sand for years. They do not grow at all until heavy rain finally wakes them.” Which clue helps you understand “dormant”?
options: “do not grow at all until heavy rain”
questions.why: Not growing until something wakes them shows dormant means inactive.

questions.stem: Thick fur is an ____ that helps arctic foxes live in the snow.
questions.why: The noun “adaptation” fits after “an”; it names a helpful feature.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “frigid”?

rows.text: icy
freezing
scorching
hot

questions.why: Frigid means very cold; scorching and hot are its opposites.

questions.stem: True or false: “Penguins huddle together in the frigid wind to stay warm” uses “frigid” correctly.
questions.why: Frigid wind is extremely cold wind.

questions.stem: Which TWO things insulate an animal from the cold? Choose two.
questions.why: Fat and feathers trap warmth and insulate the body.

questions.stem: “Deep in the ocean, the octopus is agile. It squeezes through tiny cracks and darts away from danger in a flash.” What does “agile” mean here?
questions.why: Darting and squeezing through cracks show quick, easy movement.

questions.stem: The tortoise digs a burrow where it will ____ until spring returns.
questions.why: The base verb “hibernate” fits after “will.”

questions.stem: Match each vocabulary word with its antonym (opposite): “agile,” “dormant,” and “frigid.”
questions.why: An antonym has the opposite meaning.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Fish forage in the desert sand for water,” the word “forage” is used correctly.
questions.why: Fish forage in water, not in desert sand.

questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how a chipmunk gets ready to hibernate.
sequence: It forages for nuts and seeds in autumn.
It hides a cache of food in its burrow.
It lines the burrow with leaves that insulate it.
It sleeps through the frigid winter.
questions.why: Gathering, storing, insulating, and then sleeping is the order.

questions.stem: “Unlike the busy hummingbird, which flies all day, the bat in the cave remained dormant all winter long.” Which word signals a context clue of contrast for “dormant”?
questions.why: “Unlike” tells you dormant means the opposite of busy.

questions.stem: Is the context clue for each key word a definition clue or an example clue?

rows.text: “Blubber insulates, or keeps warm, the whale's body.”
“A cache, or hidden supply, was found in the tree.”
“Adaptations, such as webbed feet and gills, help animals swim.”
“Animals forage for food like berries, insects, and roots.”

questions.why: Definition clues explain the word; example clues give examples of it.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph about polar bears: “Polar bears live in frigid places. Thick fur insulates their bodies. They are agile swimmers and hunt seals. In summer they forage in the warm cache of the Arctic sea.”
segments: Polar bears live in frigid places.
They are agile swimmers and hunt seals.
In summer they forage in the warm cache of the Arctic sea.
questions.correction: In summer they forage in the cold waters of the Arctic sea.
questions.why: A cache is a hidden supply, not a body of water.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: “hibernate” is to “bear” as “forage” is to ____.
questions.why: Bears hibernate; a hungry goat forages for food.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph: “The scientist found a hidden ____ of seeds inside a hollow log. A small mouse had stored them there. It would eat them when food was hard to find.” Which word BEST fits the blank?
questions.why: A cache is a hidden store, which matches the stored seeds.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses “cache” as a hidden supply.

segments.text: The crow kept a cache of shiny stones in its nest.
We sat in the cache at the beach.
The runner was cache and quick.
Our teacher will cache the class to the park.

questions.why: Cache is a noun naming a hidden collection.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the context clue type that explains “adaptation,” “frigid,” or “agile.”

pairs.left: “An adaptation is a feature that helps an animal survive.”
“The frigid water, unlike the warm bath, made him shiver.”
“The agile monkey, which leaped and swung easily, reached the fruit.”

questions.why: Writers use definitions, contrasts, and descriptions as clues.

questions.stem: Part A: In “The deep ocean is frigid; no sunlight reaches it, and the water is near freezing,” what does “frigid” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: In “The deep ocean is frigid; no sunlight reaches it, and the water is near freezing,” what does “frigid” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: very cold

options.label: B
options.text: very dark

options.label: C
options.text: very deep

options.label: D
options.text: very salty

partB.stem: Part B: Which clue best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “the deep ocean”

options.label: B
options.text: “the water is near freezing”

options.label: C
options.text: “is”

options.label: D
options.text: “no sunlight reaches it”

questions.why: Near freezing directly shows that frigid means very cold.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “insulates” with the most precise meaning? Choose two.
options: The ice insulates the lake by melting it quickly.
The sun insulates the desert sand until it burns.
Snow insulates a rabbit's burrow by keeping the cold wind out.
A whale's blubber insulates it in icy seas.
questions.why: Insulates means keeps heat in or cold out, not heats or melts.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph about deep-sea life: “Some sea animals have an amazing adaptation. They glow in the dark to find food. Others stay dormant to save energy. The squid is frigid, darting fast to catch its prey.”
segments: Some sea animals have an amazing adaptation.
They glow in the dark to find food.
Others stay dormant to save energy.
The squid is frigid, darting fast to catch its prey.
questions.correction: The squid is agile, darting fast to catch its prey.
questions.why: Agile means quick and nimble; frigid means very cold.

questions.stem: “The car horn blares outside the bakery, and everyone jumps.” What does “blares” mean?
options: plays a soft and gentle tune
questions.why: Something that blares makes a loud, harsh sound.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “blares,” “errand,” “exchange,” and “connection.”

pairs.right: a short trip to do a job
to give one thing and get another back
a link between people or things

questions.why: Knowing each meaning helps you understand the word in any sentence.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Mama sent Khalid on an errand to buy fresh bread,” the word “errand” means a short trip to get something done.
questions.why: An errand is a short trip to do a task for someone.

questions.stem: At the book fair, Sara and Lina ____ their favorite books so each girl has something new to read.
questions.why: To exchange is to give something and get something back.

questions.stem: Does each sentence use “imagery” (words that help you see, hear, smell, taste, or feel), or not?

rows.text: The golden dunes glowed under a pink evening sky.
We went to the market on Tuesday.
Warm cardamom coffee steamed in the tiny cups.
The meeting lasted one hour.

questions.why: Imagery uses sense details to paint a picture in the reader's mind.

questions.stem: Which word means almost the same as “connection”?
questions.why: A connection is a link between things or people.

questions.stem: Match each poetry term—“personification,” “assonance,” “consonance,” and “imagery”—with an example line.

pairs.right: The wind whispered secrets to the palms.
Go slow over the open road.
The black truck struck the rock.
Cold, salty spray stung my cheeks.

questions.why: Each poetry device creates a different effect in a line.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “The radio blares the morning news so loudly that the baby wakes up” uses “blares” correctly.
questions.why: A very loud radio blares, which could wake a baby.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use personification? Choose two.
options: The old clock struck twelve at noon.
Big waves washed over the sand castle.
The old clock grumbled as it struck noon.
The sea reached out and grabbed the sand castle.
questions.why: Personification gives human actions, like grumbling or grabbing, to things that are not human.

questions.stem: Grandpa's tales about life in Jeddah long ago gave me a strong ____ to my family's past.
questions.why: A connection is a link, here between a child and family history.

questions.stem: “Noor had one more errand before dinner. She still needed to pick up her brother's shoes from the repair shop.” What does “errand” most likely mean?
options: a short trip to get something done
a long holiday spent far away from home
a gift brought for a family
questions.why: Picking up shoes is a short trip to do a job, which is an errand.

questions.stem: Is the key word (“exchange,” “blares,” or “connection”) used as a noun or a verb in each sentence?

rows.text: The student exchange brought pupils from Oman to Riyadh.
Let's exchange phone numbers with the new neighbors.
The loudspeaker blares the start of the race.
A strong connection keeps the video call clear.

questions.why: A noun names a thing; a verb shows an action.

questions.stem: The phrase “the cool blue moon” is an example of ____ because the “oo” vowel sound repeats.
questions.why: Assonance is the repetition of vowel sounds.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Pick a thick black stick,” the repeated “ck” sound at the ends of words is an example of consonance.
questions.why: Consonance is the repetition of consonant sounds, often at the ends of words.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are antonyms of “blares” when talking about sound? Choose two.
questions.why: Whispers and murmurs are soft, the opposite of blares.

questions.stem: “Our class did a cultural exchange with a school in Japan. We sent dates and Arabic calligraphy, and they sent us paper cranes.” What does “exchange” mean here?
options: traveling by airplane to a faraway country
a race between two teams of pupils
giving and receiving things in return
a test given at the end of the year
questions.why: Each school gave and received gifts, which is an exchange.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “connection”?
questions.why: After “will” we need the verb connect, not the noun connection.

questions.stem: Put these sounds in order from the softest to the one that blares the loudest.
sequence: a cat purring on the sofa
a teacher speaking to the class
a fire alarm that blares in the hall
questions.why: Blares describes the loudest, harshest sound.

questions.stem: Does each line show personification, assonance, or consonance?

rows.text: The tired sun sank into its sandy bed.
Low tones float over the old boat.
The milk spilled and filled the hall.

questions.why: Personification gives human traits; assonance repeats vowels; consonance repeats consonants.

questions.stem: True or false: “Imagery” is language that appeals only to the sense of sight.
questions.why: Imagery can appeal to all five senses: sight, sound, smell, taste, and touch.

questions.stem: Which word best shows that the siren is very loud and harsh? “The siren ____ through the empty streets at midnight.”
questions.why: Blares carries the strongest sense of a loud, harsh noise.

questions.stem: In each sentence, does “exchange” mean “a swap or trade” or “a place where money or goods are traded”?

rows.text: The stock exchange opened at ten o'clock.
We exchange gifts with our cousins at Eid.
Travelers changed riyals at the currency exchange in the airport.
The players exchange shirts after the match.

questions.why: Exchange has several meanings; the rest of the sentence shows which one fits.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: whispers is to quiet as blares is to ____.
questions.why: Whispers are quiet; something that blares is loud.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the lines: “The old door groaned when we pushed it, / and the wind sighed softly through the hall.” Which device do these lines mainly use?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the lines: “The old door groaned when we pushed it, / and the wind sighed softly through the hall.” Which device do these lines mainly use?

options.label: A
options.text: rhyme

options.label: B
options.text: personification

options.label: C
options.text: assonance

options.label: D
options.text: consonance

partB.stem: Part B: Which word from the lines about the door and the wind best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: old

options.label: B
options.text: hall

options.label: C
options.text: pushed

options.label: D
options.text: sighed

questions.why: Doors and wind cannot really groan or sigh; giving them human actions is personification.

questions.stem: Find the misused key word in this short paragraph about an errand: “Hessa ran a quick errand to buy milk for her grandmother. At the shop, she gave coins in exchange for a cold bottle. Outside, a car horn imagery loudly at a slow driver. Hessa smiled and hurried home.”
segments: Hessa ran a quick errand to buy milk for her grandmother.
At the shop, she gave coins in exchange for a cold bottle.
Outside, a car horn imagery loudly at a slow driver.
questions.correction: Outside, a car horn blared loudly at a slow driver.
questions.why: A horn blares; imagery is a writing device, not a sound.

questions.stem: Which TWO lines use personification to show the desert's mood? Choose two.
options: The dunes slept peacefully under a blanket of stars.
The dunes were as gold as honey in the sunset.
Thousands of stars shone above the quiet dunes.
The hot wind complained as it pushed across the sand.
questions.why: Sleeping and complaining are human actions, so those lines use personification.

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? “Our pen-pal letters built a warm ____ between students in Abha and students in Kenya, even though they never met.”
questions.why: A connection is a bond or link between people.

questions.stem: Which word gives the fridge a human action (personification)? “All night the old fridge ____ in the dark kitchen, keeping the milk cold.”
questions.why: Snoring is something people do, so it personifies the fridge.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order to build a paragraph that uses “imagery” and “connection.”
sequence: Fatima opened a book about life in Morocco.
Rich imagery let her almost smell the spices in the busy markets.
She felt a new connection to children who lived far away.
The next day, she wrote her own poem about the trip she imagined.
questions.why: The paragraph moves from reading, to the imagery, to the feeling, to a result.

questions.stem: True or false: The line “Slow boats float home” uses both assonance and personification.
questions.why: The long “o” sound is assonance, but nothing is given a human action, so there is no personification.

questions.stem: “The two football clubs from Riyadh have been rivals for many years, and their matches always sell out.” What does “rival” mean?
options: a coach who trains young players
a referee who judges the match
a fan who cheers loudly from the stands
a competitor who wants the same win
questions.why: A rival competes with you for the same goal.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “rival,” “loyalty,” “devastating,” and “evade.”

pairs.right: to escape or keep away from

questions.why: Knowing each meaning helps you read the word in new sentences.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The fountain's perpetual flow never stopped, day or night,” the word “perpetual” means never ending.
questions.why: Perpetual means continuing forever or without stopping.

questions.stem: Yasir sat ____ by the window, thinking quietly about the choice he had to make.
questions.why: Pensively means in a deeply thoughtful way.

questions.stem: Does each action show loyalty or not?

rows.text: Mansour defends his friend when others tease him.
Reem tells her teammate's secret to the whole class.
A fan supports the local team even in a losing season.
Hadi leaves his partner to finish the project alone.

questions.why: Loyalty means staying faithful and supportive.

questions.stem: Which word means almost the same as “evade”?
questions.why: To evade is to avoid or escape something.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe a barrage? Choose two.
options: The teacher asked a single, simple question.
One raindrop landed on the window.
Reporters fired a barrage of questions at the coach after the match.
A barrage of hailstones pounded the car roof.
questions.why: A barrage is a heavy, nonstop stream of something.

questions.stem: The teacher's calm explanation helped ____ our fear of the difficult exam.
questions.why: To dispel is to make a feeling or idea go away.

questions.stem: True or false: Losing the final by one point felt devastating to the team, so they were thrilled and celebrated all night.
questions.why: Something devastating causes deep pain, not joy.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “perpetual,” “barrage,” or “pensive” in it.

pairs.left: The desert wind made a perpetual hum.
A barrage of messages filled her phone.
Grandfather looked pensive as he watched the sunset.

questions.why: Context helps show each word's meaning.

questions.stem: “The fox tried to evade the hunters. It slipped through the bushes, doubled back along the creek, and hid in a hollow log.” What does “evade” mean?
options: to attack someone or fight back against
to escape or keep away from
questions.why: Hiding and doubling back are ways to evade, or escape.

questions.stem: Is each pair a synonym pair or an antonym pair for “perpetual,” “loyalty,” “dispel,” “evade,” and “pensive”?

rows.text: perpetual — endless
loyalty — betrayal
dispel — scatter
evade — confront
pensive — thoughtful

questions.why: Synonyms share a meaning; antonyms are opposites.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “loyalty”?
questions.why: After “showed great” we need the noun loyalty.

questions.stem: The earthquake had a ____ effect on the small village; almost every house was destroyed.
questions.why: Devastating describes enormous damage.

questions.stem: Which TWO words belong to the same word family as “rival”? Choose two.
questions.why: Rivalry and rivaled share the base word rival.

questions.stem: Which word is an antonym of “pensive”?
questions.why: Pensive means deep in thought, so carefree is the opposite.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “The cat evaded the dog by squeezing under the fence” uses “evaded” correctly.
questions.why: The cat escaped the dog, so it evaded it.

questions.stem: Put these outcomes in order from the least painful to the most devastating.
sequence: a small disappointment
a painful setback
a devastating loss
questions.why: Devastating is the strongest word for loss or pain.

questions.stem: Match each form of “rival,” “loyalty,” “evade,” and “perpetual” with its meaning.

pairs.right: trying to avoid a direct answer

questions.why: Suffixes change a word's form and part of speech.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “dispel” correctly?
options: The cook dispelled the soup into four bowls.
The bright lights helped dispel the darkness of the cave.
We plan to dispel the fast train to Dammam early tomorrow morning.
She dispelled her name on the paper before class.
questions.why: To dispel is to drive away, as light drives away darkness.

questions.stem: Which word shows the heaviest attack of words? “The critic launched a ____ of complaints against the new stadium design.”
questions.why: A barrage is a heavy, nonstop stream, much stronger than a handful or trickle.

questions.stem: In each sentence, does “barrage” mean “a heavy, steady stream” or “a barrier built across a river”?

rows.text: The barrage across the river controls flooding.
A barrage of camera flashes greeted the champion.
Engineers inspected the concrete barrage near the dam.
The fans let out a barrage of cheers.

questions.why: Barrage is a multiple-meaning word; context shows which meaning fits.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: ally is to friend as rival is to ____.
questions.why: An ally is a friend; a rival is a competitor.

questions.stem: Part A: “Even after Huda's team beat ours, our rivalry did not damage our friendship; we still studied together every evening.” What does “rivalry” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: “Even after Huda's team beat ours, our rivalry did not damage our friendship; we still studied together every evening.” What does “rivalry” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: a long friendship with no disagreements

options.label: B
options.text: competition between people or groups

options.label: C
options.text: a study group that meets each night

options.label: D
options.text: a prize given to the winning side

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase in the sentence about Huda's team best helps you understand “rivalry”?

options.label: A
options.text: every evening

options.label: B
options.text: we still studied together

options.label: C
options.text: Huda's team beat ours

options.label: D
options.text: our friendship

questions.why: Beating another team shows competition, which is rivalry.

questions.stem: Find the misused key word in this paragraph: “Before the final, Majid felt pensive and sat silently thinking about the match. His coach tried to dispel his worries with a smile. During the game, Majid stayed loyal by evading every pass from his teammates. Even so, the team won, and the crowd cheered.”
segments: Before the final, Majid felt pensive and sat silently thinking about the match.
His coach tried to dispel his worries with a smile.
During the game, Majid stayed loyal by evading every pass from his teammates.
Even so, the team won, and the crowd cheered.
questions.correction: During the game, Majid stayed loyal by passing to his teammates.
questions.why: Evading your teammates' passes is not loyal, so the word is misused.

questions.stem: Which word makes this sentence most precise? “Our grandmother's ____ kindness never ran out; she helped neighbors every single day for fifty years.”
questions.why: Perpetual means never ending, which fits fifty years of daily help.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “devastating” figuratively, not about physical destruction? Choose two.
options: Her devastating smile won over the whole audience.
The news of the cancelled trip was devastating to the class.
The devastating flood washed away three bridges.
A devastating fire burned the old forest.
questions.why: Figurative uses describe a strong effect on feelings, not real damage.

questions.stem: True or false: A person who gives an evasive answer (from “evade”) replies clearly and directly.
questions.why: An evasive answer avoids the question instead of answering it.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order to build a paragraph that uses “rival,” “dispel,” and “loyalty.”
sequence: Two chess players from Jeddah had been rivals since grade four.
Before the national final, a rumor said one of them had cheated.
His rival quickly spoke up to dispel the rumor.
That act of loyalty made their friendship stronger than ever.
questions.why: The paragraph moves from background, to problem, to action, to result.

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? “After hearing the sad news, Rami grew ____; he stared at the sea for an hour, lost in deep thought.”
questions.why: Pensive means quietly lost in serious thought.

questions.stem: “Huda's mother is an activist who works to protect sea turtles on the Red Sea coast.” What is an “activist”?
options: a person who works for a cause or change
a person who sells goods at a market
a person who writes reports for TV news
a person who repairs cars and trucks
questions.why: An activist works hard to bring about change for a cause.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “advocate,” “initiative,” “persevere,” and “contribute.”

pairs.right: to speak up in support of something
the ability to start something on your own

questions.why: Knowing each meaning helps you use the words correctly.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Faisal showed determination by practicing his assembly speech every day until it was perfect,” the word “determination” means refusing to give up.
questions.why: Determination is a firm purpose to reach a goal.

questions.stem: Each student will ____ one book to the new class library.
questions.why: To contribute is to give something to help a shared goal.

questions.stem: Does each action show the ability to persevere, or does it show giving up?

rows.text: Salem kept fixing his robot after it failed five times.
Reem stopped learning to swim after one try.
The runner finished the marathon despite sore legs.
Omar quit the puzzle when it got hard.

questions.why: To persevere is to keep trying even when it is hard.

questions.stem: Which word means almost the same as “inspire”?
questions.why: To inspire is to motivate someone to act.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences show someone taking initiative? Choose two.
options: Without being asked, Lama organized a beach cleanup.
Noor waited for someone else to fix the broken swing.
Ziyad started a reading club when he saw the library was empty.
Badr cleaned his room after his father asked him three times.
questions.why: Initiative means starting something on your own, without being told.

questions.stem: Planting trees around the school had a big ____ on summer temperatures in the yard.
questions.why: An impact is a strong effect.

questions.stem: True or false: An advocate for clean water is someone who argues against having clean water.
questions.why: An advocate speaks up in support of something.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “inspire,” “impact,” or “determination” in it.

pairs.left: The coach's speech inspired the team.
pairs.right: filled with the desire to do something

pairs.left: The meteor's impact left a deep crater.
pairs.right: the force of one object hitting another

pairs.left: Her determination helped her finish the climb.
pairs.right: firm purpose to reach a goal

questions.why: Context shows the meaning of each word.

questions.stem: “Ali wanted to contribute to the charity drive. He gave half of his savings and spent Saturday packing food boxes.” What does “contribute” mean?
options: to watch something from far away
to collect money and food from others
to give or add something to help
to count items in a large box
questions.why: Giving savings and time are ways to contribute.

questions.stem: Is the key word (“advocate,” “inspire,” “impact,” or “contribute”) used as a noun or a verb in each sentence?

rows.text: Teachers advocate for safer crossings near schools.
She is a strong advocate for reading.
Their kindness will inspire others.
The project's impact was huge.
Your help will contribute a lot.

questions.why: Some words, like advocate, can be either a noun or a verb.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “determination”?
segments: to finish the science fair project
questions.why: After “Her” we need the noun determination.

questions.stem: The student council took the ____ to start a recycling program before anyone asked them.
questions.why: Taking the initiative means starting something on your own.

questions.stem: Which TWO words or phrases are antonyms of “persevere”? Choose two.
questions.why: To persevere is to keep going, so quit and give up are opposites.

questions.stem: Which word is closest in meaning to “advocate” in “Dr. Rania is an advocate for children's health”?
questions.why: An advocate is a champion or supporter of a cause.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “The heavy rain had an impact on the football schedule, so the match was moved to Friday” uses “impact” correctly.
questions.why: The rain had an effect on the schedule, so impact fits.

questions.stem: Put these steps of a young activist's beach campaign in order.
sequence: Noticing plastic litter piling up on the beach.
Taking the initiative to form a cleanup team.
Persevering through weeks of hot weekend work.
Seeing the impact: a cleaner beach and returning crabs.
questions.why: A campaign moves from a problem, to action, to effort, to results.

questions.stem: Match each form of “inspire,” “contribute,” “persevere,” and “activist” with its meaning.

pairs.right: something that gives you courage or ideas
continuing even when it is hard
action taken to bring about change

questions.why: Suffixes such as -tion, -ance, and -ism form nouns.

questions.stem: True or false: A person with determination usually gives up as soon as a task becomes difficult.
questions.why: Determination means sticking with a goal.

questions.stem: Which word best describes someone who publicly speaks up for a cause, rather than simply agreeing with it?
questions.why: An advocate actively speaks up in support of a cause.

questions.stem: In each sentence, does “impact” mean “a strong effect” or “a hit or collision”?

rows.text: The new library had a positive impact on reading scores.
The impact of the ball cracked the window.
Social media has a big impact on how teens shop.
Seat belts protect riders during the impact of a crash.

questions.why: Impact has a literal and a figurative meaning.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: teacher is to educate as advocate is to ____.
questions.why: A teacher educates; an advocate supports a cause.

questions.stem: Part A: “At eleven, Tariq noticed that older neighbors could not carry groceries up the stairs. Without waiting for adults, he organized a delivery team of friends.” Which word best describes Tariq?

partA.stem: Part A: “At eleven, Tariq noticed that older neighbors could not carry groceries up the stairs. Without waiting for adults, he organized a delivery team of friends.” Which word best describes Tariq?

options.label: A
options.text: showing initiative

options.label: B
options.text: showing fear

options.label: C
options.text: showing pride

options.label: D
options.text: showing laziness

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase about Tariq's delivery team best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: up the stairs

options.label: B
options.text: carry groceries

options.label: C
options.text: older neighbors

options.label: D
options.text: Without waiting for adults

questions.why: Acting without waiting to be told shows initiative.

questions.stem: Find the misused key word in this paragraph: “Rawan is an activist who works to save mangrove forests. She advocates for laws that protect the coastline. Her speeches inspire many students to volunteer. Sadly, her hard work has had no impact, because the forests are now growing again.”
segments: Rawan is an activist who works to save mangrove forests.
She advocates for laws that protect the coastline.
Her speeches inspire many students to volunteer.
Sadly, her hard work has had no impact, because the forests are now growing again.
questions.correction: Her hard work has had a great impact, because the forests are now growing again.
questions.why: If the forests are growing again, her work had a strong impact.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences show both determination and initiative? Choose two.
options: Without being told, Dana designed a water filter and kept improving it after each failure.
Fahad noticed his school had no ramp, wrote to the principal himself, and kept writing until one was built.
Saad started a garden but quit after the first plant died.
Maha finished her homework because her teacher checked it.
questions.why: Initiative is starting on your own; determination is not quitting.

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? “The village's water problem was solved because each family agreed to ____ a few riyals every month to repair the well.”
questions.why: Families gave money to help, so contribute is precise.

questions.stem: True or false: “Persevere” and “determination” are close in meaning, but “persevere” names an action while “determination” names a quality.
questions.why: Persevere is a verb; determination is a noun naming a quality.

questions.stem: Put these actions in order from the smallest to the largest contribution to a food bank.
sequence: donating one can of beans
volunteering for a single afternoon
organizing a citywide food drive as an activist
questions.why: A larger contribution gives more time, effort, or goods.

questions.stem: Which word makes this sentence most precise? “Her brave speech ____ hundreds of students to start recycling clubs at their schools.”
questions.why: To inspire is to move people to act.

questions.stem: “The sun will emerge from behind the clouds after the rain.” What does “emerge” mean?
questions.why: To emerge is to come out into view.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “emerge,” “fragile,” “conceal,” and “transform.”
questions.why: Knowing each meaning helps you read the words in new sentences.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Pack the fragile glass vase in soft paper,” the word “fragile” means easily broken.
questions.why: Fragile things break easily, so they need careful packing.

questions.stem: Sara wrapped the ____ old manuscript gently so its thin pages would not tear.
questions.why: Delicate means easily damaged and needing care.

questions.stem: In each sentence, does “shed” mean “a small building for storage” or “to let something fall off”?

rows.text: Grandpa keeps his tools in the shed.
Snakes shed their skin as they grow.
Palm trees shed old fronds.
We painted the garden shed green.

questions.why: Shed is a multiple-meaning word: a noun or a verb.

questions.stem: Which word is an antonym of “conceal”?
questions.why: To conceal is to hide, so reveal is the opposite.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “patient” to mean a person receiving medical care? Choose two.
options: The fisherman was patient as he waited for a bite.
Be patient while the bread bakes.
The nurse checked the patient's temperature.
The dentist called the next patient into the room.
questions.why: Patient can be a noun (a person under care) or an adjective (calm while waiting).

questions.stem: Heat and pressure can ____ soft mud into hard rock over millions of years.
questions.why: To transform is to change completely.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The actors bowed on the stage,” the word “stage” means a step in a process.
questions.why: Here stage means a raised platform where actors perform.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “stage” in it.

pairs.left: The band played on the stage.
A tadpole is an early stage of a frog's life.
The students will stage a play about Al-Idrisi.

questions.why: Stage is a multiple-meaning word; context shows the meaning.

questions.stem: “The leopard's spotted coat helps it conceal itself in the tall grass. Its prey walks right past without seeing it.” What does “conceal” mean?
questions.why: The prey does not see the leopard, so conceal means hide.

questions.stem: Is each pair a synonym pair or an antonym pair for “fragile,” “conceal,” “emerge,” “delicate,” and “transform”?

rows.text: fragile — sturdy
conceal — hide
emerge — appear
delicate — rough
transform — change

questions.why: Synonyms share a meaning; antonyms are opposites.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “transform”?
questions.why: After “The city's” we need the noun transformation.

questions.stem: The newborn kitten looked so ____ that Omar held it with both hands very carefully.
questions.why: Delicate means fragile and in need of gentle care.

questions.stem: Which TWO words use the prefix “trans-” with the meaning “across or change,” as in “transform”? Choose two.
questions.why: Trans- means across or change; trash and train only begin with similar letters.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “patient” as an adjective?
options: Be patient while the paint dries.
Each patient got a cup of water.
The doctor visited a young patient.
questions.why: As an adjective, patient describes someone calm while waiting.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Trees shed their leaves in autumn,” the word “shed” is a verb.
questions.why: Here shed is an action: the trees drop their leaves.

questions.stem: Put these steps in the growth of a date palm in order, using “emerge” and “stage.”
sequence: A seed sprouts in moist soil.
A young shoot emerges above the ground.
The palm reaches the stage where it produces dates.
questions.why: Growth moves from seed, to shoot, to fruit.

questions.stem: Match each form of “emerge,” “fragile,” “conceal,” and “transform” with its meaning.
questions.why: Suffixes like -ence, -ity, -ment, and -ation form nouns.

questions.stem: The diver watched an octopus ____ itself by changing color to match the rocks.
questions.why: Changing color to blend in is a way to conceal, or hide.

questions.stem: In each sentence, which meaning of “delicate” is used?

rows.text: The delicate lace tore when it caught on a nail.
Talking about the lost match was a delicate subject.
Rose water gave the pudding a delicate flavor.

questions.why: Delicate has several related meanings; context decides.

questions.stem: Which word best tells a mover to handle the ancient pottery gently? “Carry this box carefully; the pottery inside is ____.”
questions.why: Fragile means easily broken, which calls for gentle handling.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: enter is to exit as conceal is to ____.
questions.why: Enter and exit are opposites, as are conceal and reveal.

questions.stem: Part A: “The director decided to stage the final scene in total darkness. Only one lamp lit the actor's face.” What does “stage” mean here?

partA.stem: Part A: “The director decided to stage the final scene in total darkness. Only one lamp lit the actor's face.” What does “stage” mean here?

options.label: A
options.text: a section of a rocket

options.label: B
options.text: to plan and present a performance

options.label: C
options.text: a raised platform for actors

options.label: D
options.text: a step in development

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase about the director's final scene best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Only one lamp

options.label: B
options.text: The director decided

options.label: C
options.text: the actor's face

options.label: D
options.text: in total darkness

questions.why: A director decides how to present a scene, so stage is a verb meaning to present.

questions.stem: Find the misused key word in this paragraph: “Every spring, the old camel begins to shed its thick winter hair. Underneath, a lighter coat starts to emerge. The camel stays patient as the herders brush it. Its fragile hide easily handles the burning desert sun.”
segments: Every spring, the old camel begins to shed its thick winter hair.
Underneath, a lighter coat starts to emerge.
The camel stays patient as the herders brush it.
Its fragile hide easily handles the burning desert sun.
questions.correction: Its tough hide easily handles the burning desert sun.
questions.why: A fragile hide could not easily handle harsh sun; the word should mean strong.

questions.stem: In which sentence does “shed” mean “to give off or send out”?
options: We stored the bicycles in the shed.
The lantern shed a warm light over the tent.
The goat shed its winter coat.
He shed his heavy wool jacket because the afternoon was hot.
questions.why: A lantern sheds light by sending it out.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “emerge” to mean “become known”? Choose two.
options: It emerged that the old map was a copy.
The miners emerged from the tunnel at noon.
A turtle emerged from the waves.
New facts emerged during the investigation.
questions.why: Emerge can mean to come out physically or to become known.

questions.stem: Which word best shows a complete change? “In ten years, the empty desert land will ____ into a green farm full of date palms.”
questions.why: Transform means to change completely in form or appearance.

questions.stem: Put these objects in order from the least fragile to the most fragile.
sequence: a steel pipe
a plastic cup
a thin glass ornament
questions.why: Fragile things break easily; thin glass breaks most easily.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The doctor asked the patient to be patient,” the word “patient” has the same meaning both times.
questions.why: First it is a noun (a person in care); then an adjective (calm while waiting).

questions.stem: “Grandma used a needle to stitch a button back onto my shirt.” What does “stitch” mean?
questions.why: To stitch is to sew with a needle and thread.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “fragment,” “cherish,” “frayed,” and “legacy.”

pairs.right: something handed down from the past

questions.why: Knowing each meaning helps you use the words.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Old photos of my grandparents are things I cherish,” the word “cherish” means to love and care for.
questions.why: To cherish something is to treasure it.

questions.stem: The rope was so ____ at the ends that its threads were coming loose.
questions.why: Frayed means worn so threads come loose.

questions.stem: Is each item part of a family's heritage or not?

rows.text: Sadu weaving patterns passed down for generations
a kabsa recipe from great-grandmother
a plastic bag from today's shopping
a pencil bought yesterday

questions.why: Heritage is what is passed down from earlier generations.

questions.stem: Which word means almost the same as “embrace” in “The friends embraced at the airport”?
questions.why: To embrace someone is to hug them.

questions.stem: Which TWO things could be described as intricate? Choose two.
options: a carpet with thousands of tiny knotted shapes
a mashrabiya window with detailed carved patterns
questions.why: Intricate means having many small, detailed parts.

questions.stem: The archaeologist found a small ____ of a clay pot buried in the sand near AlUla.
questions.why: A fragment is a small broken piece.

questions.stem: True or false: A legacy is something that disappears as soon as a person leaves.
questions.why: A legacy lasts and is passed on after a person is gone.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “stitch” in it.

pairs.left: Each stitch in the scarf was neat and even.
After running, Majed got a stitch in his side.
Dad will stitch the torn tent.

questions.why: Stitch is a multiple-meaning word.

questions.stem: “My grandfather's old cloak was frayed. Its edges were worn thin, and loose threads hung down.” What does “frayed” mean?
options: worn and loose at the edges
heavy and warm for cold nights
questions.why: Worn edges and loose threads describe something frayed.

questions.stem: Is each pair a synonym pair or an antonym pair for “cherish,” “frayed,” “intricate,” “fragment,” and “embrace”?

rows.text: cherish — treasure
frayed — brand-new
intricate — simple
fragment — piece
embrace — reject

questions.why: Synonyms share a meaning; antonyms are opposites.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “intricate”?
questions.why: An adjective (intricate), not an adverb, describes the noun pattern.

questions.stem: The new museum in Riyadh helps young people learn about the Kingdom's rich ____.
questions.why: Heritage is the history and traditions passed down.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “embrace” to mean “accept willingly”? Choose two.
options: The school embraced the new science program.
The aunts embraced at the airport.
Hamad embraced the chance to learn Chinese.
questions.why: Embrace can mean to hug or to gladly accept an idea.

questions.stem: Which word is in the same word family as “fragment” and means “broken into pieces”?
questions.why: Fragmented comes from fragment and means broken into parts.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “The scientist left a legacy of discoveries that students still study today” uses “legacy” correctly.
questions.why: Discoveries that last after a person is gone are a legacy.

questions.stem: Put these steps of making a family quilt in order.
sequence: Gather fragments of old family clothes.
Arrange the pieces into an intricate design.
Stitch the pieces together.
Give the finished quilt to a child as a heritage gift.
questions.why: A quilt is gathered, arranged, sewn, and then passed on.

questions.stem: Match each form of “cherish,” “fragment,” “intricate,” and “stitch” with its meaning.

pairs.right: the quality of having many detailed parts

questions.why: Suffixes change a word's form and part of speech.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “cherish” correctly?
options: I cherish the watch my father gave me before he retired.
Please cherish the trash out to the bin before dinner tonight.
We cherish the ball across the field during the match.
The plumber will cherish the leaking pipe in the kitchen.
questions.why: We cherish things we love and treasure.

questions.stem: Which word gives the warmest, most loving feeling? “She ____ every letter her grandmother ever wrote to her.”
questions.why: Cherishes shows deep love, not just ownership.

questions.stem: In each sentence, does “frayed” mean “worn at the edges” or “strained and tense”?

rows.text: After the long flight delay, everyone's nerves were frayed.
The frayed carpet edge caught my toe.
Tempers frayed during the heated debate.
The frayed collar showed years of wear.

questions.why: Frayed can describe cloth or, figuratively, feelings.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: simple is to plain as intricate is to ____.
questions.why: Plain is a synonym of simple; complex is a synonym of intricate.

questions.stem: Part A: “The museum's oldest Sadu tent is a legacy from Bedouin weavers. Its patterns were passed down from mothers to daughters for centuries.” What does “legacy” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: “The museum's oldest Sadu tent is a legacy from Bedouin weavers. Its patterns were passed down from mothers to daughters for centuries.” What does “legacy” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: something handed down from the past

options.label: B
options.text: a story told only once

options.label: C
options.text: a new design made this year

options.label: D
options.text: a price paid for a tent

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase about the Sadu tent best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Bedouin weavers

options.label: B
options.text: The museum's oldest

options.label: C
options.text: passed down from mothers to daughters

options.label: D
options.text: Sadu tent

questions.why: Something passed down over generations is a legacy.

questions.stem: Find the misused key word in this paragraph: “My aunt keeps a box of fragments from old family dresses. She says each scrap is part of our heritage. Last winter, she stitched them into an intricate quilt. She frays the quilt so much that she hangs it on the wall.”
segments: My aunt keeps a box of fragments from old family dresses.
She says each scrap is part of our heritage.
Last winter, she stitched them into an intricate quilt.
She frays the quilt so much that she hangs it on the wall.
questions.correction: She cherishes the quilt so much that she hangs it on the wall.
questions.why: Hanging a quilt on the wall shows she cherishes it; frayed means worn out.

questions.stem: Which word makes this sentence most precise? “The carpet's ____ design had hundreds of tiny diamonds, stars, and vines woven together.”
questions.why: Intricate describes a design with many detailed parts.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “stitch” or “fragment” figuratively? Choose two.
options: A fragment of glass lay on the floor.
Only fragments of the old song remained in her memory.
The coach stitched together a team from players of five schools.
The tailor stitched a hem on the thobe.
questions.why: Figurative uses apply the words to ideas, not real thread or broken objects.

questions.stem: True or false: In the line “The quilt embraced the sleeping child like warm arms,” the quilt is given a human action, which is personification.
questions.why: Embracing is a human action, so the line uses personification.

questions.stem: Put these words in order from the weakest to the strongest feeling of love for an object, ending with “cherish.”
sequence: like
value
cherish
questions.why: Cherish shows the deepest love and care.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “heritage” most precisely?
options: The heritage of yesterday's exciting football match was two goals to one.
My heritage is that I bought new shoes at the mall yesterday.
She put her heritage in her backpack and walked to class.
Traditional Najdi architecture is part of Saudi Arabia's heritage.
questions.why: Heritage is traditions and culture passed down through history.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Reem was hesitant to jump into the cold pool, so she stood at the edge for a long time.” What does “hesitant” mean?
questions.why: A hesitant person pauses because they are unsure.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “migrant,” “enroll,” “corridor,” and “savor.”

pairs.right: a person who moves from place to place for work
to sign up as a member or student

questions.why: Knowing each meaning helps you picture what is happening.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Faisal walked down the long corridor to reach the school library,” a “corridor” is a hallway.
questions.why: A corridor is a long hallway with rooms along it.

questions.stem: Every morning, Lina follows the same ____: she prays, eats breakfast, and packs her school bag.
questions.why: A routine is a set of actions done the same way regularly.

questions.stem: Does each sentence show someone acting “instinctively” or after careful planning?

rows.text: Omar pulled his hand back from the hot pan without thinking.
The cat leaped away the moment it heard a loud bang.
Huda wrote a list before shopping for the camping trip.
The hikers studied the map for an hour before setting out.

questions.why: Acting instinctively means acting naturally, without stopping to think.

questions.stem: “Grandfather asked Yusuf to accompany him to the date market in Riyadh.” Which words mean the same as “accompany”?
questions.why: To accompany someone is to go along with them.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe a “migrant”? Choose two.
options: Each spring, the worker moved to a new farm to pick fruit.
The baker has run the same shop on one street for thirty years.
The farmhand traveled from town to town wherever there was a harvest.
Nora has lived in the same house in Dammam since she was born.
questions.why: A migrant moves from place to place, often to find work.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “savor,” “enroll,” or “accompany” in it.

pairs.left: Sami ate the dates slowly to savor their sweetness.
Parents can enroll their children at the new school in August.
pairs.right: to sign up as a member

pairs.left: A teacher will accompany the class on the museum trip.

questions.why: Each meaning fits the way the word is used in its sentence.

questions.stem: Before the school year starts, Mother will ____ my little brother in first grade.
questions.why: To enroll a child is to sign the child up for school.

questions.stem: True or false: A student who is hesitant to answer raises a hand quickly and shouts out the answer.
questions.why: A hesitant student pauses and holds back, not rushing to answer.

questions.stem: “Migrant birds such as white storks pass over the Arabian Peninsula each autumn. They fly thousands of kilometers to warmer lands and return in spring.” Which words best help you understand “migrant”?
options: “pass over the Arabian Peninsula each autumn”
“fly thousands of kilometers to warmer lands”
questions.why: Flying far to other lands shows that migrant animals move from place to place.

questions.stem: The nurse moved ____ to catch the falling tray; she did not stop to think about it.
questions.why: “Did not stop to think” signals an instinctive action.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are antonyms of “hesitant”? Choose two.
questions.why: Confident and certain people act without holding back, the opposite of hesitant.

questions.stem: In each sentence, is the form of “enroll,” “routine,” or “accompany” used as a noun or a verb?

rows.text: Enrollment in the new science club reached fifty students.
Students may enroll in the art class online.
Her evening routine includes a walk after sunset.
The museum guide will accompany the visitors.

questions.why: Suffixes such as -ment can change a verb into a noun.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Laila savored her last week at the seaside in Al Khobar,” the word “savored” shows that she enjoyed the week and wanted it to last.
questions.why: To savor an experience is to enjoy it slowly and fully.

questions.stem: “The new student felt lost in the long corridor. Classroom doors lined both sides, and he could not remember which one was his.” What is a corridor?
options: a passage with rooms on each side
a small office for the teachers
a narrow staircase between two floors
questions.why: The clue “doors lined both sides” shows that a corridor is a hallway.

questions.stem: Match each word with its antonym: “hesitant,” “savor,” “routine,” and “accompany.”
questions.why: Antonyms are words with opposite meanings.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about a desert fox uses a vocabulary word incorrectly?
segments: When the fox heard the eagle,
and savored there until the danger passed.
questions.correction: and stayed there until the danger passed.
questions.why: Savor means to enjoy something; the fox simply stayed hidden.

questions.stem: The ____ workers followed the harvest, picking grapes in one valley in June and dates in another region in August.
questions.why: Workers who move with the harvest are migrant workers.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use “routine” correctly? Choose three.
options: Feeding the camels at dawn is a daily routine on the farm.
Winning the World Cup once was a routine for the tiny team.
The surprise sandstorm was a routine that nobody expected.
Brushing my teeth before bed is part of my nightly routine.
The doctor said the check-up was routine and nothing to worry about.
questions.why: A routine is something regular and expected, not a surprise or rare event.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “savor” to mean enjoying a moment or experience rather than food?
options: Mona slowly savored the warm bread fresh from the oven.
Khalid savored every spoonful of his mother's lentil soup.
The runners savored their win long after the race ended.
The thirsty children savored their cold mango juice at noon.
questions.why: Savor can describe enjoying a feeling or event, not only a taste.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: Migrant is to move as resident is to ____.
questions.why: A migrant moves; a resident stays in one place.

questions.stem: Does each word come from the Latin root migr, meaning “to move,” like “migrant”?

rows.text: migration
immigrate
mirror
midnight
emigrant

columns.text: Does not have the root migr

questions.why: Words with migr are about moving from one place to another.

questions.stem: Which sentence in this paragraph about Hamad's first day at a new school uses a key word incorrectly?
segments: Hamad's first day at the new school made him nervous.
He walked slowly down the corridor, hesitant to open the classroom door.
A kind teacher offered to accompany him inside.
By lunchtime, he had already savored his fears and joined a game of football.
questions.correction: By lunchtime, he had already forgotten his fears and joined a game of football.
questions.why: People do not savor fears they want to leave behind; savor means to enjoy.

questions.stem: Part A: In “The volunteer instinctively reached for the child's hand as the crowd surged forward,” what does “instinctively” suggest about the action?

partA.stem: Part A: In “The volunteer instinctively reached for the child's hand as the crowd surged forward,” what does “instinctively” suggest about the action?

options.label: A
options.text: It followed written instructions.

options.label: B
options.text: It was done unwillingly and slowly.

options.label: C
options.text: It happened naturally, without planning.

options.label: D
options.text: It was practiced for many weeks.

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase from that sentence about the volunteer best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “the child's hand”

options.label: B
options.text: “reached for”

options.label: C
options.text: “as the crowd surged forward”

options.label: D
options.text: “The volunteer”

questions.why: A sudden surge left no time to plan, so the action was instinctive.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “routine” to mean “ordinary and not exciting”?
options: The dancers practiced a new routine for the show.
The guard found the long night shift dull and routine.
Her morning routine starts with a glass of water.
Each night the family routine begins with homework.
questions.why: As an adjective, routine can mean ordinary or dull.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are closest in meaning to “instinctively” as in “The goalkeeper instinctively dived to the left”? Choose two.
questions.why: Instinctive actions happen automatically, without a plan.

questions.stem: The new student was not afraid exactly, just ____; she paused at the door for a moment before stepping in.
questions.why: Hesitant describes a short pause from uncertainty, milder than terrified.

questions.stem: Put these words in order from the weakest to the strongest feeling of enjoyment, ending with “savor.”
sequence: tolerate
accept
enjoy
savor
questions.why: Savor is the strongest: enjoying something fully and slowly.

questions.stem: Match each use of “corridor” with its meaning.

pairs.left: The hotel corridor had soft carpets.
The train runs along the coastal corridor from city to city.
pairs.right: a long strip of land used as a travel route

pairs.left: Animals use a green corridor of trees to cross between two forests.
pairs.right: a narrow strip of natural land linking habitats

questions.why: Corridor has several related meanings, all about a long passage.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “The twins wore identical uniforms, so their teacher could not tell them apart.” What does “identical” mean?
questions.why: Identical things are exactly the same.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “identical,” “distinguish,” “resemble,” “unique,” and “independent.”

pairs.right: able to act on one's own

questions.why: Each word describes how people or things are alike or different.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Huda and her cousin resemble each other because they both have curly hair and dark eyes,” “resemble” means to look alike.
questions.why: To resemble someone is to look like them.

questions.stem: Every fingerprint is ____; no two people in the world share the same pattern.
questions.why: Unique means the only one of its kind.

questions.stem: Does each sentence show someone being “independent” or depending on others?

rows.text: Majed packs his own lunch and walks to school by himself.
The baby bird waits in the nest for its mother to bring food.
Rana solved the hard puzzle without asking for help.
My little brother needs help to tie his shoes.

questions.why: Independent people do things on their own.

questions.stem: “A bird watcher can distinguish a falcon from a hawk by the shape of its wings.” What does “distinguish” mean?
questions.why: To distinguish is to see how things are different.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe something done by an “individual” rather than a group? Choose two.
options: Salem built the model airplane all by himself.
The whole team carried the trophy around the field.

The independent student finished her project early.
Each handmade rug has its own uniqueness.

questions.why: Suffixes like -ance and -ness form nouns.

questions.why: An individual is one person considered alone.

questions.stem: “Nada and Nour are twins, but Nada is quiet and loves painting while Nour is loud and loves sports. Each girl has her own identity.” What does “identity” mean?

the qualities that make a person who she is
the clothes a person wears to school
the people a person lives with
questions.why: The details about each girl's personality explain identity.

questions.stem: Match each word with its antonym: “identical,” “independent,” “unique,” and “distinguish.”
questions.why: Antonyms have opposite meanings.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about two falcons at a falcon show uses a vocabulary word incorrectly?
segments: could distinguish one from the other.
questions.why: Birds that are hard to tell apart are identical, not unique.

questions.stem: Some people say the twins ____ their father, with the same tall build and warm smile.
questions.why: To resemble is to look like someone.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use “unique” correctly? Choose three.
options: The artist's unique style made her paintings easy to recognize.
Each person's voice has a unique sound.
The Edge of the World cliffs near Riyadh offer a unique view of the desert.
All the pencils in the box were unique, exactly the same color and size.
The bus was unique, just like every other bus in the city.
questions.why: Unique means unlike anything else, not the same as others.

questions.stem: Which word describes Faris's style in the most positive way? “Faris always wears a bright scarf that no one else would choose; his style is ____.”
questions.why: Unique has a positive connotation; the others suggest something is wrong.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: Identical is to different as dependent is to ____.
questions.why: Both pairs are antonyms.

unique

identity
incomplete

One twin may prefer to work in groups, while the other is more independent.
Their parents learn to resemble them by small details, such as a freckle or a voice.
questions.correction: Their parents learn to distinguish them by small details, such as a freckle or a voice.
questions.why: Parents tell twins apart, so the word should be distinguish.

questions.stem: Part A: In “Though the twins dressed alike, Samar wanted her teachers to see her individuality,” what does “individuality” mean?

options.label: C

questions.why: Individuality comes from individual plus -ity, “the quality of being.”

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “distinguish” to mean “to make oneself known for doing something well”?

In fog, it is hard to distinguish one car from another.

Can you distinguish the sound of a flute from the sound of a violin?
questions.why: To distinguish yourself is to stand out by excellent work.

questions.stem: Which TWO choices are closest in meaning to “resemble” as in “The rock formations resemble giant mushrooms”? Choose two.

questions.stem: To solve the water problem in the village, the engineer looked at it from a farmer's ____ instead of only her own.
questions.why: A perspective is a point of view.

questions.stem: Put these words in order from the most alike to the least alike, starting with “identical.”
sequence: identical
similar
different
completely unlike
questions.why: Identical is the strongest word for sameness.

questions.stem: Match each word built from “identity” or “identical” with its meaning.

pairs.right: a card or proof that shows who someone is

questions.why: Words from the same root share a core meaning of “the same.”

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “When Sultan dropped his pen, gravity pulled it down to the floor.” What does “gravity” mean?
options: the light that helps us see objects
the wind that blows things across a room
the sound that falling objects make
the force that pulls things toward Earth
questions.why: Gravity is the pull that makes objects fall.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “mass,” “impact,” “vibration,” and “simultaneous.”

pairs.right: the amount of matter in an object
the force of one thing hitting another

questions.why: These science words help describe motion and force.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The fans stood up simultaneously when the goal was scored,” “simultaneously” means one at a time, slowly.
questions.why: Simultaneously means all at the same time.

questions.stem: The doors and windows rattled from the ____ when the heavy truck rumbled past the house.
questions.why: A vibration is a shaking movement.

questions.stem: Is each example a push or a pull, the two kinds of “force”?

rows.text: A player kicks a football across the field.
A magnet draws a paper clip toward it.
Mother opens the fridge door by its handle.
Wind presses against a boat's sail.

questions.why: A force is a push or a pull.

questions.stem: “An elephant has much more mass than a mouse.” What does “mass” mean in this sentence?
questions.why: Mass is the amount of matter in an object.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe events that are “simultaneous”? Choose two.
options: The two runners crossed the finish line at the exact same moment.
The two fireworks burst in the sky at the very same instant.
Ahmed ate breakfast, and an hour later he went to school.
First the bell rang, and later the students left.
questions.why: Simultaneous events happen at the same time.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “force,” “impact,” or “gravity” in it.

Gravity keeps the Moon circling Earth.
pairs.right: the pull between objects with mass

questions.why: Each meaning fits its sentence.

questions.stem: The ball hit the wall with a loud thud, and the ____ knocked a picture off its hook.
questions.why: An impact is the force of a hit.

questions.stem: True or false: A negligible amount of sugar is so small that it hardly matters.
questions.why: Negligible means so small it can be ignored.

options: “less than the width of a hair”
“Scientists measured the movement of the bridge”
questions.why: Something thinner than a hair is too small to matter.

questions.why: A hypothetical question imagines a possible situation.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are antonyms of “negligible”? Choose two.
questions.why: Significant and enormous mean large or important.

questions.stem: Is the form of “gravity,” “vibration,” or “impact” in each sentence a noun, a verb, or an adjective?

Phones vibrate when a message arrives.
The vibration from the drill shook the shelf.
Heavy rain can impact the date of the match.

questions.why: The same word family can appear as different parts of speech.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Every student in the hall clapped simultaneously, and the sound was like a single thunderclap,” the clapping happened at the same time.
questions.why: One single sound shows that everyone clapped at once.

questions.stem: “Astronauts on the Moon can jump much higher than on Earth. The Moon has less mass, so its gravity is weaker.” Using context, what is the relationship between “mass” and “gravity”?
options: Mass and gravity are not related.
questions.why: Less mass gives weaker gravity, so more mass gives stronger gravity.

questions.stem: Match each word with its antonym: “simultaneous,” “negligible,” and “hypothetical.”
questions.why: Antonyms have opposite meanings.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about an earthquake sensor uses a vocabulary word incorrectly?
segments: The sensor in the university lab
that no one in the building felt it.
questions.why: A shake too small to feel is negligible, not hypothetical.

questions.stem: If all the fans in the stadium jumped ____, the stands would shake more than if they jumped one at a time.
questions.why: Jumping simultaneously means jumping together at once.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use “force” correctly? Choose three.
options: The force was a gentle color painted on the wall.
The garden's force smelled of roses and mint.
It takes more force to lift a full bucket than an empty one.
The force of the waves moved the small boat toward the shore.
Friction is a force that slows down a sliding box.
questions.why: Force is a push or pull, not a color or a smell.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “mass” to mean “a large crowd or amount” rather than its science meaning?
options: A brick has more mass than a sponge of the same size.
Scientists carefully measured the mass of the rock in kilograms.
The mass of an object stays the same on the Moon.
A mass of fans filled the streets after the final match.
questions.why: Mass can also mean a large group gathered together.

questions.why: A vibration is a shake; an impact is a hit.

questions.stem: Which sentence in this paragraph about the whole world jumping at once uses a key word incorrectly?
