Scientists say the effect would be negligible, because Earth's mass is enormous compared with all the people on it.
Even if every person landed simultaneously, the planet would barely shift.
The only clear effect would be a gravity that seismographs could record.
questions.correction: The only clear effect would be a vibration that seismographs could record.
questions.why: Seismographs record shaking, which is a vibration.

slight
noticeable

to move toward something as if pulled
very serious or heavy in importance

questions.why: The root grav means heavy.

questions.why: Each meaning fits its sentence.

questions.stem: Match each word with its antonym: “aggressive,” “exclude,” “isolate,” and “intervene.”

questions.why: To intervene is to step in to change what is happening.

questions.why: Both pairs are antonyms.

A brave bystander can make a difference by telling a trusted adult.
Schools that teach empathy help students intimidate one another's feelings.
questions.correction: Schools that teach empathy help students understand one another's feelings.
questions.why: Empathy helps students understand feelings, not intimidate others.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are closest in meaning to “intimidate” as in “Loud threats were used to intimidate the smaller team”? Choose two.

questions.stem: Put these words in order from the gentlest behavior to the most forceful, ending with “aggressive.”
sequence: polite
firm
pushy
aggressive
questions.why: Aggressive is the strongest, most forceful word.

questions.stem: Match each word built on the root of “exclude” (clud/clus = close or shut) with its meaning.

the act of shutting someone out
to close or bring to an end

questions.why: The root clud/clus means to close or shut.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “It took courage for Yara to speak in front of the whole school for the first time.” What does “courage” mean?
options: the ability to run very fast
a fear of meeting new people
a loud and clear speaking voice
questions.why: Courage is bravery in a difficult moment.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “activist,” “resilient,” “eloquent,” and “injustice.”

able to recover after hard times

questions.stem: True or false: In “The young plant was resilient and grew back after the sandstorm,” “resilient” means the plant recovered after harm.

Omar quit the swim class because the water was cold.

questions.why: To persevere is to keep going despite difficulty.

a map used to find the way
a large group of friendly travelers

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “eloquent,” “activist,” or “inspire” in it.

pairs.right: skilled at speaking clearly and movingly

pairs.left: The young activist collected signatures to protect the city's mangrove trees.

pairs.right: to fill with the wish to do something

questions.why: Each meaning fits its sentence.

questions.stem: Even after failing her driving test twice, Asma decided to ____ until she passed.

questions.stem: True or false: An eloquent speaker mumbles and forgets what to say.

questions.stem: “The young activist spent her weekends writing to leaders and organizing beach clean-ups. She wanted to change how people treated the coastline.” Which clue best helps you understand “activist”?

Inspiration can come from a walk in nature.

in an angry and loud way

in a clear and powerful way

questions.stem: Match each word with its antonym: “courage,” “persevere,” “eloquent,” and “injustice.”

options.label: B
options.text: “Despite years of setbacks”

options.label: C
options.text: “the young scientist”

options.label: D
options.text: “finally”

questions.why: Continuing despite setbacks is what persevering means.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “inspire” in its science meaning, “to breathe in”?
options: Her poems about the sea inspire readers to care for nature.
Doctors listen as patients inspire deeply through the nose.
Great leaders inspire others to act.
The view inspired the young painter.
questions.why: Inspire comes from a Latin word meaning “to breathe into.”

questions.stem: Which TWO words are closest in meaning to “resilient” as in “The resilient village rebuilt its homes after the flood”? Choose two.
questions.why: Resilient means tough and able to recover.

questions.stem: The young ____ spoke at a public meeting, asking the city to build a library for the girls in her neighborhood.
questions.why: An activist speaks up to bring about change.

questions.stem: Put these words in order from the weakest to the strongest form of not giving up, ending with “determination.”
sequence: interest
effort
commitment
determination
questions.why: Determination is the strongest commitment to a goal.

questions.stem: Match each noun formed from “persevere,” “resilient,” or “eloquent” with its meaning.

pairs.right: the quality of continuing to try

questions.why: Suffixes like -ance and -ence turn words into nouns.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “The children waited for the Eid holiday with great anticipation, counting the days on the calendar.” What does “anticipation” mean?
options: fear of something in the past
questions.why: Anticipation is the excited feeling of waiting for something to happen.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “anticipation,” “isolated,” “frail,” and “vivid.”
questions.why: Each meaning describes a feeling, place, or image.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The lighthouse stood isolated on a small rock far out at sea,” the word “isolated” means alone and far from others.
questions.why: Something isolated is set apart, far from other things.

questions.stem: Grandfather felt ____ after his long illness, so he walked slowly with a cane.
questions.why: Frail means weak, which explains why he needed a cane.

questions.stem: Is each scene “dreary” or not dreary?

rows.text: a gray, rainy afternoon with nothing to do
an empty classroom with dim lights on a cold day
a sunny beach day with friends in Al Khobar
a colorful festival with music and games

questions.why: Dreary describes something dull, gloomy, and sad.

questions.stem: “Nora's painting of the Red Sea coral reef was so vivid that the fish seemed to swim off the paper.” Which phrase means the same as “vivid”?
questions.why: A vivid picture is bright and looks real.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences show someone feeling “envious”? Choose two.
options: Huda clapped happily for her sister's success.
Sami wished he owned a new bicycle like his cousin's.
Omar shared his snacks with everyone at lunch.
Lina frowned when her classmate won the prize she wanted.
questions.why: Envious people want what someone else has.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “resentment,” “remorse,” or “envious” in it.

pairs.left: Majid felt resentment when he was blamed unfairly.
Rakan felt remorse after he lied to his mother.
Salma was envious of her friend's new tablet.

questions.why: Each word names a different feeling.

questions.stem: After breaking his neighbor's window with a football, Khalid felt deep ____ and offered to pay for the repair.
questions.why: Remorse is regret for something wrong you did.

questions.stem: True or false: A person who feels resentment toward a friend feels warm and thankful toward that friend.
questions.why: Resentment is bitter anger, not thankfulness.

questions.stem: “The desert village was isolated. The nearest town was a three-hour drive away, and no phone signal reached it.” Which clue best helps you understand “isolated”?
questions.why: Being hours away from any town shows that the village is isolated.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “frail”?

rows.text: weak
delicate
sturdy
strong

questions.why: Frail means weak, so sturdy and strong are opposites.

questions.stem: The museum guide described the ancient Nabataean tombs of Al-Ula so ____ that the students could picture them clearly.
questions.why: The adverb vividly describes how the guide spoke.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about the football match uses the wrong form of “anticipation”?
questions.why: After the adjective eager, we need the noun anticipation.

questions.stem: True or false: “The players felt remorse after the team won the championship fairly” uses “remorse” correctly.
questions.why: Remorse is regret for wrongdoing, and winning fairly is not wrong.

questions.stem: Which word is the best antonym of “dreary”?
questions.why: Dreary means gloomy, so cheerful is its opposite.

questions.stem: Which TWO words have almost the same meaning as “resentment”? Choose two.
questions.why: Resentment is bitter, unfriendly feeling.

questions.stem: Put the sentences in order to show how a camper's feeling changed from “anticipation” to “remorse.”
sequence: Faisal packed his tent, full of anticipation for the desert trip.
At camp, he ignored his father's warning and left the cooler open.
By morning, wild cats had eaten all the food.
Faisal felt remorse and apologized to his family.
questions.why: The feelings follow the events: excitement, a mistake, the result, then regret.

questions.stem: Match each form of “envious” with its part of speech.
questions.why: Suffixes like -ous and -ly change the part of speech.

questions.stem: When the storm left the mountain village ____ from the rest of the region, helicopters brought water and food.
questions.why: Isolated means cut off from others.

questions.stem: Which word shows a deeper, longer-lasting bitterness than “annoyance”?
questions.why: Resentment is a strong, lasting bitterness, much stronger than annoyance.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: joy is to sorrow as vivid is to ____.
questions.why: Joy and sorrow are opposites, and dull is the opposite of vivid.

questions.stem: Which sentence in this paragraph about a hospital visit misuses a vocabulary word (frail, vivid, envious)?
segments: My grandmother was frail after her surgery.
The doctors kept her room quiet and calm.
When we visited, she told us vivid stories about her childhood.
She felt envious that so many relatives came to see her.
questions.correction: She felt grateful that so many relatives came to see her.
questions.why: Envious means wanting what others have; she felt thankful, not envious.

questions.stem: In “The peace between the two neighbors was frail after the argument,” what does “frail” mean?
questions.why: Here frail is used figuratively: the peace could break easily.

questions.stem: Does each sentence use “isolated” to describe a place or a person's feeling?

rows.text: The isolated island had no airport.
Reem felt isolated during her first week at a new school.
An isolated farm sat alone on the wide plain.
Bader felt isolated when his friends stopped calling.

questions.why: Isolated can describe a far-off place or a lonely feeling.

questions.stem: What does “dreary” suggest in “The dreary week of sandstorms kept everyone indoors, staring at the same dusty windows”?

partA.stem: What does “dreary” suggest in “The dreary week of sandstorms kept everyone indoors, staring at the same dusty windows”?

options.label: A
options.text: dangerous and deadly

options.label: B
options.text: warm and peaceful

options.label: C
options.text: exciting and loud

options.label: D
options.text: dull and depressing

partB.stem: Which phrase best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “staring at the same dusty windows”

options.label: B
options.text: “week of sandstorms”

options.label: C
options.text: “kept everyone”

options.label: D
options.text: “dreary week”

questions.why: Staring at the same windows shows how dull and gloomy the week felt.

questions.stem: The suffix -ly turns an adjective into an adverb. Which TWO sentences use “vividly” or “enviously” correctly? Choose two.
options: The colors of the flag were vividly.
Mona remembered her trip to Abha vividly.
He was enviously of his friend's prize.
The boy looked enviously at his brother's new phone.
questions.why: Adverbs describe how an action is done, not what something is.

questions.stem: The scientist waited for the rover's first photos of Mars with breathless ____, refreshing her screen every few seconds.
questions.why: Anticipation is excited waiting, the best fit for refreshing the screen.

questions.stem: Put the sentences in order so the paragraph about “resentment” makes sense.
sequence: Yousef was not chosen for the robotics team.
At first, resentment toward the winners grew inside him.
Then his coach showed him how to improve his design.
Over time, his resentment faded, and he joined the team the next year.
questions.why: The paragraph moves from the cause, to the feeling, to the change.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Her apology was full of remorse,” replacing “remorse” with “regret” keeps nearly the same meaning.
questions.why: Remorse and regret are close synonyms; remorse is a little stronger.

questions.stem: “The famous football player signed shirts for every fan; he was a true celebrity in Riyadh.” What is a “celebrity”?
questions.why: A celebrity is a famous person.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “celebrity,” “integrity,” “publicity,” and “genuine.”

pairs.right: attention from the public or media

questions.why: Each word is useful when talking about fame and character.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Winning the national science fair was a great achievement for Reem,” the word “achievement” means something done successfully through effort.
questions.why: An achievement is a success reached by hard work.

questions.stem: Hassan always tells the truth, even when it is hard; he is a person of great ____.
questions.why: Integrity means being honest and doing what is right.

questions.stem: Is each item “genuine” or not genuine?

rows.text: a real gold coin from an old market
a plastic toy made to look like a diamond
a sincere thank-you from a friend
a fake smile hiding anger

questions.why: Genuine means real or sincere, not fake.

questions.stem: “Many children idolize astronauts and hang their pictures on bedroom walls.” What does “idolize” mean?
questions.why: To idolize someone is to admire them greatly.

questions.stem: Which TWO actions show the “influence” of a coach on a team? Choose two.
options: The stadium lights turn on every night at seven.
Rain falls on the field during the second half.
The players copy the coach's habit of training early.
The team starts eating healthy food because the coach advised it.
questions.why: Influence is the power to change how others think or act.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “publicity,” “admirable,” or “idolize” in it.

pairs.left: The new science museum got publicity on TV.
Her kindness to the elderly was admirable.
Young fans idolize the champion swimmer.

questions.why: Each meaning fits how the word is used.

questions.stem: Helping clean the beach every weekend is an ____ habit that the whole town respects.
questions.why: Admirable means deserving respect.

questions.stem: True or false: A company that wants publicity hopes that nobody will hear about its new product.
questions.why: Publicity is public attention, so a company wants many people to hear.

questions.stem: “The athlete's influence reached far beyond the stadium. After she spoke about reading, thousands of young fans visited their libraries.” Which clue best helps you understand “influence”?
questions.why: The fans' changed actions show her influence.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “genuine”?

rows.text: real
sincere
fake
false

questions.why: Genuine means real, so fake and false are opposites.

questions.stem: Reaching the top of Jabal Sawda was the greatest ____ of the hiking club's year.
questions.why: After 'the greatest' we need the noun achievement.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about a young poet uses the wrong form of “influence”?
questions.why: The passive verb needs the past participle influenced.

questions.stem: True or false: “The singer hired a team to get more publicity for his new album” uses “publicity” correctly.
questions.why: Getting more publicity means getting more public attention.

questions.stem: Which word is the best antonym of “admirable”?
questions.why: Admirable means deserving respect; shameful is its opposite.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are closest in meaning to “integrity”? Choose two.
questions.why: Integrity is about honest, fair character, not fame or money.

questions.stem: Put the sentences in order to show how a local volunteer became a “celebrity.”
sequence: Amal started a free reading club in her neighborhood.
A news reporter wrote about her club.
The publicity brought hundreds of new members.
Soon Amal was a local celebrity, invited to speak at schools.
questions.why: Her work came first, then attention, then fame.

questions.stem: Match each form of “achievement” with its part of speech.
questions.why: The suffixes -ment and -able change the part of speech.

questions.stem: Fans should not ____ a star so much that they copy every choice he makes, even the bad ones.
questions.why: To idolize is to admire too much, which can lead to copying blindly.

questions.stem: Which word suggests that fans admire someone too much, without thinking?
questions.why: Idolize suggests extreme, sometimes blind admiration.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: honest is to integrity as famous is to ____.
questions.why: Integrity is the quality of being honest; celebrity is the state of being famous.

questions.stem: Which sentence in this paragraph about Ibn al-Haytham misuses a vocabulary word (achievement, integrity, publicity, genuine)?
segments: Ibn al-Haytham is remembered for his achievement in the science of light.
His careful experiments showed great integrity.
He did not seek publicity; he cared about the truth.
Today, his work is still genuine to scientists around the world.
questions.correction: Today, his work still has influence on scientists around the world.
questions.why: Genuine means real; the sentence means his work still affects scientists.

questions.stem: In which sentence does “genuine” mean “sincere in feeling” rather than “real, not fake”?
options: “Her genuine smile relaxed the new student.”
“The museum proved the sword was genuine.”
“Experts said the old map was genuine.”
“This wallet is made of genuine leather.”
questions.why: A genuine smile shows true feeling.

questions.stem: Does each sentence use “influence” as a noun or as a verb?

rows.text: Parents have a strong influence on their children.
Good friends can influence your choices.
The influence of the Moon causes tides.
Weather can influence how crops grow.

questions.why: As a noun it names a power; as a verb it is an action.

questions.stem: In “The charity race got wide publicity, but its true achievement was the quiet work of volunteers who trained runners for months,” what does the writer suggest about “publicity”?

partA.stem: In “The charity race got wide publicity, but its true achievement was the quiet work of volunteers who trained runners for months,” what does the writer suggest about “publicity”?

options.label: A
options.text: It harms the volunteers' work.

options.label: B
options.text: It is the main goal of the race.

options.label: C
options.text: It matters less than real effort.

options.label: D
options.text: It is the same as success.

partB.stem: Which phrase best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “for months”

options.label: B
options.text: “The charity race”

options.label: C
options.text: “got wide publicity”

options.label: D
options.text: “its true achievement was the quiet work”

questions.why: The word but shows the writer values the quiet work more than the attention.

questions.stem: The Latin root “integer” means “whole.” Which TWO meanings show how “integrity” connects to this root? Choose two.
options: having many fans on social media
being famous across the whole country
having actions that match one's values
being whole and complete in character
questions.why: A person with integrity is 'whole': words and actions agree.

questions.stem: Some fans wondered whether the star's charity visit showed ____ kindness or was just a way to gain attention.
questions.why: Genuine kindness is sincere, the opposite of acting for attention.

questions.stem: Put the sentences in order so the paragraph about why fans “idolize” stars makes sense.
sequence: Many teenagers idolize famous athletes.
They see only the wins shown on television.
They rarely see the years of hard training.
Learning about that effort helps fans admire the work, not just the fame.
questions.why: The paragraph states an idea, explains it, then concludes.

questions.stem: True or false: Calling a singer a “celebrity” is about fame, while calling a firefighter a hero is about brave actions.
questions.why: Celebrity means fame, which does not always include heroism.

questions.stem: “The school guard was devoted to his work; he arrived before sunrise every day for thirty years.” What does “devoted” mean?
questions.why: Devoted means giving great loyalty and care.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “ordinary,” “humble,” “recognition,” and “devoted.”

pairs.right: praise or notice for something done

questions.why: These words describe people and how others see them.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The small spider on the wall went unnoticed by everyone in the classroom,” the word “unnoticed” means not seen.
questions.why: Unnoticed means nobody saw or paid attention to it.

questions.stem: On most days, the walk to school is ____: the same street, the same shops, the same baker waving hello.
questions.why: Ordinary means usual and everyday.

questions.stem: Does each person show a “humble” attitude or a boastful attitude?

rows.text: a champion who thanks her coach and teammates
a student who tells everyone he is the smartest
a chef who says he is still learning
a player who shows off his medals at every chance

questions.why: Humble people do not brag.

questions.stem: “We appreciate the bus driver who drives us safely through Riyadh traffic each day.” Which word means the same as “appreciate”?
questions.why: To appreciate someone is to value them and be thankful.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe something being “overlooked”? Choose two.
options: The small mistake in the bill was missed by the cashier.
Everyone praised Majed's drawing at the art show.
The judges studied each project very carefully.
The teacher forgot to read Dana's answer, even though it was correct.
questions.why: Overlooked means missed or not given attention.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “recognition,” “significance,” or “devoted” in it.

pairs.left: The nurse received recognition for her care.
The date has great significance for our family.
He is devoted to caring for his garden.

questions.why: Each meaning fits the word in its sentence.

questions.stem: The scientist received an award in ____ of her work on desert plants.
questions.why: 'In recognition of' means as praise for.

questions.stem: True or false: Something with great significance is unimportant and easy to forget.
questions.why: Significance means importance.

questions.stem: “The quiet gardener's work often went unnoticed. People admired the flowers but never saw who planted them at dawn.” Which clue best helps you understand “unnoticed”?
questions.why: Never being seen explains unnoticed.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “ordinary”?

rows.text: common
everyday
unusual
remarkable

questions.why: Ordinary means common, so unusual and remarkable are opposites.

questions.stem: The class wrote cards to show their ____ for the school's cleaning staff.
questions.why: After 'their' we need the noun appreciation.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about an old well uses the wrong form of “significance”?
questions.why: After 'very' we need the adjective significant.

questions.stem: True or false: “The player stayed humble by bragging about every goal he scored” uses “humble” correctly.
questions.why: Bragging is the opposite of being humble.

questions.stem: Which word is the best antonym of “humble”?
questions.why: Humble means not proud; arrogant means too proud.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are closest in meaning to “overlooked”? Choose two.
questions.why: Overlooked means not noticed or ignored.

questions.stem: Put the sentences in order to show how an “overlooked” worker finally received recognition.
sequence: For years, Abu Salem quietly fixed broken desks at the school.
Few students noticed, so his work was often overlooked.
One day, the students learned how many desks he had repaired.
They gave him a certificate in recognition of his service.
questions.why: The events move from quiet work to finally being thanked.

questions.stem: Match each form of “devoted” with its part of speech.
questions.why: Suffixes change the part of speech.

questions.stem: Even though few people knew his name, the fisherman in Jizan was ____ to teaching young boys how to swim safely.
questions.why: Devoted to means giving time and love to something.

questions.stem: Which word best suggests that a person's work should have been noticed but was missed?
questions.why: Overlooked suggests someone failed to give deserved attention.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: proud is to humble as famous is to ____.
questions.why: Proud and humble are opposites; so are famous and unnoticed.

questions.stem: Which sentence in this paragraph about a school librarian misuses a vocabulary word (devoted, significance, appreciate, overlooked)?
segments: The school librarian is devoted to her students.
She stays late to help them find the right books.
Her work is humble, but it has great significance.
Many students appreciate her, so her help is overlooked.
questions.correction: Many students appreciate her, so her help is not overlooked.
questions.why: If students appreciate her, her help is noticed, not overlooked.

questions.stem: In “Our hotel room in Taif overlooked the green valley,” what does “overlooked” mean?
questions.why: Overlook can also mean to look down on a place from above.

questions.stem: Does each sentence use “overlook” to mean “fail to notice” or “have a view of”?

rows.text: Do not overlook the small print on the form.
The old fort overlooks the sea.
The judge overlooked one entry by mistake.
Our balcony overlooks the park.

questions.why: Overlook is a word with two different meanings.

questions.stem: In “The award brought recognition to the old potter, but he only smiled and said that the clay deserved the praise,” what does the potter's answer show about him?

partA.stem: In “The award brought recognition to the old potter, but he only smiled and said that the clay deserved the praise,” what does the potter's answer show about him?

options.label: A
options.text: He is unhappy.

options.label: B
options.text: He is boastful.

options.label: C
options.text: He is humble.

options.label: D

partB.stem: Which phrase best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A

options.label: C
options.text: “he only smiled”

options.label: D
options.text: “brought recognition to the old potter”

questions.why: Giving credit to the clay shows he does not want praise for himself.

questions.stem: The prefix “un-” means “not.” Which TWO words use “un-” the same way as “unnoticed”? Choose two.
questions.why: In unseen and unknown, un- means not; in under and uncle it is not a prefix.

questions.stem: The day oil was first found at Dammam has great ____ in Saudi Arabia's history.
questions.why: Significance means importance.

questions.stem: Put the sentences in order so the paragraph about why we should “appreciate” ordinary people makes sense.
sequence: Famous people often get most of our attention.
Yet ordinary people, like bakers and bus drivers, keep our days running.
Their work is easy to take for granted.
That is why we should take time to appreciate them.
questions.why: The paragraph moves from a contrast to a conclusion.

questions.stem: True or false: “Unnoticed” simply means not seen, while “overlooked” often suggests that someone should have paid attention.
questions.why: Overlooked carries a sense of a mistake or unfairness.

questions.stem: “The firefighter showed great courage when he ran into the burning building to save a cat.” What does “courage” mean?
options: fear of being in the dark
questions.why: Courage is bravery in a dangerous or hard situation.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “courage,” “sacrifice,” “compassion,” and “criteria.”
questions.why: These words help describe and judge heroes.

questions.stem: True or false: In “A selfless volunteer gave her weekends to help at the animal shelter,” the word “selfless” means caring more about others than oneself.
questions.why: Selfless people put others' needs first.

questions.stem: The ____ lifeguard swam through rough waves at a Jeddah beach to rescue a struggling swimmer.
questions.why: Valiant means very brave.

questions.stem: Does each action show “compassion” or not?

rows.text: comforting a crying younger child
laughing at someone who tripped
visiting a sick neighbor with soup
ignoring a classmate who needs help

questions.why: Compassion is caring about others who suffer.

questions.stem: “Hind showed perseverance; she practiced the hard math problems every day until she could solve them.” Which word means the same as “perseverance”?
questions.why: Perseverance means continuing until you succeed.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences show a “sacrifice”? Choose two.
options: Saad ate his favorite dessert after dinner.
Noor bought a new game for herself at the mall.
Ali gave up his football match to help his father at the shop.
Maha spent her savings on medicine for her sick cat.
questions.why: A sacrifice means giving up something you value.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “distinguish,” “criteria,” or “valiant” in it.

pairs.left: Can you distinguish a falcon from a hawk?
The judges used three criteria to score projects.
The valiant guard stood firm in the storm.

questions.why: Each meaning fits the word's sentence.

questions.stem: Twins can look so alike that even their teacher cannot ____ one from the other.
questions.why: To distinguish is to tell things apart.

questions.stem: True or false: A person with no compassion feels sorry for people who are suffering.
questions.why: Compassion is that feeling of care; without it, a person does not feel sorry.

questions.stem: “The coach listed the criteria for joining the team: good attendance, teamwork, and a positive attitude.” Which clue best helps you understand “criteria”?
questions.why: The list shows the standards a player must meet.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “courage”?

rows.text: bravery
boldness
cowardice
fear

questions.why: Courage means bravery, so cowardice and fear are opposites.

questions.stem: The ____ young girl spoke up when she saw a classmate being teased.
questions.why: The adjective courageous describes the girl.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about a doctor uses the wrong form of “compassion”?
questions.why: The adjective compassionate describes the voice.

questions.stem: True or false: “The team showed perseverance by quitting after the first loss” uses “perseverance” correctly.
questions.why: Perseverance means continuing, not quitting.

questions.stem: Which word is the best antonym of “selfless”?
questions.why: Selfless means caring for others; selfish is its opposite.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are closest in meaning to “valiant”? Choose two.
questions.why: Valiant means brave and heroic.

questions.stem: Put the sentences in order to show a climber's “perseverance.”
sequence: Turki set a goal to climb Jabal Sawda, one of the highest peaks in Saudi Arabia.
On his first try, he turned back because of heavy fog.
He trained for three more months to build his strength.
On his second try, he reached the top and watched the sunrise.
questions.why: Perseverance means trying again after a setback.

questions.stem: Match each form of “distinguish” with its meaning.
questions.why: Suffixes change both the form and the meaning.

questions.stem: The judges' main ____ for the science fair were creativity, accuracy, and clear explanation.
questions.why: Criteria are the standards used to judge.

questions.stem: Which word suggests the greatest bravery, often in a battle or a serious emergency?
questions.why: Valiant suggests heroic bravery in great danger.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: generous is to selfish as compassion is to ____.
questions.why: Generous and selfish are opposites; so are compassion and cruelty.

questions.stem: Which sentence in this paragraph about a flood rescue misuses a vocabulary word (courage, sacrifice, compassion, distinguish)?
segments: During the flood, a teenager showed courage by guiding neighbors to safety.
He made a sacrifice by leaving his own belongings behind.
His compassion for the elderly was clear as he carried their bags.
People could hardly distinguish his valiant actions, so they gave him an award.
questions.correction: People admired his valiant actions, so they gave him an award.
questions.why: Distinguish means tell apart; the sentence needs admired.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “criterion” and “criteria” correctly?
options: “One criterion are honesty; the other criteria is courage and kindness.”
“One criterion is honesty; the other criteria are courage and kindness.”
“One criterias is honesty; the other criterion is courage and kindness.”
“One criteria is honesty; the other criterion are courage and kindness.”
questions.why: Criterion is singular and criteria is plural.

questions.stem: Does each sentence describe a hero by “courage” or by “compassion”?

rows.text: He climbed a smoky stairway to reach trapped children.
She sat for hours with a lonely patient.
He drove into a sandstorm to bring water to stranded travelers.
She shared her lunch with a hungry classmate every day.

questions.why: Courage faces danger; compassion shows care.

questions.stem: In “Some say heroes must be famous, but the true test is whether a person acts selflessly when no one is watching,” which criteria for a hero does the writer support?

partA.stem: In “Some say heroes must be famous, but the true test is whether a person acts selflessly when no one is watching,” which criteria for a hero does the writer support?

options.label: A
options.text: winning many awards and prizes

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “persistent” with a negative meaning?

Her persistent practice made her a strong swimmer.
The persistent volunteers cleaned the whole beach.
A persistent cough kept Bilal awake all week.

questions.stem: Choose the best word for the blank: “Training a young horse takes patience. The rider must ____ many bumpy, disappointing days before the first smooth gallop finally arrives.”
questions.why: To get through hard days patiently is to tolerate them.

questions.stem: Put these feelings in order from mildest to strongest, showing where “frustration” fits.
sequence: mild annoyance
irritation
frustration
fury
questions.why: Frustration is stronger than irritation but weaker than fury.

questions.stem: Sort these forms of “tolerate” and “comprehend” into nouns and adjectives.

comprehensible
intolerable
comprehension

questions.why: The suffixes -ance and -sion make nouns; -ible and -able make adjectives.

questions.why: Praise needs a positive word; obstinate sounds negative, while persistent sounds admiring.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Reem aspires to become an astronaut, so she studies science every night.” What does “aspire” mean?
options: to travel far away from home
to forget about a plan quickly
questions.why: To aspire is to hope and work toward a goal.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “diligent,” “cultivate,” “priority,” and “integrity.”

pairs.right: the most important thing to do first
being honest and doing what is right

questions.why: These words describe good habits and character.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Before playing, Majed's first priority is finishing his homework,” the word “priority” means the thing he does last.
questions.why: A priority is the most important thing, done first.

questions.stem: The farmer will ____ tomatoes and peppers in the greenhouse near Al-Kharj this winter.
questions.why: To cultivate plants is to grow them.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “reflect,” “superficial,” or “conscientious” in it.

pairs.left: After the game, the team sat quietly to reflect on their mistakes.
The scratch on the car was only superficial.
A conscientious nurse checks every chart twice.

questions.why: Each meaning fits the word in its sentence.

questions.stem: Does each action show “integrity” or not?

rows.text: Lina returned the extra change the shopkeeper gave her by mistake.
Turki copied his friend's answers and said they were his own.
Sami told the coach he had touched the ball last, even though it cost a point.
Dana broke a vase and blamed her little cousin.

questions.why: Integrity means being honest even when no one is checking.

questions.stem: “The diligent beekeeper checked every hive each morning and wrote careful notes.” Which word means the same as “diligent”?
questions.why: Checking every hive daily and keeping notes shows a diligent, hard-working person.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe a “conscientious” student? Choose two.
options: Rania often leaves her library books at home on return day.
Yousef rechecks every math answer before he hands in his test.
Hamad rushes through his work so he can play outside sooner.
Amal writes each assignment in her planner so she never misses one.
questions.why: A conscientious person is careful and responsible.

questions.stem: The calm lake was so still that it seemed to ____ the mountains perfectly, like a mirror.
questions.why: To reflect can mean to show an image, as a mirror or water does.

questions.stem: “His friendship with Adel was superficial; they only talked about the weather and never shared real thoughts.” What does “superficial” mean?
questions.why: Talking only about the weather shows a shallow, superficial friendship.

questions.stem: “Mariam wants to cultivate a love of reading in her younger sisters. Every night she reads them a new book and lets them pick the next one.” What does “cultivate” mean in these sentences?
questions.why: Here cultivate means to help a quality grow, not to farm.

questions.stem: Mr. Nasser praised the class for their ____ when they finished the long science report carefully and on time.
questions.why: After “their,” a noun is needed: diligence.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Kareem aspires to be a pilot,” the word “aspires” could be replaced with “hopes and works.”
questions.why: To aspire is to hope for and work toward something.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “superficial”?

rows.text: shallow
surface-level
profound
thorough

questions.why: Superficial means shallow; profound and thorough mean deep.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are antonyms of “diligent”? Choose two.
questions.why: Lazy and careless are opposites of diligent.

questions.why: “Thinking about” shows that reflect means to think carefully.

questions.stem: With exams, football practice, and a cousin's visit all on Thursday, Lama had to decide which one was her top ____.
questions.why: When choosing what matters most, you choose your priority.

questions.stem: Sort these forms of “reflect” and “aspire” by part of speech.

rows.text: reflection
aspire
aspiration
reflective
aspiring

questions.why: Suffixes -tion and -ation form nouns; -ive and -ing (before a noun) can form adjectives.

questions.stem: True or false: A conscientious worker leaves tasks half-finished because details do not matter to her.
questions.why: A conscientious worker cares about details and finishes tasks well.

questions.stem: “The museum guide gave only a ____ tour, so the visitors learned little about the ancient town of Al-Ula.” Which word best fits the blank?
questions.why: A superficial tour stays on the surface, so visitors learn little.

questions.stem: Which word has the most positive connotation for someone who works carefully and follows their conscience?
questions.why: Conscientious praises careful, responsible work; fussy and picky sound critical.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph about “integrity” and “aspire”: “Hessa aspires to become a judge. She knows a judge needs integrity, so she always tells the truth. Last week she showed her superficial honesty by admitting she had broken a classmate's ruler.”

She knows a judge needs integrity,

Last week she showed her superficial honesty
by admitting she had broken a classmate's ruler.
questions.correction: Last week she showed her deep honesty
questions.why: Admitting a mistake shows real, deep honesty, not superficial honesty.

questions.stem: “Reflect” has more than one meaning. Which TWO sentences use “reflect” to mean “show or be a sign of”? Choose two.
options: Snow can reflect sunlight and hurt your eyes.
Please reflect on your choices before you answer.
Your neat handwriting reflects how carefully you work.
The team's trophies reflect years of hard training.
questions.why: Reflect can mean to throw back light, to think, or to show a sign of something.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: careless is to diligent as shallow is to ____.
questions.why: Careless is the opposite of diligent, and shallow is the opposite of profound.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses “cultivate” correctly.

segments.text: Rashed hopes to cultivate patience by practicing calligraphy.
The storm will cultivate the old palm tree tonight.
Please cultivate the light when you leave the room.
The runner cultivated across the finish line first.

questions.why: Cultivate can mean to develop a quality, such as patience.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “priority” correctly?
options: He walked slowly with great priority.
She painted the wall a bright priority.
Safety is the first priority when building a bridge.
The priority of the cake was soft and sweet.
questions.why: A priority is something placed first in importance.

questions.stem: Choose the best word for the blank: “Hamza's grandfather gave him advice. He said, ‘Do not judge people by their clothes. Looks are ____; what matters is a person's honesty and kindness.’”
questions.why: Looks are only on the surface, which is what superficial means.

questions.stem: Put these words in order from weakest to strongest wish, showing where “aspire” fits.
sequence: wonder about
hope for
aspire to
be determined to achieve
questions.why: Aspiring is stronger than hoping, but being determined to achieve something is stronger still.

questions.stem: The prefix “super-” means “above” or “over.” Which words use “super-” with that meaning, like “superficial” (on the surface)?

superficial
supper
supply

columns.text: Uses “super-” to mean above or over

questions.why: Supervise means to watch over; supper and supply do not use the prefix “super-.”

questions.stem: Which part misuses a word? “The conscientious volunteers will reflect the garden, plant new seeds, and cultivate the young trees with care.”

questions.why: Reflect means to think or show back; it does not describe garden work.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “The courageous lifeguard swam through high waves to reach the swimmer.” What does “courageous” mean?
questions.why: Swimming through high waves to help someone is brave.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “prejudice,” “restraint,” “adversity,” and “retaliate.”

pairs.right: an unfair opinion formed without knowing the facts
control over your actions or feelings
to hit back or get revenge

questions.why: These words describe how people face unfair treatment.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Even when the crowd laughed at him, the old poet kept his dignity,” the word “dignity” means calm self-respect.
questions.why: Dignity is calm self-respect, even when others are rude.

questions.stem: In some places long ago, ____ laws kept people of different races in separate schools and buses.
questions.why: Segregation means keeping groups apart by law or custom.

questions.stem: “The older boys tried to provoke Fahad by calling him names, but he walked away.” What does “provoke” mean?

to teach someone a new board game
to help someone feel calm again
to make someone angry on purpose
questions.why: Calling names to upset someone is trying to provoke them.

questions.stem: Does each person show “restraint” or not?

rows.text: Saud wanted to shout at the referee but stayed silent.
Muna ate the whole box of dates before dinner.
Waleed slammed the door when he lost the game.
The goalkeeper kept calm after a rough tackle.

questions.why: Restraint means holding back when you want to react.

questions.stem: “Many farmers faced adversity when the drought dried up their wells.” Which word means the same as “adversity”?
questions.why: A drought brings hardship, which is adversity.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences show someone who decided not to “retaliate”? Choose two.
options: When a player pushed him, Rayan pushed back even harder.
After his sister hid his shoes, Ammar hid her bag to get even.
After her brother took her pencil, Joud asked politely for it back.
When a player pushed him, Zaid simply got up and kept playing.
questions.why: To retaliate is to strike back; staying calm means not retaliating.

questions.stem: Judging a new classmate before even speaking to him is a kind of ____.
questions.why: Prejudice is judging someone unfairly before knowing them.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “courageous,” “dignity,” or “segregation” in it.

pairs.left: The courageous girl spoke up for the new student.
He accepted the loss with dignity and shook hands.
Segregation kept the two groups in separate neighborhoods.

questions.why: Each meaning matches its sentence.

questions.stem: “The champion boxer showed great restraint. When his opponent shouted insults, he did not answer; he simply nodded and waited for the bell.” Which clue best helps the reader understand “restraint”?
questions.why: Not answering insults shows self-control, or restraint.

questions.stem: The nurse's ____ act of running into the smoky building saved two children.
questions.why: Before the noun “act,” an adjective is needed: courageous.

questions.stem: True or false: A person who treats everyone fairly, no matter where they come from, is showing prejudice.
questions.why: Prejudice is unfair judgment, so fair treatment is the opposite.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “adversity”?

rows.text: misfortune
hardship
good fortune
ease

questions.why: Adversity means hardship; ease and good fortune are its opposites.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are synonyms of “provoke”? Choose two.
questions.why: To provoke is to anger or irritate; soothe and calm are opposites.

questions.stem: “The scientist faced many years of adversity. Her lab burned down, and she lost her funding. Still, she never stopped her research.” What does “adversity” mean in these sentences?
questions.why: A burned lab and lost funding are serious troubles, or adversity.

questions.why: “Get back at” someone means to strike back, or retaliate.

provoke

questions.why: The suffix -tion makes nouns; -ive and -ed can make adjectives.

questions.stem: Which word best describes someone who stays calm when insulted, rather than someone who is just quiet?
questions.why: Restrained means actively holding back a reaction, not just being quiet.

The crowd waited to see if he would retaliate.
and calmly walked back to his position.
questions.why: Calmly walking away shows restraint, not prejudice.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “provoke” to mean “cause or bring about,” not “make someone angry”? Choose two.
options: His teasing provoked his little brother to tears of anger.
Do not provoke the guard dog by poking the fence.
The new speed bump provoked complaints from drivers.
The surprising news provoked a long discussion in class.
questions.why: Provoke can mean to cause a reaction, not only to anger someone.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: fear is to courageous as pride is to ____.
questions.why: A courageous person overcomes fear; a humble person sets aside pride.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses “segregation” correctly.

questions.why: Segregation is the separation of groups of people.

questions.stem: Which word is the most precise choice in this sentence: “Refusing to let a girl join the robotics team just because she is a girl is an example of ____.”
questions.why: Prejudice names an unfair judgment about a whole group.

questions.stem: Choose the best word for the blank: “The first female pilots faced many doubts. People said they could not fly well. With ____ and skill, the pilots proved them wrong and earned respect.”
questions.why: Proving critics wrong with calm self-respect shows dignity.

reply politely
argue loudly

questions.why: Propel, project, and provoke push something forward or out.

questions.why: Segregation is a noun and does not fit; a calm, dignified hero would forgive.

able to speak easily and well
questions.why: A fluent speaker uses a language easily and smoothly.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “isolated,” “translate,” “mimic,” and “hesitant.”

to copy how someone speaks or acts
slow to act because you are unsure

questions.why: These words describe learning a new language.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Nada felt embarrassed when she tripped in front of the whole class,” the word “embarrassed” means proud and happy.
questions.why: Embarrassed means feeling awkward or ashamed in front of others.

questions.stem: Rami speaks Arabic at home and English at school, so he is ____.
questions.why: Bilingual means able to use two languages.

questions.stem: “The small village was isolated; the nearest town was a three-hour drive across the desert.” What does “isolated” mean?

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences show someone being “hesitant”? Choose two.

Ziyad ran straight to the front to try the new ride first.
Faris stood at the edge of the pool for a long time before jumping in.

questions.why: Hesitant people pause because they are unsure.

questions.stem: Our guide in Cairo helped us ____ the menu from Arabic into English for our visitors.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “fluent,” “anxious,” or “bilingual” in it.

He felt anxious before his first day at a new school.
The bilingual sign was written in Arabic and English.

questions.why: Each meaning fits the word in its sentence.

questions.stem: “Laila felt isolated at her new school in London. She ate lunch alone and had no one to talk to during break.” Which clue best helps the reader understand “isolated”?

questions.stem: The comedian's perfect ____ of famous voices made the audience laugh.
questions.why: After “perfect,” a noun is needed, and mimicry is the noun form.

questions.stem: True or false: A person who is fluent in English must stop and search for almost every word.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “anxious”?

rows.text: worried
uneasy
relaxed
confident

questions.why: Anxious means worried; relaxed and confident are its opposites.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are antonyms of “hesitant”? Choose two.
questions.why: Eager and decisive people act without pausing.

questions.stem: “Ahmed's face turned red when he realized he had called his teacher ‘Mom.’ He wanted to hide under his desk.” Which word best describes how Ahmed felt?
questions.why: A red face and wanting to hide show embarrassment.

options.label: A

translate

questions.stem: Sultan felt ____ when his phone rang loudly in the middle of the quiet library.

questions.stem: Which word describes the strongest feeling of shame in front of others?
questions.why: Humiliated is stronger than embarrassed, uncomfortable, or awkward.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph about “fluent” and “translate”: “When my grandmother visits the doctor, I translate for her. She speaks only Arabic, but I am fluent in English too. Sometimes I feel hesitant about my skill, because the doctor smiles and thanks me.”

questions.why: A doctor's thanks makes someone proud, not hesitant.

questions.stem: The prefix “bi-” means “two.” Which TWO words use “bi-” to mean “two,” like “bilingual”? Choose two.
questions.why: Bicycle has two wheels, and biweekly means every two weeks.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: speaker is to fluent as dancer is to ____.
questions.why: A skilled speaker is fluent; a skilled dancer is graceful.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses “mimic” correctly.

questions.why: To mimic is to copy someone's sounds or actions.

questions.stem: Which word is the most precise choice for this sentence: “The scientist working alone on an island station for six months felt completely ____.”
questions.why: Isolated describes being cut off from others by distance.

questions.stem: Choose the best word for the blank: “On her first day in Japan, Rawan could read only a few signs. She felt ____ about asking for directions, so she walked in circles for an hour.”

questions.stem: Put these feelings in order from mildest to strongest, showing where “anxious” fits.
sequence: a little uneasy
anxious
very frightened
panicked
questions.why: Anxious is stronger than uneasy but weaker than frightened or panicked.

questions.stem: The prefix “trans-” means “across.” Which words use “trans-” with this meaning, like “translate” (to carry across into another language)?

transfer
translate
track

questions.stem: “Loose rocks on the mountain road are a hazard for drivers.” What is a hazard?

a thing that can cause harm
a sign that shows drivers the way
a place for travelers to rest
questions.why: A hazard is something dangerous that can hurt people, like falling rocks.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The river will alter its path after the flood,” the word “alter” means the river will stay exactly the same.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about a valley with the meaning of its multiple-meaning word: “bank,” “drop,” and “face.”

questions.stem: Under which heading would a reader find out how rock pieces are carried away?
