questions.why: Rock is broken first (weathering), then moved (erosion), then dropped (deposition).

questions.stem: What does the diagram in “How Wind and Water Change Rock” show? Choose two.
options: a tall rock breaking into small pieces
people building a wall to stop the wind
wind and a river carrying pieces to a beach
a volcano erupting near a small town
questions.why: The diagram shows the rock breaking and the pieces being carried to a beach.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “severe” correctly?
options: The severe breeze gently cooled the children at the park.
Ali was severe happy to see his cousins after school.
The kitten was so severe that it purred on my lap.
The severe sandstorm closed the airport for a whole day.
questions.why: Severe means very strong or serious, like a sandstorm that closes an airport.

questions.stem: Scientists watch volcanoes closely because eruptions can be ____; they sometimes happen with very little warning.
questions.why: Unpredictable means no one can know ahead of time when it will happen.

questions.stem: In each sentence about water in the land, does “spring” mean a place where water comes out of the ground or a season of the year?

rows.text: Travelers filled their bottles at the cool spring.
Wildflowers bloom in the desert in spring.
The oasis gets its water from an underground spring.
Heavy rain sometimes falls in early spring.

questions.why: The other words in the sentence show which meaning of “spring” is used.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about an earthquake drill has an error with a key word?
segments: the students learned that a building can collapsed
so they practiced hiding under their desks.
questions.correction: the students learned that a building can collapse
questions.why: After “can,” use the base form of the verb: “can collapse.”

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe a crisis? Choose two.
options: The class plans a trip to the science museum next week.
A flood cuts off the only road to a village, and food runs low.
A family plants new palm trees in their garden after school.
A fire spreads through a market, and hundreds of people must leave fast.
questions.why: A crisis is a time of great danger or trouble that needs action right away.

questions.stem: Match each key word from a news report about a flood with a detail that shows it: “destruction,” “substantial,” “crisis,” “hazard.”

pairs.right: Houses and roads are broken and ruined.
The water rose by almost two meters.
Families need help right away to stay safe.
A fallen power line lies in the water.

questions.why: Each detail is an example of what the key word means.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentences. “The weather in the mountains is unpredictable. A sunny morning can turn into a storm by noon.” What does “unpredictable” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentences. “The weather in the mountains is unpredictable. A sunny morning can turn into a storm by noon.” What does “unpredictable” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: always the same from day to day

options.label: B
options.text: easy to see from far away

options.label: C
options.text: very hot and dry all the time

options.label: D
options.text: not able to be known ahead of time

partB.stem: Part B: Which words best help the reader understand “unpredictable”?

options.label: A
options.text: The weather

options.label: B
options.text: can turn into a storm by noon

options.label: C
options.text: A sunny morning

options.label: D
options.text: in the mountains

questions.why: A sunny morning that suddenly becomes a storm shows the weather cannot be known ahead of time.

questions.stem: Which word is the closest synonym of “alter”?
questions.why: To alter something is to change it.

questions.stem: The earthquake caused ____ damage; more than half of the buildings in the town had to be rebuilt.
questions.why: Substantial means large in amount, like damage to half of a town.

questions.stem: Put the steps a town follows to prepare for a flood hazard in a sensible order.
sequence: Scientists measure how fast the river is rising.
Leaders warn families that a flood may come.
Families move to higher ground with emergency bags.
Workers clean up after the water goes down.
questions.why: Monitoring comes first, then warnings, then moving to safety, then cleanup.

questions.stem: Part A: How is creep different from a landslide?

partA.stem: Part A: How is creep different from a landslide?

options.label: A
options.text: Creep moves soil slowly over years, but a landslide moves it in minutes.

options.label: B
options.text: Creep destroys homes quickly, but a landslide only makes posts lean.

options.label: C
options.text: Creep is caused by gravity, but a landslide is caused by strong wind.

options.label: D
options.text: Creep happens on flat land, but a landslide happens on steep hills.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Suddenly, an entire hillside can slide down in less than a minute.

options.label: B
options.text: Scientists call this slow movement creep.

options.label: C
options.text: Roads may collapse, and homes can be buried.

options.label: D
options.text: Both creep and landslides are caused by gravity pulling soil and rock downhill.

questions.why: The landslide happens in less than a minute, while creep takes years.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Two Kinds of Change on a Mountain” that tell how creep and landslides are alike.

segments.text: Both creep and landslides are caused by gravity pulling soil and rock downhill.
A landslide is very different.
Both are more likely on steep slopes with few plants to hold the ground in place.
Families have years to notice the problem and repair their land.

questions.why: Words like “both” signal how two things are alike.

questions.stem: Why did the author include the heading “How They Are Alike”?
options: to introduce a list of ways that families can repair their land
to signal that the section explains what the two changes share
to explain how scientists chose the name for slow movement
to show that the section tells which change is more dangerous
questions.why: Headings tell readers what a section is about, here the ways creep and landslides are alike.

questions.stem: In “Two Kinds of Change on a Mountain,” does each detail describe creep, a landslide, or both?

rows.text: Fence posts begin to lean.
A hillside slides down in less than a minute.
Gravity pulls soil downhill.
Roads may collapse.

questions.why: Sorting details by topic helps readers compare and contrast.

questions.stem: What information does the diagram add to the passage?
options: It shows the time each change takes, side by side.
It lists the steps for repairing a leaning wall.
It tells where in Saudi Arabia creep usually happens.
It explains why plants help hold the soil in place.
questions.why: The labels “years” and “minutes” compare how long each change takes.

questions.stem: The word “rock” has more than one meaning. Which TWO sentences use “rock” as a verb meaning to move back and forth? Choose two.
options: The small earthquake made the lamps rock on the tables.
Strong waves rock the fishing boats in the harbor.
A huge rock rolled onto the mountain road.
Weathering slowly breaks the rock into sand.
questions.why: When “rock” is an action, it means to move back and forth; as a noun it means stone.

questions.stem: Find the misused key word in this short report about a sandstorm.
segments: A severe sandstorm swept across the city.
Strong winds caused substantial damage to signs.
Drivers faced a hazard because they could not see.
The storm was so unpredictable that everyone knew exactly when it would arrive.
questions.correction: The storm was so unpredictable that no one knew when it would arrive.
questions.why: Something unpredictable cannot be known ahead of time, so no one knew when it would come.

questions.stem: The city's quick emergency plan turned a possible ____ into a small problem, and no one was hurt when the dam began to leak.
questions.why: A crisis is a dangerous situation; good planning kept it small.

questions.stem: True or false: “Destruction” and “collapse” both describe things breaking down, but “destruction” is a noun and “collapse” can be used as a verb.
questions.why: Destruction names the damage (noun); collapse can name the action of falling (verb).

questions.stem: Which sentence best contrasts weathering with a volcanic eruption?
options: Weathering is caused by lava cooling, while an eruption is caused by wind and rain.
Weathering and eruptions both happen deep inside the Earth and slowly turn rock into lava.
An eruption is a kind of weathering that happens only near the ocean shore.
Weathering changes rock little by little, while an eruption can alter land in hours.
questions.why: A contrast shows a difference: weathering is slow, but an eruption is fast.

questions.stem: “Sara hesitated before she raised her hand to answer.” What did Sara do?
options: She raised her hand quickly without thinking.
She left the classroom to find her teacher.
She waited a moment because she was unsure.
She shouted the answer across the room.
questions.why: To hesitate is to pause because you are not sure.

questions.stem: When Ahmad saw his sister working hard on her science project, it gave him the ____ to start his own.
questions.why: Inspiration is something that makes you want to do or create something.

questions.stem: Match each idiom about friends and feelings with its meaning: “break the ice,” “butterflies in my stomach,” “see eye to eye.”

pairs.right: start talking in a friendly way

questions.why: An idiom has a meaning different from its exact words.

questions.stem: True or false: If Noor's mother advises her about the talent show, she gives Noor ideas about what to do.
questions.why: To advise someone is to give them helpful ideas or suggestions.

questions.stem: Is each problem a character might face in a school story an internal conflict or an external conflict?

rows.text: Huda cannot decide whether to tell her friend the truth.
A storm cancels the school trip.
Two brothers argue over who gets the bike.
Faris is afraid to sing in front of the class.

questions.why: An internal conflict happens inside a character's mind; an external conflict is with someone or something else.

questions.stem: What is Sara's main conflict in “Lina's Plan”?
options: She cannot find the clay she needs for her camel.
She wants her own project but is afraid to tell Lina.
She and Lina disagree about which colors to use.
She is angry that Ms. Huda cancelled the art exhibition.
questions.why: Sara's problem is inside her: she wants something different but fears hurting Lina.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Lina's Plan” shows that Sara is worried about her friend's feelings?

segments.text: At home, she stared at the lump of clay sitting on her desk, and her stomach felt tight.
If she told Lina the truth, would her friend feel disappointed?
Sara opened her mouth, then closed it again.
The next morning, Lina proudly waved a sketch of the picture in the air.

questions.why: Sara's question shows she is afraid Lina will be disappointed.

questions.stem: Part A: What will Sara most likely do next?

partA.stem: Part A: What will Sara most likely do next?

options.label: A
options.text: ask Ms. Huda to choose a project for her

options.label: B
options.text: paint the sky in Lina's picture without a word

options.label: C
options.text: show Lina the clay camel and explain her idea

options.label: D
options.text: throw the clay camel away and forget about it

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Lina and Sara had been best friends since the first day of first grade.

options.label: B
options.text: She held her clay camel behind her back and took a deep breath.

options.label: C
options.text: When Ms. Huda announced the school art exhibition, Lina immediately clapped her hands.

options.label: D
options.text: “You can paint the sky,” she announced.

questions.why: Taking a deep breath while holding the camel suggests Sara is getting ready to speak up.

questions.stem: Put these events from “Lina's Plan” in order.
sequence: Ms. Huda announces the school art exhibition.
Lina says they will paint one picture together.
Sara stares at her clay at home and feels worried.
Lina tells Sara she can paint the sky.
questions.why: Following the order of events helps readers understand the plot.

questions.stem: Which TWO details from “Lina's Plan” show that Lina makes decisions for both girls? Choose two.
options: Lina claps her hands at the news.
Lina has been Sara's friend since first grade.
Lina tells Sara that she can paint the sky.
Lina says she has already chosen the colors.
questions.why: Choosing the colors and Sara's part shows Lina deciding for both of them.

questions.stem: Majed felt ____ when he tripped on the stage and everyone laughed, but his friends helped him up and he finished his poem.
questions.why: Humiliated means very embarrassed in front of others.

questions.stem: Which idiom means “to feel too nervous to do something you planned”?
questions.why: To get cold feet is to become too nervous to go ahead with a plan.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about Khalid's costume in the school play has an error?
segments: The new costume was too tight,
questions.why: An adverb like “uncomfortably” describes how someone moves.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences show a character being accountable? Choose two.
options: Tala blames her little brother for the mess she made.
Omar forgets his homework and says the dog ate it.
Rana admits she broke the vase and offers to pay for it.
Bilal promised to bring snacks, so he packed them the night before.
questions.why: Being accountable means taking responsibility for what you do.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentences. “Basma desperately wanted to join the art club. She asked the teacher three times and even made a poster to show her skill.” What does “desperately” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentences. “Basma desperately wanted to join the art club. She asked the teacher three times and even made a poster to show her skill.” What does “desperately” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: in a slow, careful way

options.label: B
options.text: in a calm and quiet way

options.label: C
options.text: with a very strong need

options.label: D
options.text: without any interest

partB.stem: Part B: Which detail best helps the reader understand “desperately”?

options.label: A
options.text: She made something.

options.label: B
options.text: She wanted to join the art club.

options.label: C
options.text: She asked the teacher three times.

options.label: D
options.text: She talked to the teacher.

questions.why: Asking three times shows how strongly Basma wanted to join.

questions.stem: Match each clue from a story about a school contest with the most likely prediction.

pairs.left: Nasser practices his speech every night in front of a mirror.
pairs.right: He will speak well at the contest.

pairs.left: Reem hesitated when her friend asked to share the stage.
pairs.right: She feels unsure and may say no.

pairs.left: Hamad forgot to fix his broken guitar string.
pairs.right: He will have trouble during his song.

questions.why: Good predictions use clues about what characters say and do.

questions.stem: Does each sentence about a talent show use an idiom or only literal words?

rows.text: Dana was over the moon when she won.
Dana smiled when she won first place.
Yasir told his friend to break a leg before the show.
Yasir wished his friend good luck before the show.

questions.why: Idioms like “over the moon” do not mean exactly what the words say.

questions.stem: After his grandmother praised his drawings, Tamer's ____ grew, and he finally entered the art contest.
questions.why: Self-esteem is how much you believe in yourself.

questions.stem: Put these plot events about Zain and the poetry contest in order.
sequence: Zain writes a poem for the school poetry contest.
His friend Ali keeps telling him to change every line.
Zain decides to read the poem the way he wrote it.
The judges smile, and Zain and Ali shake hands after the show.
questions.why: A plot moves from the beginning to the conflict, the turning point, and the resolution.

questions.stem: True or false: A character who feels humiliated after a mistake on stage feels proud and happy about what happened.
questions.why: Humiliated means deeply embarrassed, not proud.

questions.stem: Part A: What does the idiom “caught between a rock and a hard place” mean as it is used in the story?

partA.stem: Part A: What does the idiom “caught between a rock and a hard place” mean as it is used in the story?

options.label: A
options.text: very excited about a new game

options.label: B
options.text: angry at a friend for a long time

options.label: C
options.text: stuck under a pile of heavy stones

options.label: D
options.text: facing two choices that both seem difficult

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Then he read the date again.

options.label: B
options.text: He loved chess, but playing football for the school had always been his dream.

options.label: C
options.text: The next morning, Yousef found Majed beside the school gate.

options.label: D
options.text: Finally, he knocked quietly on his grandfather's door.

questions.why: Yousef loves both chess and football, so either choice is hard.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe Yousef's internal conflict? Choose two.
options: He wants to try out for football but does not want to let Majed down.
Majed refuses to play chess with anyone else.
Coach Adel will not let him join the football team.
He worries that telling the truth will hurt his friendship.
questions.why: An internal conflict is a struggle inside a character's own mind.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Same Saturday” best helps the reader predict that Yousef will tell Majed the truth?

segments.text: “Tell Majed honestly how you feel,” Grandfather said gently.
The tryouts were on the same Saturday as the city chess tournament.
Majed, his partner on the chess team, was already making confident plans.
That night he could not sleep a wink.

questions.why: Grandfather's advice is a clue that Yousef will speak honestly.

questions.stem: What does the idiom “could not sleep a wink” show about Yousef?
options: He was too worried to rest.
He had a cold and kept coughing.
He was excited about the gold cup.
questions.why: Not sleeping a wink means not sleeping at all, which shows worry.

questions.stem: How does Grandfather's advice affect the plot?
options: It makes Yousef give up football and stay with chess.
It causes Majed to change the date of the tournament.
It helps Yousef choose to face the problem honestly.
It shows that Yousef is angry with his grandfather.
questions.why: The advice leads Yousef to the turning point: speaking from the heart.

questions.stem: Find the misused key word in this short paragraph about a spelling bee.
segments: Mariam hesitated before spelling the last word.
She remembered her teacher's advise to go slowly.
She spelled it correctly and won the trophy.
questions.correction: She remembered her teacher's advice to go slowly.
questions.why: “Advise” is the verb; “advice” is the noun that names the helpful idea.

questions.stem: Even though Nawaf felt nervous, he refused to let one mistake ruin his ____; he reminded himself of all the songs he had performed well.
questions.why: Remembering past successes protects a person's self-esteem.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses an idiom to show that a character is being honest about her feelings?
options: “I will paint the sky blue,” Huda told her friend.
“We should practice after school,” Huda told her friend.
“I need to get this off my chest,” Huda told her friend.
“The show starts at four o'clock,” Huda told her friend.
questions.why: To get something off your chest means to finally say what you have been feeling.

questions.stem: Which part of speech is each key word from a talent-show story: “inspiration,” “hesitated,” “desperately,” “uncomfortably,” “advise”?

rows.text: inspiration
hesitated
desperately
uncomfortably
advise

questions.why: Many adverbs end in -ly, and many nouns end in -tion.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Faisal was accountable for the team's lost ball, so he searched the field until he found it,” Faisal takes responsibility for the problem.
questions.why: An accountable person accepts responsibility and fixes the problem.

questions.stem: The students sold homemade cookies to raise ____ for a new water cooler at school.
questions.why: Funds are money collected for a purpose.

questions.stem: Match each word with a suffix to its meaning: “helpful,” “careless,” “seller.”
questions.why: The suffix -ful means full of, -less means without, and -er can mean a person who.

questions.stem: True or false: A compassionate shop owner who gives free meals to hungry workers cares about other people.
questions.why: Compassionate means caring about others and wanting to help them.

questions.stem: Which word has a suffix that means “able to be”?
questions.why: The suffix -able means able to be, so washable means able to be washed.

questions.stem: Is each sentence about a juice shop the central idea or a supporting detail?

rows.text: The juice shop helps its neighborhood in many ways.
It gives free juice to hospital workers on Fridays.
It pays students to work during the summer.

questions.why: The central idea is the big point; details are examples that support it.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of “Businesses Can Be Good Neighbors”?
options: Customers should only shop at big stores.
Bakeries should give all their bread away.
Older people need to learn to use computers.
Helping others can make a business stronger.
questions.why: The author says helping others makes a business stronger, and every section supports that.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Businesses Can Be Good Neighbors” best supports the idea that kindness helps a business earn customers?

segments.text: When customers see a shop helping others, they want to shop there again.
A computer shop offers free weekend classes for older people.
Many grandparents have learned to video call their families.
A business needs to earn money, but it can also help the people around it.

questions.why: This sentence links helping others to customers coming back.

questions.stem: Match each heading in “Businesses Can Be Good Neighbors” with the detail found under it.

pairs.right: A bakery gives extra bread to a food bank.
A computer shop offers free classes.
Customers want to shop there again.

questions.why: Headings tell what each section is about, so they help readers find details.

questions.stem: Part A: Which detail supports the claim that helping others is good for a community?

partA.stem: Part A: Which detail supports the claim that helping others is good for a community?

options.label: A
options.text: A computer shop sells many new laptops.

options.label: B
options.text: Customers shop at the same store each week.

options.label: C
options.text: A business needs to earn money to survive.

options.label: D
options.text: Families in need get fresh bread from a bakery.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: A business needs to earn money, but it can also help the people around it.

options.label: B
options.text: Kindness brings in new customers.

options.label: C
options.text: When customers see a shop helping others, they want to shop there again.

options.label: D
options.text: Families in need get fresh bread, and nothing goes to waste.

questions.why: The bread helps families in the community, which supports the claim.

questions.stem: In “Businesses Can Be Good Neighbors,” the author's opinion is that every business should ____.
options: find one way to give back
questions.why: The conclusion states the author's opinion: every business should give back.

questions.stem: The new app that turns old phones into weather stations is an ____ idea that no one had tried before.
questions.why: Innovative means new and creative.

questions.stem: Which TWO words end with a suffix that turns a verb into a noun? Choose two.
questions.why: The suffixes -tion and -ment turn verbs (donate, pay) into nouns.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about a bakery's morning routine has an error?
segments: the bakers follow the same routine:
they mix the dough, shape the loaves,
questions.why: Verbs in a list should match: mix, shape, and bake.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Collecting old clothes for every family in the village was a huge undertaking,” the word “undertaking” means a big job that takes a lot of work.
questions.why: An undertaking is a large task or project someone takes on.

questions.stem: Which word uses the suffix -al to mean “having the quality of”?
questions.why: Exceptional means having the quality of an exception, or being unusually good.

questions.stem: Match each word built from “compassion,” “exception,” and “innovate” with its part of speech.
questions.why: Suffixes like -ate, -ly, and -ion change a word's part of speech.

questions.stem: Opening a small food truck that also trains young cooks was an ____ that made money and helped the community.
questions.why: An enterprise is a business or project.

questions.stem: Put the steps in the process a toy company used to donate toys to a children's hospital in order.
sequence: The company asked the hospital what toys the children needed.
Workers set aside one toy from every box sold.
Volunteers packed the toys into gift bags.
Nurses gave the gift bags to the children.
questions.why: A process is a series of steps done in order.

questions.stem: Which choice would be the best heading for a section about how a business raised money for charity?
options: Raising Funds for a Good Cause
Colors of the New Shop Logo
questions.why: A good heading names the main topic of the section.

questions.stem: A paragraph's central idea is “The Riyadh book shop's weekly routine helps both readers and the community.” Which TWO details best support this central idea? Choose two.
options: Every Tuesday, the shop gives free books to a children's library.
Each morning, staff read stories to young children before school.
The walls of the shop are painted a bright green color.
The shop owner was born in a small town by the sea.
questions.why: Supporting details must connect to the central idea, not just describe the shop.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the central idea of “Why Giving Can Be Good Business”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the central idea of “Why Giving Can Be Good Business”?

options.label: A
options.text: A business can be successful and kind at the same time.

options.label: B
options.text: Children should buy their shoes from companies in Jeddah.

options.label: C
options.text: Big brands always sell more shoes than small companies.

options.label: D
options.text: Companies must keep all of their money to succeed.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The company also donated thousands of pairs to schools.

options.label: B
options.text: Some people believe a company must keep every riyal it earns to be successful.

options.label: C
options.text: However, the story of a small sports shoe company in Jeddah shows another path.

options.label: D
options.text: This example proves that a business does not have to choose between profit and kindness.

questions.why: The author's conclusion states the central idea directly.

questions.stem: According to the bar graph, how many more pairs of shoes were sold in 2023 than in 2021?
Select two sentences from “Why Giving Can Be Good Business” that support the idea that customers liked the company's promise.

segments.text: Some people believe a company must keep every riyal it earns to be successful.
Many shoppers liked this idea and chose the company over larger brands.
As the graph shows, sales grew every year after the promise began.
The company also donated thousands of pairs to schools.

questions.why: Shoppers choosing the company and rising sales show customers liked the promise.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the section with the heading “The Numbers Tell the Story”?
options: to describe how the shoes are made in factories
to explain why some people disagree with the author
to compare the prices of shoes at different stores
to give evidence that sales grew after the promise
questions.why: The graph and its section give number evidence for the author's claim.

questions.stem: In “Why Giving Can Be Good Business,” is each statement the author's claim or evidence that supports it?

rows.text: A business does not have to choose between profit and kindness.
The company sold 9,000 pairs in 2023.
The company gave thousands of pairs to schools.
When companies help people, customers reward them.

questions.why: A claim is what the author wants you to believe; evidence is the facts that back it up.

questions.stem: Find the error in this sentence about an exceptional young business owner.
questions.why: The adjective “innovative” describes the business; “innovation” is a noun.

questions.stem: Adding the suffix -ly to “routine” makes “routinely,” so “The shop routinely gives away bread” means the shop gives it away ____.
questions.why: Something done routinely is done regularly as part of a habit.

questions.stem: Which word BEST replaces “very good” in this sentence? “Hessa's plan to sell plants and give the money to a hospital was very good, better than any other plan in the contest.”
questions.why: Exceptional means much better than usual.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The factory will process the dates and pack them into boxes,” the word “process” is a noun that names a series of steps.
questions.why: Here “process” is a verb meaning to prepare or treat something.

questions.stem: Which THREE details would best support the central idea “Compassionate businesses make their communities stronger”? Choose three.
options: A toy shop changes the color of its sign.
A clothing store moves to a bigger building.
A pharmacy delivers free medicine to elderly neighbors.
A market gives its unsold fruit to a shelter.
A café adds a new flavor of juice.
A restaurant trains young people who need jobs.
questions.why: Each supporting detail shows a business helping its community.

questions.stem: The owl sat still on the branch, waiting to ____ on the mouse below.
questions.why: To pounce is to jump suddenly to catch something.

questions.stem: What does the prefix un- mean in the word “unsafe”?
questions.why: The prefix un- means not, so unsafe means not safe.

questions.stem: True or false: A rabbit is the prey of a hawk because the hawk hunts and eats it.
questions.why: Prey is an animal that is hunted by another animal.

questions.stem: Match each animal with the adaptation that helps it survive: polar bear, chameleon, hedgehog.
questions.why: Adaptations are body parts or behaviors that help animals survive.

questions.stem: Does the prefix in each word mean “not” or “again”?

rows.text: unhappy
refill
unable
rebuild

questions.why: The prefix un- means not; re- means again.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of “Built for the Desert”?
options: Camels are the only desert animals strong enough to walk far across soft, deep sand dunes.
Desert animals have adaptations that help them live with heat and little water.
The Arabian desert is hotter than any other place in the world.
The sand cat sleeps in a burrow when the sun is strong.
questions.why: Every section shows an adaptation that helps an animal survive desert heat or dryness.

questions.stem: Which sentence in “Built for the Desert” explains how the sand cat's large ears help it survive?

segments.text: The sand cat's large ears help it hear prey moving under the sand.
Many animals, such as the sand cat, rest in underground burrows when the sun is strong.
They come out to hunt at night, when the air is much cooler.
These special features are called adaptations.

questions.why: The photo caption tells exactly what the ears do.

questions.stem: Match each heading in “Built for the Desert” with the animal described in that section.
questions.why: Headings help readers find information about each adaptation.

questions.stem: Part A: Which is the best summary of the section “Finding Water”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which is the best summary of the section “Finding Water”?

options.label: A
options.text: Water is easy to find in the desert if animals know where to look.

options.label: B
options.text: The oryx eats only dry plants and never needs any water at all.

options.label: C
options.text: The oryx drinks from desert rivers every morning before the heat begins.

options.label: D
options.text: The oryx can live for weeks without drinking because its food gives it water.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Water is difficult to find in the desert.

options.label: B
options.text: Soft sand is hard to walk on.

options.label: C
options.text: It gets the water it needs from the plants it eats.

options.label: D
options.text: They come out to hunt at night, when the air is much cooler.

questions.why: A summary tells the most important ideas of a section in a few words.

questions.stem: Put the sections of “Built for the Desert” in the order they appear.
sequence: Staying Cool
Finding Water
Moving on Sand
questions.why: Headings show how the article is organized.

questions.stem: The bright colors on some frogs warn birds that the frogs are ____ and will make them sick.
questions.why: Poisonous animals can make others sick, and bright colors warn predators.

questions.stem: Which TWO words have a prefix that means “not”? Choose two.
questions.why: The prefixes un- and non- both mean not.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about a spider's web has an error?
segments: When an insect lands in the web,
questions.why: A singular subject like “the spider” needs a verb ending in -s.

questions.stem: Which sentence best summarizes these sentences? “Snowshoe hares have brown fur in summer. In winter, their fur turns white. The white fur matches the snow, so foxes have trouble seeing them.”
options: Snowshoe hares have brown fur during the warm summer months.
Foxes cannot see very well when heavy snow falls on the ground in winter.
Snowshoe hares like snow more than they like summer weather.
The hare's fur changes color with the seasons to hide it from predators.
questions.why: A summary combines the key ideas: the fur changes so predators cannot see the hare.

questions.stem: True or false: The word “extraordinary” uses the prefix extra-, so it means “beyond ordinary,” or very unusual.
questions.why: Extra- means beyond, so extraordinary means beyond the ordinary.

questions.stem: Match each key word from an article about animal survival with an example: “camouflaged,” “vibrations,” “dribbles.”

pairs.right: A green insect sits still on a green leaf.
A snake feels the ground shake as a mouse runs.
Water slowly drips from a thirsty camel's mouth.

questions.why: Each example shows what the key word means.

questions.stem: A cheetah can run 100 kilometers an hour, an ____ speed that no other land animal can match.
questions.why: Extraordinary means far beyond what is usual.

questions.stem: Put the steps of how a camouflaged crab spider catches a bee in order.
sequence: The white spider sits still on a white flower.
A bee lands on the flower to drink nectar.
The bee does not notice the spider.
The spider pounces and catches the bee.
questions.why: The spider's camouflage lets it wait unseen until it can pounce.

questions.stem: Which caption would best go with a photo of a hedgehog rolled into a ball?
options: Hedgehogs eat beetles, worms, and other small creatures at night.
Hedgehogs are small animals that live in many parts of the world.
When it senses danger, a hedgehog rolls up so its spines face out.
This photo was taken in a garden on a sunny afternoon last May.
questions.why: A useful caption explains what the photo shows and why it matters.

questions.stem: True or false: A predator that hunts at night may use its sense of hearing to find prey in the dark.
questions.why: Many night predators, like owls, use hearing to find prey.

questions.stem: Part A: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?

partA.stem: Part A: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?

options.label: A
options.text: The octopus is the fastest swimmer on the coral reef.

options.label: B
options.text: Camouflage helps reef animals hide from danger or catch food.

options.label: C
options.text: Sharks are the most dangerous animals in the Red Sea.

options.label: D
options.text: Stonefish change color to match the sand on the sea floor.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The coral reefs of the Red Sea are full of color, but they are also full of danger.

options.label: B
options.text: When a shark swims near, the octopus can look exactly like a rock or a patch of sand.

options.label: C
options.text: The octopus can change the color and pattern of its skin in less than a second.

options.label: D
options.text: Whether they are hiding from predators or waiting for prey, these animals show how camouflage helps them stay alive.

questions.why: The last sentence pulls together both examples into the central idea.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Masters of Disguise in the Red Sea” that explain how the stonefish uses camouflage to catch prey.

segments.text: The octopus can change the color and pattern of its skin in less than a second.
The stonefish does not change color, but its lumpy body looks like a rock covered with algae.
When a shark swims near, the octopus can look exactly like a rock or a patch of sand.
Small fish swim right up to it, and the stonefish swallows them in a flash.

questions.why: The stonefish looks like a rock, so small fish come close enough to be caught.

questions.stem: What do the photo and caption add to the article?
options: They let the reader see how well the stonefish blends with rocks.
They show how quickly the octopus can change its skin color and pattern.
They show where stonefish lay their eggs.
They explain why sharks swim near the coral reefs.
questions.why: The photo and caption help readers see the camouflage described in the text.

questions.stem: In “Masters of Disguise in the Red Sea,” does each detail describe the octopus, the stonefish, or both?

rows.text: changes the color of its skin
has a lumpy body that looks like a rock
uses camouflage to survive
swallows small fish in a flash

questions.why: Sorting details helps readers see how the two animals are alike and different.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences belong in a summary of “Masters of Disguise in the Red Sea”? Choose two.
options: The stonefish's shape helps it hide and catch fish.
The octopus changes color to look like rocks or sand.
The Red Sea reefs are full of bright colors.
A shark is a large fish with sharp teeth.
questions.why: A summary keeps the important ideas and leaves out small details.

questions.stem: Find the misused key word in this short paragraph about a desert snake.
segments: The horned viper hides under the sand.
Only its eyes show, so it is camouflaged.
When a lizard walks by, the snake feels its vibrations.
Then the viper pounces and becomes the prey.
questions.correction: Then the viper pounces and catches its prey.
questions.why: The viper is the predator; the lizard it catches is the prey.

questions.stem: When the camel finally reaches the water trough, it drinks so fast that water ____ from its lips onto the sand.
questions.why: Dribbles means falls in small drops.

questions.stem: The prefix pre- means “before.” Which word means “to tell what will happen before it happens”?
questions.why: Predict combines pre- (before) and dict (say).

questions.stem: Is each detail about the fennec fox important enough for a summary or only a minor detail?

rows.text: Its huge ears let heat escape and help it hear prey.
Its thick fur keeps it warm on cold desert nights.
One fennec fox at a zoo was named Sunny.
Some people think fennec foxes look like cartoons.

questions.why: A summary includes details about adaptations, not fun facts that do not matter.

questions.stem: Part A: “The young gazelle is extraordinary at sensing danger. Its large ears pick up tiny vibrations, and it runs before a predator can pounce.” What is the central idea of these sentences?

partA.stem: Part A: “The young gazelle is extraordinary at sensing danger. Its large ears pick up tiny vibrations, and it runs before a predator can pounce.” What is the central idea of these sentences?

options.label: A
options.text: Gazelles like running more than resting.

options.label: B
options.text: Gazelles have the largest ears of any animal.

options.label: C
options.text: Predators can never catch young gazelles.

options.label: D
options.text: The gazelle's senses help it escape predators.

partB.stem: Part B: Which detail best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The gazelle is young.

options.label: B
options.text: Its large ears pick up tiny vibrations.

options.label: C
options.text: Gazelles have ears.

options.label: D
options.text: Predators pounce on animals.

questions.why: The ears sense vibrations, which lets the gazelle escape in time.

questions.stem: Which word is an antonym of “annoyed”?
questions.why: Annoyed means bothered; pleased means the opposite.

questions.stem: Match each part of a play with what it does: cast of characters, stage directions, dialogue.

pairs.right: lists the people or animals who appear
tell actors how to move or speak

questions.why: Plays use special parts to tell actors what to do and say.

questions.stem: The puppy was ____ after a long day, so it growled when the children tried to play with it.
questions.why: Cranky means grumpy and easily annoyed, often when tired.

questions.stem: True or false: “Hot” and “cold” are antonyms because they have opposite meanings.
questions.why: Antonyms are words with opposite meanings.

questions.stem: In a play about a lazy grasshopper, is each line dialogue or a stage direction?

rows.text: GRASSHOPPER: Let's sing all day!
(The ant carries a heavy seed.)
ANT: I must work while the sun shines.
(Wind blows, and leaves fall.)

questions.why: Stage directions are usually in parentheses; dialogue follows a character's name.

questions.stem: What is the theme of “The Bee and the Butterfly”?
options: Butterflies are more beautiful and graceful than bees.
Gardens are full of flowers in the spring.
It is always fun to rest in the warm spring sunshine.
Working ahead helps you get ready for hard times.
questions.why: Bee's hard work saves both friends when the cold comes.

questions.stem: Which stage direction in “The Bee and the Butterfly” shows that Butterfly is cold?

segments.text: (stretching her wings)
(laughing)
(shivering)
(opening the door of her hive)

questions.why: Shivering is what a body does when it is cold.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does Bee keep working instead of resting?

partA.stem: Part A: Why does Bee keep working instead of resting?

options.label: A
options.text: She wants to win a flying race.

options.label: B
options.text: She does not like Butterfly very much.

options.label: C
options.text: She is lost and cannot find her hive.

options.label: D
options.text: She wants to store honey before the cold days.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Next spring, we will work together.

options.label: B
options.text: Come and relax in the sunshine with me!

options.label: C
options.text: I cannot rest yet, because I must store honey before the cold days come.

options.label: D
options.text: The cold days are far away, and there is plenty of time.

questions.why: Bee says she must store honey before the cold days.

questions.stem: Put these events from “The Bee and the Butterfly” in order.
sequence: Bee carries nectar back to her hive.
Butterfly asks Bee to rest in the sunshine.
The flowers fade, and a chilly wind blows.
Bee shares her saved honey with Butterfly.
questions.why: The narrator's lines help show how time passes in a play.

questions.stem: Which TWO questions can be answered by reading the setting of “The Bee and the Butterfly”? Choose two.
options: Where does the play take place?
Why does Bee share her honey?
What season is it at the start?
How does Butterfly feel at the end?
questions.why: The setting tells where and when a play takes place.

questions.stem: The ____ in the stadium grew louder as the fans cheered the winning goal.
questions.why: A commotion is a noisy, excited disturbance.

questions.stem: Which pair of words are antonyms?
questions.why: Frustrated and satisfied have opposite meanings; the others are synonyms.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about Uncle Fahad's cooking has an error?
segments: asks him to cook it on holidays.
questions.why: The singular subject “specialty” needs the singular verb “is.”

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “frustrated”?

rows.text: upset
calm
discouraged
satisfied

questions.why: Synonyms have similar meanings; antonyms have opposite meanings.

questions.stem: True or false: In a play, a narrator may speak to the audience to explain what is happening.
questions.why: A narrator in a play often tells the audience about events or time passing.

questions.stem: Match each short fable with its theme.

pairs.left: A crow drops pebbles into a jug until the water rises and it can drink.
A selfish dog drops its bone while trying to grab another dog's bone.
pairs.right: Greed can make you lose what you have.

pairs.left: A tiny mouse frees a trapped lion by chewing the net.
pairs.right: Even small friends can be a big help.

questions.why: A theme is the lesson the characters' actions teach.

questions.stem: Grasshopper's lazy ____ changed after the dry season; he began waking early to help gather seeds.
questions.why: An attitude is the way someone thinks and acts about something.

questions.stem: A student reads a play and wants to ask questions about its theme. Which TWO questions would help? Choose two.
options: What lesson does the main character learn by the end?
How many actors are in the cast?
What color is the stage curtain?
How do the characters' choices lead to good or bad results?
questions.why: Questions about lessons and results of choices lead readers to the theme.

questions.stem: Put these lines from a short play about two camels in order.
sequence: NARRATOR: Two camels prepare for a long trip across the desert.
FIRST CAMEL: I will drink plenty of water before we leave.
SECOND CAMEL (annoyed): Why waste time? Let's go now!
NARRATOR: Days later, only the first camel still has strength to walk.
questions.why: The plan, the argument, and then the result make the play's order clear.

questions.stem: Which word is the best antonym of “familiar” in this sentence? “The road to Grandmother's house was familiar to Badr.”
questions.why: Familiar means well known; strange means not known.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the theme of “The Well in the Oasis”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the theme of “The Well in the Oasis”?

options.label: A
options.text: Wells in an oasis never run dry, even in the summer.

options.label: B
options.text: It is better to rest in the shade than to dig in the sun.

options.label: C
options.text: Neighbors should always share their tea with each other.

options.label: D
options.text: Planning ahead and working hard prepare you for hard times.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Come and join me for a cup of tea.

options.label: B
options.text: The sun burns, and the water in the well sinks lower every day.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the cool season, and the well is full of water.

options.label: D
options.text: I am saving water now, because the hot summer always brings a terrible drought.

questions.why: Sami plans ahead, and his saved water helps both farmers in summer.

questions.stem: Which line from “The Well in the Oasis” shows that Raed's attitude has changed?

segments.text: Why worry, Sami?
The well has never run dry.
My trees are dying, and I do not know what to do!
I will never laugh at hard work again.

questions.why: Raed now respects hard work instead of laughing at it.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of words in parentheses, such as “(lying in the shade of a palm tree)”?
options: to name the setting of each scene
to list all the characters in order
to show the words a character says aloud
to tell what a character is doing
questions.why: Stage directions in parentheses tell actors how to move or act.

questions.stem: In “The Well in the Oasis,” the word “careful” in the cast list is an antonym of ____, which describes Raed early in the play.
questions.why: Careful and careless are opposites; Raed does not plan at first.

questions.stem: Which question would a reader most likely ask after the narrator says, “The sun burns, and the water in the well sinks lower every day”?
options: How many palm trees are on each farm?
Who dug the well between the two farms?
What will happen to Raed's trees without water?
Why does Sami grow dates on his farm instead of oranges?
questions.why: Good readers ask questions about what may happen next in the plot.

questions.stem: Find the misused key word in these lines from a play about a falcon show.
segments: TRAINER: Our falcon's specialty is diving fast.
CHILD (frustrated): Hooray, it caught the lure on the first try!
questions.correction: CHILD (excited): Hooray, it caught the lure on the first try!
questions.why: A child cheering “Hooray” is excited, not frustrated.

questions.stem: Huda was not only annoyed by the broken printer; after trying to fix it for an hour, she felt completely ____.
questions.why: Frustrated is a stronger feeling than annoyed, after trying and failing.

questions.stem: Which line from a play best shows the theme “Being selfish can leave you alone”?
options: FOX (sitting by himself): I kept all the dates, but now no one will eat with me.
FOX (yawning): I am so sleepy after this long and busy day of searching.
FOX (running): I must hurry home before the sun goes down behind the dunes.
FOX (smiling): I found a big basket of dates near the old palm tree today.
questions.why: Fox kept everything for himself and ended up alone, which shows the theme.

questions.stem: True or false: “Cranky” and “cheerful” are antonyms, so a cranky character would probably speak in a happy, friendly way.
questions.why: A cranky character is grumpy, the opposite of cheerful.

questions.stem: Are the words in each pair from a fable about a fox antonyms or synonyms?

rows.text: selfish – giving
annoyed – irritated
familiar – unknown
cranky – grouchy

questions.why: Antonyms are opposites; synonyms mean nearly the same thing.

questions.stem: Match each key word from the animal poems unit to its meaning.

pairs.right: hard but easily broken or cracked
full of details that help you picture something
reached out as far as possible
using imagination to make something new

questions.why: These words help readers talk about how poets describe animals.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: The dry autumn leaf was so ____ that it cracked when Huda stepped on it.
questions.why: Something brittle breaks or cracks easily.

questions.stem: True or false: A simile compares two things by using the word like or as.
questions.why: “As fast as the wind” is a simile because it uses as.

questions.stem: Which sentence about a kitten contains a simile?
options: The kitten slept on a soft cloud-shaped pillow.
The soft kitten slept beside the window.
The kitten was a soft cloud of fur.
The kitten was as soft as a cloud.
questions.why: Only the first sentence compares using as.

questions.stem: Decide whether each line about an animal is a simile or a metaphor.

rows.text: The cheetah ran like the wind.
The owl is a night watchman.
The turtle's shell is as hard as stone.
The bee is a busy little worker.

questions.why: Similes use like or as; metaphors say one thing is another.

questions.stem: Match each poetry term to what it describes.

pairs.right: words that end with the same sound
the pattern of strong and weak beats in a line
a comparison that uses like or as
a comparison that says one thing is another

questions.why: Poets use these tools to create sound and pictures.

questions.stem: Which two words rhyme with the word flight? Choose two.
questions.why: Bright and night end with the same -ight sound as flight.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: The poet used ____ words such as glittering, rough, and enormous so readers could picture the eagle.
questions.why: Descriptive words help readers picture something.

questions.stem: Find the word used incorrectly in the sentence about Salem's eagle poem.
questions.why: A poem full of new ideas is creative, not brittle.

questions.stem: Which line from a poem about an eagle uses a metaphor?
options: The eagle flies as high as the clouds.
The eagle builds its nest on a high cliff.
The eagle is a king of the mountain air.
The eagle looks like a dark kite in the sky.
questions.why: Calling the eagle a king is a metaphor; it does not use like or as.

questions.stem: Part A: Which idea does the poet express about the falcon's wings in “The Desert Falcon”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which idea does the poet express about the falcon's wings in “The Desert Falcon”?

options.label: A
options.text: She has small wings that cannot lift her.

options.label: B
options.text: She uses the wind to glide with great ease.

options.label: C
options.text: She shines because her wings are metal.

options.label: D
options.text: She is tired after flying over the sea.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Then suddenly she tumbles down, an arrow from the sky,

options.label: B
options.text: I watch her from my window, and I hold my breathing still,

options.label: C
options.text: Her outstretched wings are silver sails that catch the winds below.

options.label: D
options.text: The frightened lizards scatter as the hunter rushes by.

questions.why: Sails catch the wind, so the metaphor shows the falcon gliding easily.

questions.stem: Select the line from “The Desert Falcon” that contains a simile.

segments.text: Above the golden dunes the falcon circles, calm and slow,
Her eyes are polished lanterns, searching every rocky ledge,
She hovers like a question mark beside the canyon's edge.
Then suddenly she tumbles down, an arrow from the sky,

questions.why: The falcon is compared to a question mark using like.

questions.stem: For “The Desert Falcon,” decide whether each phrase is a simile or a metaphor.

rows.text: her eyes are polished lanterns
hovers like a question mark
an arrow from the sky

questions.why: Only the question-mark phrase uses like.

questions.stem: Which pair of words from “The Desert Falcon” shows the poem's rhyme pattern?
questions.why: Each pair of lines ends in rhyming words, such as slow and below.

questions.stem: How does the speaker of “The Desert Falcon” feel about the falcon?
options: The speaker admires her and wishes to be as brave.
The speaker is bored and would rather watch lizards.
The speaker fears her and wants her to fly away.
The speaker pities her because she must hunt to eat.
questions.why: The speaker wishes for the falcon's courage and skill.

questions.stem: Put the lines of this haiku about a sea turtle in a sensible 5-7-5 order: “to the sandy shore,” “Slow turtle swims on,” “through the warm and silver waves.”
sequence: Slow turtle swims on
through the warm and silver waves
to the sandy shore
questions.why: A haiku has three lines of five, seven, and five syllables.

questions.stem: True or false: A haiku is a short poem of three lines that usually has five, seven, and five syllables.
questions.why: That syllable pattern is the usual structure of a haiku.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: When Ali read his poem aloud, he tapped his desk to keep the steady ____ of each line.
questions.why: Meter is the steady pattern of beats in a line of poetry.

questions.stem: Which two features would most likely appear in a lyric poem about a chimpanzee? Choose two.
options: descriptive words that create a picture
characters speaking lines on a stage
a list of facts with headings and a chart
the speaker's feelings about the chimpanzee
questions.why: Lyric poems share feelings and use descriptive language.

questions.stem: Read the line: “The young chimp was a little acrobat in the treetops.” What does the metaphor tell the reader?
options: The chimp was smaller than the other chimps.
The chimp performed tricks for visitors in a show.
The chimp moved with quick and skillful jumps.
The chimp liked to sleep high in the treetops.
questions.why: An acrobat jumps and swings with skill, so the chimp moves the same way.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the camel's perspective in “The Camel's Song”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the camel's perspective in “The Camel's Song”?

options.label: A
options.text: It is afraid of the stars and the long, dark nights.

options.label: B
options.text: It is proud of its strength and thinks people misjudge it.

options.label: C
options.text: It is angry that the caravans travel too slowly.

options.label: D
options.text: It is tired of the desert and wants to ride in trucks.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: But I can cross the empty miles that you will never understand.

options.label: B
options.text: The desert is my library, the stars are my old friends,

options.label: C
options.text: My lashes are like curtains that protect me from the haze.

options.label: D
options.text: You hurry in your noisy trucks and grumble at the heat,

questions.why: The camel answers people who call it slow by boasting of what it can do.

questions.stem: Select two lines from “The Camel's Song” that use metaphors.

segments.text: My humps are patient storehouses that keep me strong for days,
My lashes are like curtains that protect me from the haze.
The desert is my library, the stars are my old friends,
While I go gently forward on my wide and padded feet.

questions.why: These lines say one thing is another without like or as.

questions.stem: Decide whether each detail in “The Camel's Song” describes the camel or the people.

rows.text: hurry in noisy trucks
go gently forward on padded feet
grumble at the heat
carry every caravan

questions.why: The poem contrasts the calm camel with the hurried people.

questions.stem: Which two statements about the structure of “The Camel's Song” are correct? Choose two.
options: The lines do not rhyme, so it is free verse.
The poem is divided into two stanzas of four lines.
Each pair of lines ends with rhyming words.
Each line has exactly five syllables like a haiku.
questions.why: The poem has two four-line stanzas made of rhyming pairs.

questions.stem: Why does the poet most likely use the camel as the speaker instead of a person?
options: to explain scientific facts about how camels store water
to make the poem shorter and easier to memorize
to show that people and camels never travel together
to let readers see the desert through the camel's eyes
questions.why: A camel speaker shares the animal's own perspective.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence that explains what a metaphor is.
segments: by using the word like or as,
such as “the moon is a lamp.”
questions.correction: without using the word like or as,
questions.why: A metaphor does not use like or as; a simile does.

questions.stem: Read each line from a poem about a desert fox and decide whether it uses a simile, a metaphor, or neither.

rows.text: Its ears are radar dishes turning in the dark.
It slips across the sand as quietly as smoke.
It hunts for beetles when the evening cools.
Its tail is a soft brush sweeping its tracks away.

questions.why: Look for like or as (simile) or a direct comparison (metaphor).

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: The eagle landed with its wings ____, then slowly folded them against its body.
questions.why: Outstretched wings are spread wide open.

questions.stem: True or false: Two lines of poetry that have the same meter must also rhyme.
questions.why: Meter is the beat pattern; lines can share a beat without rhyming.

questions.stem: A poem is spoken by a hungry eagle looking down at a field. Which line best shows the eagle's perspective?
options: The farmer counts his sheep and hopes the eagle stays away.
The eagle looks so fierce and proud that children stop to stare.
Below me, tiny dinners run and hide in golden grass.
The field is warm and quiet under the afternoon sun.
questions.why: Only the first line shows how the eagle itself sees the field.

questions.stem: Match each key word about helping after a storm to its meaning.

Order Returns

Teams could compete fairly.

One set of laws was written.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are synonyms for gleaming? Choose two.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Wire Comes to Millbrook” that tells when the story takes place.

Her father, the town doctor, stood beside her with his arms folded.

children talking on telephones at school
workers stringing black wires along a dusty main road

questions.stem: Based on the father's words, what will most likely happen later in the story?

The telephone will spoil good conversation.

a feeling of warmth and safety

options.text: because it was easy to defend

options.label: C
options.text: Later leaders wished the first group had studied the land more carefully

options.label: D
options.text: on low, swampy land

questions.why: The leaders wished the settlers had checked the land first.

questions.stem: Read the sentences from a student's report on Jamestown. Select the two sentences that are evidence from a document.

segments.text: A settler's 1608 letter says, “We have but little food left.”
I think the settlers were very brave.
A 1610 report states that the fort's walls were repaired.
Jamestown is my favorite topic in history.

questions.why: Letters and reports are documents; opinions are not evidence.

questions.stem: Find the word that is used incorrectly in the sentence about the settlers' first shelter.
questions.why: A shelter that gets replaced is temporary, not permanent.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: Historians call the years when Jamestown was founded the colonial ____.
questions.why: An era is a period of time in history.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses expedition correctly?
options: He opened the expedition to let fresh air into the room.
The expedition on the wall showed the time of the meeting.
She ate a large expedition of rice and warm lentil soup for dinner last night with her family.
The explorers set out on an expedition to find the source of the great river.
questions.why: An expedition is a long trip for a special purpose.

questions.stem: Match each energy word to its meaning: renewable, consume, installed.

pairs.right: able to be replaced by nature
put in place and set up to use

questions.why: These three words often appear when people talk about energy.

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? “Large factories ____ huge amounts of coal and oil every day.”
questions.why: To consume something is to use it up, as factories use up fuel.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “Workers installed solar panels on the roof of the school,” installed means the workers took the panels away.
questions.why: Installed means the workers put the panels in place so they could be used.

questions.stem: The new light bulb is more ____ because it uses less electricity to make the same amount of light.
questions.why: Something efficient does a job well without wasting energy.

questions.stem: Decide whether each energy source is renewable or not renewable.

rows.text: sunlight
wind
coal
oil

questions.why: Sunlight and wind are replaced by nature; coal and oil take millions of years to form.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of “Power from the Playground Roof”?
options: Air conditioners are the most important machines in a hot school building.
Students should always close the doors when they leave a classroom.
The school found ways to use cleaner energy and waste less of it.
Workers can put many solar panels on a roof in only two days.
questions.why: Most details tell how the school used solar power and saved energy.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Power from the Playground Roof” that gives an example of a small choice that saves energy.

segments.text: They turn off lights when they leave a room.
Workers installed forty panels in just two days.
The air conditioners ran all day, and the lights stayed on even when rooms were empty.
A solar panel is made of special cells.

questions.why: Turning off lights is one of the small choices the students made.

questions.stem: Part A: Which question does the sidebar in “Power from the Playground Roof” answer?

partA.stem: Part A: Which question does the sidebar in “Power from the Playground Roof” answer?

options.label: A
options.text: How many students attend Al-Noor School?

options.label: B
options.text: How does a solar panel make electricity?

options.label: C
options.text: When will the school add more panels?

options.label: D
options.text: Who paid for the new solar panels?

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: They close the doors so cool air stays inside.

options.label: B
options.text: Workers installed forty panels in just two days.

options.label: C
options.text: The students wanted to find a cleaner way to get energy.

options.label: D
options.text: When sunlight hits the cells, they make a small electric current.

questions.why: A sidebar gives extra facts; this one explains how solar cells work.

questions.stem: In “Power from the Playground Roof,” the word installed means that the workers ____ the panels.
options: put in place and set up
questions.why: Installed means put in place so it can be used.

questions.stem: Which details from “Power from the Playground Roof” support the idea that the school now uses energy more wisely? Choose two.
options: The work on the roof took two days.
The school is named Al-Noor School.
The panels turn sunlight into electricity for the classrooms.
Students turn off the lights when they leave a room.
questions.why: Relevant details support the central idea; the name and the time are not about using energy wisely.

questions.stem: Match each Latin or Greek prefix to its meaning: re-, bio-, tele-, trans-.
questions.why: Knowing a prefix helps you figure out a new word.

questions.stem: The prefix re- in renewable tells you that this kind of energy can be ____.
questions.why: Re- means again, so renewable energy can be replaced and used again.

questions.stem: Is the prefix in each energy word from Latin or from Greek: renewable, biofuel, transform, telephone?

rows.text: renewable (re-)
biofuel (bio-)
transform (trans-)
telephone (tele-)

questions.why: Re- and trans- come from Latin; bio- and tele- come from Greek.

questions.stem: Biofuel is made from plants. What does the prefix bio- in biofuel tell you?
options: The fuel is used again after it burns.
The fuel can travel across very long distances.
The fuel is tiny and hard to see.
The fuel comes from living things.
questions.why: Bio- means life, so biofuel comes from living things such as plants.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong prefix? “The old factory was converted into a museum, but the huge building was unefficient to heat.”
questions.why: The prefix in- (not un-) is added to efficient to mean “not efficient.”

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of “Wind at Work”?
options: Some people think rows of wind turbines spoil the view of open land.
Wind power is a useful renewable energy source, but it has problems to solve.
Windmills in Persia were used long ago to grind grain into flour for bread.
The blades of many turbines are longer than a basketball court.
questions.why: The article explains the benefits and the problems of wind power.

questions.stem: Part A: In “Wind at Work,” what is one consequence of the wind not blowing all the time?

partA.stem: Part A: In “Wind at Work,” what is one consequence of the wind not blowing all the time?

options.label: A
options.text: Turbines send smoke into the air.

options.label: B
options.text: People build more windmills to grind grain.

options.label: C
options.text: Turbines cannot make electricity every hour.

options.label: D
options.text: The blades break during calm weather.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Wind power has many benefits.

options.label: B
options.text: The wind does not blow all the time, so turbines cannot make electricity every hour of the day.

options.label: C
options.text: Centuries ago, windmills in Persia used moving air to grind grain into flour.

options.label: D
options.text: Today, tall wind turbines do a different job.

questions.why: The word so signals the consequence: no wind means no electricity.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Wind at Work” that describe disadvantages of wind energy.

segments.text: The wind does not blow all the time, so turbines cannot make electricity every hour of the day.
Some people also feel that long rows of turbines spoil the view of open land.
Wind is renewable, so it will never run out, and turbines do not send smoke into the air.
Their long blades spin when the wind blows, and a machine inside the turbine converts that motion into electricity.

questions.why: Calm days and spoiled views are the two problems the article names.

questions.stem: In paragraph 1 of “Wind at Work,” the word converts means ____.
options: changes from one form into another
stores for use at a later time
questions.why: The machine changes the motion of the blades into electricity.

questions.stem: Decide whether each question can be answered using “Wind at Work.”

rows.text: What did windmills in Persia do long ago?
How are engineers trying to help on calm days?
How much money does one turbine cost?
Which country has the most wind turbines?

questions.why: Good readers check whether a text answers their questions or whether they need another source.

questions.stem: Which sentences use the word consequences correctly? Choose two.
options: Before you choose a plan, think about the consequences of each one.
Burning coal has serious consequences for the air we breathe.
The consequences of the solar panels were bright and blue.
Our class will consequences the energy plan on Monday.
questions.why: Consequences are the results or effects of an action.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses coincidence correctly?
options: We used a coincidence to measure how much energy our house used.
The coincidence of the turbine spun quickly in the strong wind.
By coincidence, both teams chose wind power on the same day.
Ali planned the coincidence carefully for many weeks.
questions.why: A coincidence is a surprising event that happens by chance, not by plan.

questions.stem: The scientist could hardly believe that one small panel could power the whole water pump. She said it was ____.
questions.why: Incredible means hard to believe.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “The new engine consumes less fuel” means the engine uses up less fuel than before.
questions.why: Consume means to use up.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence does not make sense? “The engineers installed a more efficient heater, so the house consumed more energy than before.”
questions.why: An efficient heater wastes less, so the house would use less energy.

questions.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses the central idea of “The Biofuel Debate”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses the central idea of “The Biofuel Debate”?

options.label: A
options.text: Biofuels are always the best choice for every country.

options.label: B
options.text: Used cooking oil should be poured into drains and rivers.

options.label: C
options.text: Biofuels have both benefits and drawbacks that people must weigh.

options.label: D
options.text: Debates are won by the team that speaks the loudest.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Biofuels are fuels made from plants or from waste such as used cooking oil.

options.label: B
options.text: Reem's team found several advantages.

options.label: C
options.text: On the day of the debate, both teams spoke clearly and listened politely.

options.label: D
options.text: Every energy source has costs and benefits, and wise choices come from comparing them carefully.

questions.why: The class's final agreement states the central idea.

questions.stem: Which details from “The Biofuel Debate” support the argument against biofuels? Choose two.
options: Growing fuel crops takes a great deal of land and water.
Some biofuels cost more to make than gasoline.
Turning waste into fuel keeps oil out of rivers.
questions.why: Faisal's team used land, water, and cost as reasons against biofuels.

questions.stem: Put the events of “The Biofuel Debate” in order.
sequence: Mr. Hamdan's class learns it will debate biofuels.
The class splits into two teams.
The teams research advantages and problems.
Both teams speak and listen at the debate.
The class agrees that every energy source has costs and benefits.
questions.why: The debate is prepared, held, and then the class reaches an agreement.

questions.stem: A reader asks, “Why might biofuels be a poor choice in a dry country?” Which answer does “The Biofuel Debate” give?
options: Dry countries do not have any used cooking oil to turn into fuel.
The water used for fuel crops may be needed to grow food.
Biofuel crops cannot grow at all when the weather is hot and sunny.
Gasoline is easier to find in dry countries than in wet ones.
questions.why: Paragraph 3 explains that water might be needed more for food.

questions.stem: In “The Biofuel Debate,” Reem's team says biofuels are ____ because plants grow back each season.
questions.why: Renewable sources can be replaced by nature.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning: ancestors, retreated, endurance, honor.

pairs.right: family members who lived long ago
the power to keep going through hard times

questions.why: These words describe people, their past, and their actions.

questions.stem: The camels showed great ____ as they walked across the hot sand for three days without stopping.
questions.why: Endurance is the ability to keep going for a long time.

questions.stem: In the sentence “The fox retreated into its den when the hunters came near,” what does retreated mean?
options: slept for a very long time
went back to a safe place
questions.why: Retreated means moved back or away from danger.

questions.stem: True or false: Your ancestors are the people in your family who will be born in the future.
questions.why: Ancestors are family members who lived long before you.

questions.stem: Sort these words from a historical story by connotation: honor, despised, irritating, endurance.

rows.text: honor
despised
irritating
endurance

questions.why: Connotation is the feeling a word gives; honor and endurance feel positive.

questions.stem: Where and when does “The Caravan at Hail” take place?
options: near the town of Hail in the spring of 1870
at Salim's home on the first day of school
in a busy city market on a cold winter night
on a ship sailing north to trade horses in 1890
questions.why: The first sentence tells the time and place.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Caravan at Hail” that best helps the reader picture the setting.

segments.text: The sun was hot, and the wind blew sand into his eyes.
Salim's father was searching for his older brother, Khalid.
Salim's father dropped the rope he was holding.
His family was whole again.

questions.why: Details about the hot sun and blowing sand describe the desert setting.

questions.stem: In “The Caravan at Hail,” the word irritating shows that the blowing sand was ____.
questions.why: Irritating describes something that bothers you.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the theme of “The Caravan at Hail”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the theme of “The Caravan at Hail”?

options.label: A
options.text: Family bonds stay strong even after many years apart.

options.label: B
options.text: Children should never complain during long trips.

options.label: C
options.text: Trading horses is the best way to earn money.

options.label: D
options.text: Travel by camel is the fastest way to cross the desert.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Khalid had left home to trade horses in the north, and no letters had come back.

options.label: B
options.text: Twelve-year-old Salim walked beside his father.

options.label: C
options.text: The two brothers hugged for a long time, and Salim smiled.

options.label: D
options.text: Salim found the sand irritating, but he did not complain.

questions.why: After twenty years, the brothers' hug shows their bond is still strong.

questions.stem: Put the events of “The Caravan at Hail” in order.
sequence: The caravan moves slowly toward Hail.
The caravan reaches the town well.
A gray-bearded man looks up and whispers a name.
The two brothers hug for a long time.
questions.why: The reunion happens after the caravan arrives at the well.

questions.stem: The words disliked and despised have similar denotations. How are their connotations different?
options: Disliked shows a much stronger feeling than despised.
Both words show exactly the same strength of feeling.
Despised shows a much stronger feeling than disliked.
Despised is a happy word, but disliked is a sad one.
questions.why: Despised means hated, which is stronger than disliked.

questions.stem: Choose the word with the most positive connotation: “The runner kept going for all forty-two kilometers. She showed great ____.”
questions.why: Endurance praises the runner; stubbornness and tiredness sound negative.

questions.stem: Which sentences use a word with a negative connotation to describe a character? Choose two.
options: The travelers showed endurance on the long climb.
The guide despised the lazy traders who refused to help.
