Hana found her cousin's constant humming irritating.
The chief spoke with honor about his ancestors.
questions.why: Despised and irritating carry negative feelings.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses a word incorrectly? “Because only five players arrived, the team had to forfeit the match, and the other team forfeited the trophy.”
segments: the team had to forfeit the match,
questions.why: To forfeit is to lose or give something up, so the other team won.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The intensity of the storm frightened the travelers,” the word intensity describes how strong the storm was.
questions.why: Intensity means great strength or force.

questions.stem: Part A: Why are mostly women, children, and old men in Darin at the start of “Waiting on the Pearl Coast”?

partA.stem: Part A: Why are mostly women, children, and old men in Darin at the start of “Waiting on the Pearl Coast”?

options.label: A
options.text: The men are building new coral-stone houses.

options.label: B
options.text: The men have moved to a cooler town.

options.label: C
options.text: The men have gone to sea to dive for pearls.

options.label: D
options.text: The men are resting in the shade.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: People rushed down to the beach, shouting and waving.

options.label: B
options.text: Most of the men had sailed away months earlier to dive for pearls.

options.label: C
options.text: In the summer of 1925, the town of Darin sat quietly beside the warm waters of the Gulf.

options.label: D
options.text: Her father's boat had been gone since spring.

questions.why: The setting is a pearl-diving town whose men are away at sea.

questions.stem: Which details from “Waiting on the Pearl Coast” help the reader picture the setting? Choose two.
options: she held his hand and would not let it go
the narrow lanes between the coral-stone houses
Mariam ran faster than she had ever run
the smell of salt and seaweed
questions.why: Setting details describe the place, not the characters' actions.

questions.stem: How does the setting affect Mariam in “Waiting on the Pearl Coast”?
options: Because the lanes are narrow, she cannot run down to the beach to meet the boats.
Because the town is by the sea, she can watch each evening for her father's boat.
Because it is summer, she sails away with the other divers to look for pearls.
Because the day is very hot, she sleeps in the shade with the cats all afternoon.
questions.why: Living beside the sea lets Mariam watch for her father every evening.

questions.stem: In paragraph 2 of “Waiting on the Pearl Coast,” the daytime heat has great intensity. This means the heat is ____.
questions.why: Intensity means great strength; the heat was so strong even cats hid.

questions.stem: In “Waiting on the Pearl Coast,” is each statement a theme of the story or a detail from the story?

rows.text: Love for family helps people endure long separations.
The men sailed away in the spring.
Patient waiting can bring a joyful reward.
Mariam climbs onto the roof every evening.

questions.why: A theme is a message about life; a detail is a fact from the story.

questions.stem: Match each sentence to the meaning of the key word it uses: forfeit, honor, retreated, intensity.

pairs.left: She will forfeit her turn if she is late.
We honor our ancestors by keeping their traditions.
The scouts retreated before the storm arrived.
The intensity of the sun made the sand too hot to touch.

questions.why: Context in each sentence shows the meaning of the key word.

questions.stem: Choose the word with a positive connotation that best completes the sentence: “The guide was ____ as he led the travelers calmly through the dangerous mountain pass.”
questions.why: Courageous praises the guide; reckless and careless suggest he was foolish.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses despised correctly?
options: The travelers despised the cool water after their long, thirsty walk.
The villagers despised the thieves who stole their horses.
The chief despised his sister and hugged her with great joy.
The children despised their grandmother's warm, delicious bread.
questions.why: Despised means strongly disliked, which fits feelings about thieves.

questions.stem: For each statement about the words endurance and irritating, choose whether it describes denotation or connotation.

rows.text: Endurance means the ability to last through something difficult.
Endurance makes a reader admire a character's strength.
Irritating means causing someone to feel annoyed.
Irritating makes a reader feel that something is unpleasant.

questions.why: Denotation is the exact meaning; connotation is the feeling the word adds.

questions.stem: True or false: Calling a person “stubborn” instead of “determined” gives the description a more positive connotation.
questions.why: Stubborn sounds negative; determined sounds positive.

questions.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses the theme of “Many Voices”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses the theme of “Many Voices”?

options.label: A
options.text: Old sailors always tell the most exciting stories.

options.label: B
options.text: Great achievements often depend on many people working together.

options.label: C
options.text: Maps of the world never include small harbors.

options.label: D
options.text: Learning a second language is easy for young children.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: At first he found the work dull.

options.label: B
options.text: Many sailors spoke too quickly, and some argued about distances.

options.label: C
options.text: Travelers from many lands came to his workshop to describe the rivers, mountains, and cities they had seen.

options.label: D
options.text: “A map is made by many voices,” he said.

questions.why: Al-Idrisi says the map needs many voices, including Yusuf's.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Many Voices” that show how Yusuf's feelings about his work change.

segments.text: Yusuf despised the long afternoons of copying numbers.
From then on, Yusuf listened to every traveler with patience, proud to be one of those voices.
The geographer thanked him warmly.
Yusuf, a boy who spoke both Arabic and Greek, was hired to help.

questions.why: Yusuf first despises the work and later feels proud of it.

questions.stem: Why does the author use the word despised instead of disliked in paragraph 2 of “Many Voices”?
options: to explain why the sailors argued about the distances
to show how strongly Yusuf hated the dull work at first
to show that Yusuf secretly enjoyed copying the numbers
to suggest that Yusuf was angry with al-Idrisi himself
questions.why: Despised has a stronger negative connotation than disliked.

questions.stem: How does the setting of al-Idrisi's workshop in Palermo help develop the theme of “Many Voices”?
options: Palermo is far from the sea, so sailors rarely visit and the map stays unfinished.
The workshop is quiet and empty, so Yusuf can do his work alone without any help.
Travelers from many lands meet there, so knowledge from many people comes together.
The year is 1150, so there are no maps of the world and no one knows about harbors.
questions.why: The busy workshop brings many voices together, which is the theme.

questions.stem: Put the events of “Many Voices” in order.
sequence: Yusuf is hired to help in the workshop.
Yusuf grows bored with copying numbers.
An old sailor describes an unknown harbor.
Al-Idrisi adds the harbor and thanks Yusuf.
Yusuf listens to every traveler with patience.
questions.why: Yusuf's attitude changes after al-Idrisi thanks him.

questions.stem: Match each poetry term to its meaning: metaphor, personification, imagery, free verse.

pairs.right: a comparison of two things without using like or as
giving human actions or feelings to something that is not human
words that help readers see, hear, smell, taste, or feel
poetry with no regular rhyme or rhythm

questions.why: Poets use these tools to make their writing vivid.

questions.stem: Early in the morning, a thin ____ covered the valley, so we could barely see the trees.
questions.why: Mist is a cloud of tiny water drops near the ground that makes things hard to see.

questions.stem: In the sentence “My little brother gobbled his breakfast before the hike,” what does gobbled mean?
questions.why: To gobble is to eat very fast.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The roots of our family go back to a small village in the mountains,” the word roots means the parts of a plant under the ground.
questions.why: Here roots means where a family comes from, its origins.

questions.stem: Is each line from a hiking poem a simile or a metaphor?

rows.text: The trail was a ribbon tied around the hill.
My legs felt as heavy as stones.
The sun is a golden coin in the sky.
The wind whistled like a teapot.

questions.why: A simile uses like or as; a metaphor says one thing is another.

questions.stem: Select the line from “Up the Green Mountain” that uses personification.

segments.text: The old juniper trees lean over the trail and whisper secrets to the wind.
My little sister skips ahead, then stops to pick tiny yellow flowers.
Early in the morning, my whole family climbs the mountain path near Abha.
My grandmother opens a basket, and we gobble warm bread with honey.

questions.why: Trees cannot really whisper secrets; that is a human action.

questions.stem: In “Up the Green Mountain,” the mist wraps around the family “like a soft gray blanket.” What does this simile help the reader understand?
options: The mist feels gentle and covers them closely.
The mist is cold, wet, and very dangerous.
The family carries blankets up the mountain.
The weather is warm and bright and sunny.
questions.why: A blanket is soft and wraps around you, like the mist.

questions.stem: Which kind of figurative language is used in each phrase from “Up the Green Mountain”?

rows.text: my father ... a camel who never tires
the clouds lie below us like a sleeping sea
the old juniper trees ... whisper secrets to the wind

questions.why: Like signals a simile; calling the father a camel is a metaphor; whispering trees are personified.

questions.stem: True or false: “Up the Green Mountain” is written in free verse because its lines do not follow a regular rhyme pattern.
questions.why: Free verse does not need rhyme or a steady beat.

questions.stem: The speaker of “Up the Green Mountain” feels ____ about the family hike.
options: bored and eager to go home
happy and close to the family
questions.why: The speaker laughs with the family and treasures the mountain.

questions.stem: Which sentences contain personification? Choose two.
options: The kitten was as quiet as a soft feather.
The old door groaned when Grandfather pushed it open.
My brother is a walking dictionary.
The moon peeked shyly from behind the clouds.
questions.why: Peeking shyly and groaning are human actions given to things.

questions.stem: In the line “Morning mist is a curtain hiding the valley,” the poet uses a ____ to compare mist to a curtain.
questions.why: The line says the mist is a curtain without using like or as.

questions.stem: Match each family idiom to its meaning.

pairs.left: a chip off the old block
pairs.right: a child who is like a parent
settle in one place to live

questions.why: An idiom means something different from its separate words.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence names the wrong poetry term? “In my poem, the line ‘The wind sang a lullaby’ is an example of a simile because the wind does something only a person can do.”
segments: the line ‘The wind sang a lullaby’
is an example of a simile
because the wind does something only a person can do.
questions.why: Giving a human action to the wind is personification, not a simile.

questions.stem: True or false: Writing about individuality means writing about the things that make a person different from everyone else.
questions.why: Individuality is what makes someone unique.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the speaker's feeling about her name change in “My Name Is Yasmin”?

partA.stem: Part A: How does the speaker's feeling about her name change in “My Name Is Yasmin”?

options.label: A
options.text: She first wants a flower name but later chooses her cousin's name.

options.label: B
options.text: She first loves her name but later wishes it came from a story.

options.label: C
options.text: She first feels angry with her grandmother but later forgives her.

options.label: D
options.text: She first wishes for a grander name but later feels proud of her own.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: My name is not a story from the past; it is a promise still growing.

options.label: B
options.text: At first, I wished my name were as grand and famous as theirs.

options.label: C
options.text: Grandmother named me Yasmin after the jasmine vine on our garden wall.

options.label: D
options.text: My cousins all have names from old family stories, but mine came from a flower.

questions.why: The later line shows her new pride; the “At first” line shows only her early feeling.

questions.stem: Select the line from “My Name Is Yasmin” that uses personification to describe the jasmine vine.

segments.text: Each spring, it climbs higher, reaching for the sun with tiny green fingers.
Grandmother named me Yasmin after the jasmine vine on our garden wall.
and its white blossoms fill the evening air with sweetness.
It is my own, and it belongs to no one else.

questions.why: The vine is given fingers and reaches like a person.

questions.stem: Which senses does the imagery in the line “and its white blossoms fill the evening air with sweetness” from “My Name Is Yasmin” appeal to? Choose two.
questions.why: White blossoms can be seen, and sweetness in the air can be smelled.

questions.stem: In “My Name Is Yasmin,” what does the metaphor “it is a promise still growing” suggest about the speaker's name?
options: Her name was promised to her by her grandmother's mother.
Her name came from an old and well-known family story.
Her name points to a future that she is still shaping.
Her name will change into a new one when she is older.
questions.why: A promise still growing looks toward the future, like a climbing vine.

questions.stem: The speaker's comparison of herself to the jasmine in “My Name Is Yasmin” shows that she values her ____.
questions.why: She is proud that her name is her own and belongs to no one else.

questions.stem: Which line uses imagery that appeals mainly to the sense of hearing?
options: The cold stream water numbs my fingers in a moment.
Dry leaves crackle and snap beneath our hiking boots.
The scent of wild mint drifts up from the valley floor.
Golden light spills across the tops of the far hills.
questions.why: Crackle and snap are sounds.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence using roots or mist is literal or figurative.

rows.text: The roots of the old olive tree push deep into the ground.
Our family's roots are planted in the village where Grandfather was born.
A light mist hung over the lake at sunrise.
My memories of that summer are a mist that is slowly fading.

questions.why: Literal words mean exactly what they say; figurative words compare or suggest.

questions.stem: Read the lines: “My brother is a hungry wolf at dinner; / he can ____ a whole plate of rice in two minutes.” Which word best fits the metaphor?
questions.why: A hungry wolf eats fast, so gobble fits the metaphor.

questions.stem: Which statements about free verse are true? Choose two.
options: Line breaks can be used to slow down or stress certain words.
It must always be divided into four-line stanzas that rhyme.
It does not need to follow a regular rhyme scheme.
Every line must have exactly the same number of syllables.
questions.why: Free verse is open in form, but poets still choose line breaks carefully.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the lines: “Grandfather says I have his dark eyes / and his loud, happy laugh. / I am a page from his old book.” What is the speaker's perspective about her family?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the lines: “Grandfather says I have his dark eyes / and his loud, happy laugh. / I am a page from his old book.” What is the speaker's perspective about her family?

options.label: A
options.text: She wants to write a book about her grandfather.

options.label: B
options.text: She thinks her grandfather's stories are boring.

options.label: C
options.text: She wishes she looked more like her grandfather.

options.label: D
options.text: She sees herself as part of her grandfather's family story.

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase from the lines contains the metaphor that supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I have his dark eyes

options.label: B
options.text: his loud, happy laugh

options.label: C
options.text: I am a page from his old book

options.label: D
options.text: Grandfather says

questions.why: Calling herself a page from his book shows she belongs to his story.

questions.stem: In “Two Views from the Dune,” whose perspective does each detail show?

rows.text: misses the city lights
sees the stars as an audience
wants the night to last forever
counts the hours until leaving

questions.why: Each speaker describes the same desert in a different way.

questions.stem: Part A: How is the sister's perspective different from the brother's in “Two Views from the Dune”?

partA.stem: Part A: How is the sister's perspective different from the brother's in “Two Views from the Dune”?

options.label: A
options.text: She is afraid of the dark, while he enjoys the quiet desert.

options.label: B
options.text: She wants to go home early, while he wants to stay longer.

options.label: C
options.text: She dislikes the cold wind, while he likes the blowing sand.

options.label: D
options.text: She finds the desert night beautiful, while he finds it unpleasant.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I count the long hours until we pack the tent and drive back home.

options.label: B
options.text: I hope this night stretches on forever, like the dunes around our tent.

options.label: C
options.text: The wind hums an old song that my grandfather once taught me.

options.label: D
options.text: The cold wind bites my ears, and the sand creeps into everything I own.

questions.why: The sister wants the night to last, which shows she loves it.

questions.stem: Select two lines from “Two Views from the Dune” that use personification.

segments.text: The cold wind bites my ears, and the sand creeps into everything I own.
The wind hums an old song that my grandfather once taught me.
I count the long hours until we pack the tent and drive back home.
I hope this night stretches on forever, like the dunes around our tent.

questions.why: Biting, creeping, and humming are actions given to wind and sand.

questions.stem: Which metaphor in “Two Views from the Dune” shows the sister's sense of wonder?
options: like the dunes around our tent
The desert at night is empty and silent
the sand creeps into everything I own
The desert at night is a giant theater
questions.why: Calling the desert a theater is a metaphor full of wonder.

questions.stem: In “Two Views from the Dune,” both speakers begin with the same words to show that they see the same place with ____ feelings.
questions.why: The same opening makes the contrast between their perspectives clear.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning: naturalist, debris, encounter, generations.

pairs.right: a person who studies plants and animals
scattered pieces of broken or leftover material
a meeting, often an unexpected one
groups of people born around the same time

questions.why: These words often appear in writing about nature and history.

questions.stem: After the storm, the beach was covered with ____ such as broken branches and torn fishing nets.
questions.why: Debris is scattered broken material.

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? “The view of the canyon at sunset was so ____ that everyone stopped talking to look.”
questions.why: Spectacular means amazing to see.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentences “The wind blew hard” and “Please wind the clock,” the word wind is pronounced the same way.
questions.why: Wind is a homograph: one rhymes with pinned, the other with find.

questions.stem: Which meaning of the homograph bat is used in each sentence?

rows.text: A bat flew out of the cave at dusk.
Omar swung the bat and hit the ball.
The naturalist counted every bat sleeping in the old barn.
Hand me the cricket bat, please.

questions.why: Homographs are spelled the same but have different meanings.

questions.stem: Why is the journal entry in “A Naturalist's Notebook” a primary source?
options: It was written many years later by a famous author of books.
It describes the crabs, a heron, and the tide at the Red Sea.
It is printed inside an article that teaches about journals.
It was written by the person who saw the crabs firsthand.
questions.why: A primary source comes from someone who was there.

questions.stem: Using the ideas in “A Naturalist's Notebook,” decide whether each item is a primary source or a secondary source.

rows.text: a student's field journal entry
a later book about mangroves written from journals
a photograph the naturalist took that day
an encyclopedia article about crabs

questions.why: Primary sources are made by eyewitnesses; secondary sources are written later by others.

questions.stem: Part A: In the journal entry in “A Naturalist's Notebook,” what caused the crabs to run into their holes?

partA.stem: Part A: In the journal entry in “A Naturalist's Notebook,” what caused the crabs to run into their holes?

options.label: A
options.text: The student came too close.

options.label: B
options.text: The sun became too hot.

options.label: C
options.text: The tide came in quickly.

options.label: D
options.text: A heron landed nearby.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: When a heron landed nearby, they all ran into their holes at once!

options.label: B
options.text: I saw at least twenty small crabs waving one giant claw.

options.label: C
options.text: In it, they record the date, the weather, and everything they observe.

options.label: D
options.text: One of their most important tools is a simple notebook called a field journal.

questions.why: The word when links the heron's landing to the crabs' running.

questions.stem: Which questions can a reader answer using “A Naturalist's Notebook”? Choose two.
options: Why is a later book about mangroves a secondary source?
What is the name of the student naturalist?
How many herons live on the Red Sea coast?
What do naturalists record in a field journal?
questions.why: Readers check whether the text gives enough information to answer a question.

questions.stem: In “A Naturalist's Notebook,” a naturalist is a scientist who ____.
options: builds tools for recording the weather
studies plants and animals where they live
writes books about events from long ago
questions.why: The first sentence defines the word naturalist.

questions.stem: The ____ cliff dropped straight down to the sea, with no ledges to stand on.
questions.why: Sheer can mean almost straight up and down.

questions.stem: Match each sentence to the meaning of the homograph sheer.

pairs.left: The climbers stared up at the sheer rock wall.
The curtains were made of sheer white cloth.
pairs.right: so thin you can see through it

pairs.left: We found the hidden spring by sheer luck.

questions.why: Context shows which meaning of sheer is being used.

questions.stem: In which sentence does the word lead rhyme with bed?
options: The guide will lead us through the forest.
The old pipes were made of heavy lead.
Our captain will lead the team onto the field.
Please lead the camels to the water trough.
questions.why: Lead (a metal) rhymes with bed; lead (to guide) rhymes with seed.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence has an error in word use? “When she read her report aloud, Maya placed special emphasize on the words ‘protect the forest.’”
segments: When she read her report aloud,
questions.why: Emphasis is the noun; emphasize is the verb.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The arrow indicated the trail to the waterfall,” indicated means pointed to or showed.
questions.why: To indicate is to point out or show.

questions.stem: Part A: In “The Plant Traveler,” what caused Ibn al-Baitar to become interested in nature?

partA.stem: Part A: In “The Plant Traveler,” what caused Ibn al-Baitar to become interested in nature?

options.label: A
options.text: He traveled across North Africa and met many local healers.

options.label: B
options.text: He read many old books that were full of mistakes about plants.

options.label: C
options.text: Scholars asked him to write a huge book about natural medicines.

options.label: D
options.text: An herbalist taught him the names of wild plants when he was a boy.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: He traveled across North Africa and into Egypt and Syria.

options.label: B
options.text: As a result, he found many mistakes that older writers had made.

options.label: C
options.text: Ibn al-Baitar was born in Málaga, in Al-Andalus, around the year 1197.

options.label: D
options.text: Because of these early lessons, he became fascinated by the natural world.

questions.why: Because of signals that the lessons caused his interest.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Plant Traveler” that tells an effect of Ibn al-Baitar's checking of earlier books.

segments.text: As a result, he found many mistakes that older writers had made.
He traveled across North Africa and into Egypt and Syria.
When he was about twenty, he left home to study plants in other lands.
Ibn al-Baitar was born in Málaga, in Al-Andalus, around the year 1197.

questions.why: As a result signals an effect.

questions.stem: Is “The Plant Traveler” a primary or a secondary source?
options: primary, because it describes real events that happened long ago
secondary, because it was written later by someone who studied his life
secondary, because it is about plants instead of about people
primary, because it names real places such as Egypt and Syria
questions.why: The writer did not live with Ibn al-Baitar, so this is a secondary source.

questions.stem: Put the events of Ibn al-Baitar's life from “The Plant Traveler” in order.
sequence: He learns the names of wild plants as a boy.
He leaves home at about age twenty.
He gathers plants and questions healers in other lands.
He writes a huge book about natural medicines.
His notes are translated into other languages.
questions.why: The article tells his life in time order.

questions.stem: In paragraph 3 of “The Plant Traveler,” the phrase “for generations” means ____.
options: for only a few short weeks
by every person in one family
questions.why: A generation is about one lifetime of people, so the book was used for a very long time.

questions.stem: Which sentences use encounter correctly? Choose two.
options: Please encounter your homework before dinner tonight.
On the trail, we had a close encounter with a family of wild foxes.
The naturalist encountered the plant to make it grow faster.
Explorers may encounter sandstorms when they cross the desert.
questions.why: To encounter is to meet or come upon, often unexpectedly.

questions.stem: Decide how the homograph bow is pronounced in each sentence.

rows.text: The naturalist tied a bow on her journal.
The actor took a bow at the end of the show.
The archer pulled back his bow.
Sailors stood at the bow of the ship.

questions.why: The meaning of bow tells you how to say it.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “The guide put special emphasis on staying away from the sheer edge.” What does the guide's emphasis show?
options: The guide whispered the warning so no one could hear it.
The guide forgot to mention this warning to anyone.
The guide thought this warning was very important.
The guide thought the cliff edge was a good place to rest.
questions.why: Emphasis is special importance given to something.

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of the homograph present in this sentence: “Every naturalist must be present at the meeting before the hike.” Present means ____.
questions.why: Being present at a meeting means being there.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The tracks indicated that a fox had passed by during the night,” the word indicated means the tracks hid what had happened.
questions.why: Indicated means showed; the tracks showed that a fox had passed.

questions.stem: Part A: In “Shields of the Shore,” what is one effect of mangrove roots slowing down waves?

partA.stem: Part A: In “Shields of the Shore,” what is one effect of mangrove roots slowing down waves?

options.label: A
options.text: The shore washes away less during storms.

options.label: B
options.text: The trees grow taller in a short time.

options.label: C
options.text: The salty water turns into fresh water.

options.label: D
options.text: The waves carry fish far out to sea.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Their tangled roots rise above the mud like the legs of a giant spider.

options.label: B
options.text: Today, scientists and volunteers are planting millions of young mangroves.

options.label: C
options.text: For many years, people cut down mangroves to build roads and harbors.

options.label: D
options.text: These roots slow down waves, so the shore behind them washes away less during storms.

questions.why: The word so links the cause (slower waves) to the effect (less washing away).

questions.stem: Match each cause from “Shields of the Shore” to its effect.

pairs.left: Roots trap mud, leaves, and debris.

pairs.right: Birds nest in the branches again.

questions.why: Each cause leads to a result described in the article.

questions.stem: Which questions are answered in “Shields of the Shore”? Choose two.
options: How do mangrove roots help the shore?
How tall can a mangrove tree grow?
Why did people cut down mangroves?
Which country planted the most mangroves?
questions.why: The article explains why mangroves were cut and how roots help, but gives no heights or rankings.

questions.stem: In paragraph 3 of “Shields of the Shore,” the word spectacular suggests that the change is ____.
questions.why: Spectacular describes something amazing to see.

questions.stem: Which detail from “Shields of the Shore” would a naturalist most likely record as a firsthand observation in a field journal?
options: Some coasts lost their natural shield long ago.
Birds are nesting in the mangrove branches again.
For many years, people cut mangroves to build roads.
Mangroves grow along the coasts of two large seas.
questions.why: A field journal records what the writer sees directly.

questions.stem: Match each money word to its meaning: savings, wages, profit, loan.

pairs.right: money put aside to use later
money left after costs are paid
money borrowed that must be paid back

questions.why: These words help describe how people earn and use money.

questions.stem: Fresh water was ____ in the desert camp, so everyone drank only a little each day.
questions.why: The clue “only a little” shows that scarce means in short supply.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses afford correctly?
options: The farmer carefully afforded the seeds into neat, straight rows.
We afford the bus every morning at seven o'clock.
We can afford the tickets because we saved our money.
She will afford the ball across the field to me.
questions.why: To afford something is to have enough money to pay for it.

questions.stem: True or false: Taking a risk means doing something even though it might not turn out well.
questions.why: A risk is a chance that something bad could happen.

questions.stem: Decide whether each item is money coming in or money going out for a small business.

rows.text: profit from selling lemons
a loan payment to the bank
money from customers who buy cookies
the cost of buying seeds

questions.why: Businesses earn money from sales and spend money on costs and loans.

questions.stem: What is the main conflict in “The Mint Garden”?
options: Huda's grandmother does not like the taste of mint in tea.
Huda wants to grow mint but does not have enough money.
Huda's brother will not let her use the apartment roof.
The neighbors refuse to buy the mint that Huda grows.
questions.why: Huda's problem is that she lacks money for pots, soil, and seeds.

questions.stem: Put the events of “The Mint Garden” in order.
sequence: The shop on Huda's street stops selling mint.
Huda decides to grow mint on the roof.
Huda counts her savings.
Huda's brother offers her a loan.
Huda sells her mint and earns a profit.
questions.why: The plot moves from the problem to the solution.

questions.stem: Part A: How is Huda's money problem solved in “The Mint Garden”?

partA.stem: Part A: How is Huda's money problem solved in “The Mint Garden”?

options.label: A
options.text: The shop gives her free soil and seeds.

options.label: B
options.text: She sells her old toys to the neighbors.

options.label: C
options.text: Her brother lends her the money she is missing.

options.label: D
options.text: Her grandmother buys all the pots and seeds.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Six weeks later, bright green leaves overflowed from every pot.

options.label: B
options.text: Now mint was scarce in the neighborhood, and her grandmother complained that her afternoon tea tasted ordinary without it.

options.label: C
options.text: Then her older brother offered her a small loan.

options.label: D
options.text: Huda counted her savings.

questions.why: The loan gives Huda the money she needs to start.

questions.stem: In “The Mint Garden,” the word scarce means ____, because the shop had stopped selling mint.
questions.why: When the only shop stops selling mint, it becomes hard to find.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Mint Garden” that shows Huda's plan was a success.

segments.text: Huda sold her mint at the door each afternoon, and soon she had paid back her brother and earned a small profit.
She had only half of what she needed.
Huda counted her savings.
Unfortunately, there was a problem, because she needed pots, soil, and seeds, and she did not have enough money to buy them.

questions.why: Paying back the loan and earning a profit show success.

questions.stem: With hard work and good weather, the farmers began to ____; they built new houses and bought more land.
questions.why: New houses and more land are clues that prosper means to do well.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Sami's wages, the money he earned for washing cars on weekends, went straight into his savings jar.” Which words are a context clue for wages?
options: the money he earned for washing cars
went straight into his savings jar
questions.why: The phrase set off by commas defines wages.

questions.stem: Which sentences give a context clue that shows the meaning of profit? Choose two.
options: The shop's profit, or the money it kept after its costs, grew each month.
After paying for the flour and sugar, Ali had fifty riyals left over as profit.
The profit made everyone at the bake sale happy.
Ali was very proud of the profit he made.
questions.why: A good context clue explains or defines the word.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses a word that does not make sense? “Because the bakery's costs were higher than its sales, the owner made a large profit that month.”
segments: the owner made a large profit
questions.why: When costs are higher than sales, there is no profit.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Water was scarce, so the travelers shared every drop carefully,” the clue “shared every drop carefully” suggests that scarce means plentiful.
questions.why: People share every drop when there is very little, so scarce means in short supply.

questions.stem: Part A: What problem does Faris face after he opens his stand in “The Bicycle Doctor”?

partA.stem: Part A: What problem does Faris face after he opens his stand in “The Bicycle Doctor”?

options.label: A
options.text: The repair shop copies his idea.

options.label: B
options.text: His uncle refuses to teach him.

options.label: C
options.text: He runs out of tubes and tools.

options.label: D
options.text: No customers come on the first day.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The only repair shop in town was far away, and few families could afford the bus fare to get there.

options.label: B
options.text: On the first Saturday, nobody came.

options.label: C
options.text: Faris knew how to repair bicycles because his uncle, a patient mechanic, had taught him.

options.label: D
options.text: He decided to open a small repair stand in front of his apartment building, charging a few riyals for each repair to cover the cost of tubes and tools.

questions.why: The stand is ready, but no one comes.

questions.stem: How is the conflict resolved in “The Bicycle Doctor”?
options: Faris moves his stand to the busy repair shop across town.
Faris and Majid put up signs so people learn about the stand.
Faris lowers his prices so that more families can afford repairs.
Majid buys new bicycles for all the children who need them.
questions.why: Once people know about the stand, customers arrive.

questions.stem: Which events in “The Bicycle Doctor” happen before Faris opens his stand? Choose two.
options: His uncle teaches him to fix bikes.
Children line up with broken bicycles.
He sees children pushing broken bicycles.
questions.why: Faris learns his skill and notices the need before opening the stand.

questions.stem: In paragraph 1 of “The Bicycle Doctor,” the phrase “few families could afford the bus fare” suggests that afford means ____.
options: have enough money to pay for
questions.why: The bus fare is a cost, so afford is about having enough money.

questions.stem: In “The Bicycle Doctor,” is each event part of the conflict or part of the resolution?

rows.text: Nobody comes to the stand on the first Saturday.
Faris wonders if he wasted his savings.
Faris and Majid paint bright signs.
A line of children waits with broken bicycles.

questions.why: The conflict is the problem; the resolution is how it is solved.

questions.stem: Use context clues to match each sentence to the meaning of the word prosper, scarce, loan, or risk.

pairs.left: Small shops prosper when the neighborhood supports them.
Shade is scarce at noon in the open desert.
The bank gave the farmer a loan to buy a new pump.
pairs.right: money lent that must be repaid

pairs.left: Climbing without a rope is a risk no guide allows.
pairs.right: a chance of harm or loss

questions.why: Clues in each sentence point to the word's meaning.

questions.stem: Read: “Salma's lemonade stand earned 200 riyals, but she spent 150 riyals on lemons and cups.” Salma's profit was ____.
questions.why: Profit is what is left after costs: 200 − 150 = 50.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses context clues to show that scarce means “not enough to meet the need”?
options: Mother bought some scarce apples at the market this morning.
The scarce bird sang a lovely song from the top of the tree.
Seats were scarce at the game; hundreds of fans had to stand.
Our garden was scarce, and we enjoyed working in it every day.
questions.why: Fans standing because there were too few seats shows the meaning.

questions.stem: True or false: A shop that pays all its workers' wages and costs and still has money left over at the end of the month has made a profit.
questions.why: Money left after all costs are paid is profit.

questions.stem: Put the events of a plan for Rami's date-cookie stall in the order they most likely happen.
sequence: Rami borrows money from his aunt as a loan.
Rami buys flour and dates.
Rami bakes and sells the cookies.
Rami pays back the loan.
Rami keeps the profit.
questions.why: A loan comes first, and the profit is what remains after paying it back.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the main conflict in “Dates for the Fair”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the main conflict in “Dates for the Fair”?

options.label: A
options.text: The twins cannot find dates for their cookies.

options.label: B
options.text: The twins disagree about how many cookies to bake.

options.label: C
options.text: The hospital refuses to accept the money from the fair.

options.label: D
options.text: The school cancels the charity fair at the last minute.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: They intended to sell homemade date cookies and donate every riyal of profit to the children's hospital.

options.label: B
options.text: At the fair, every cookie had disappeared by noon.

options.label: C
options.text: But two days before the fair, they had a serious disagreement.

options.label: D
options.text: That evening, their mother asked each girl to explain her reasoning.

questions.why: The disagreement between the sisters is the conflict.

questions.stem: In “Dates for the Fair,” which sister holds each view?

rows.text: Making more cookies will earn more money.
Unsold cookies would waste their savings.
Baking two hundred cookies is the best plan.
Spending too much on flour and dates is a risk.

questions.why: Lama wants more cookies; Dana worries about the cost.

questions.stem: Put the events of “Dates for the Fair” in order.
sequence: The twins plan a stall for the charity fair.
The twins disagree about how many cookies to bake.
Their mother asks each girl to explain her reasoning.
The twins agree to bake one hundred cookies first.
Every cookie is gone by noon.
questions.why: The plot moves from conflict to compromise to result.

questions.stem: Which phrase is the best context clue for the meaning of compromise in paragraph 3 of “Dates for the Fair”?
options: every cookie was gone by noon at the charity fair
neither sister would change her mind at all
bake one hundred cookies first and make more only if
their mother asked each girl to explain her reasoning
questions.why: The plan mixes both sisters' ideas, which is what a compromise does.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Dates for the Fair” that tells how the twins' disagreement is settled.

segments.text: They would bake one hundred cookies first and make more only if the first batch sold quickly.
Neither sister would change her mind, and the kitchen grew uncomfortably silent.
Lama wanted to bake two hundred cookies.
For several weeks, the twins Lama and Dana had been planning a stall for their school's charity fair.

questions.why: The compromise ends the disagreement.

questions.stem: Match each key word about electronic devices to its meaning.

pairs.right: the chance or right to use something
facts and numbers collected to study something
to name a source as proof

questions.why: Knowing these words helps readers follow an argument about technology.

questions.stem: Our school library gives every student ____ to online books and science videos.
questions.why: Access means the chance or right to use something.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word drawbacks correctly?
options: One of the drawbacks of a small screen is that words are hard to read.
The drawbacks of the new tablet made it the best gift Huda ever got.
Omar listed the drawbacks of exercise, such as a stronger heart and lungs.
One of the drawbacks of the trip was that everyone enjoyed the museum.
questions.why: Drawbacks are problems, and hard-to-read words are a problem.

questions.stem: True or false: When you cite a website in a report, you tell readers where your information came from.
questions.why: To cite a source is to name where a fact or idea came from.

questions.stem: Sort each word about technology by the meaning of its prefix: tele- (far) or pre- (before).

rows.text: telephone
preview
television
predict

questions.why: Tele- means far, and pre- means before.

questions.stem: The Latin prefix counter- means “against.” What does the word counterpoint most likely mean?
options: the most important point at the very end
a point that agrees with every other idea
a number used to count up the results
an idea that argues against another idea
questions.why: Counter- means against, so a counterpoint argues against another point.

questions.stem: Match each Greek or Latin prefix found in technology words to its meaning.
questions.why: Prefix meanings help readers figure out new words such as microchip and internet.

questions.stem: Which words have a prefix that means “not” or “the opposite of”? Choose two.
questions.why: Un- and dis- mean not or the opposite of; re- means again and pre- means before.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about Mona's science report uses the wrong key word?
questions.why: Reasoning is the thinking that explains a conclusion; cite is a verb meaning to name a source.

questions.stem: True or false: The Greek prefix auto- means “self,” so an automatic screen dims by itself.
questions.why: Auto- means self, as in automatic and autograph.

questions.stem: Part A: Which reason does the author give to support the claim that tablets encourage reading?

partA.stem: Part A: Which reason does the author give to support the claim that tablets encourage reading?

options.label: A
options.text: Students with tablets never need to visit the library.

options.label: B
options.text: Students with tablets read for more minutes each day.

options.label: C
options.text: Students with tablets have fewer problems with their eyes.

options.label: D
options.text: Students with tablets finish their homework much faster.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Teachers can also send new lessons and practice activities to their classes in seconds.

options.label: B
options.text: In one survey of four hundred students, those who used tablets read nine more minutes each day.

options.label: C
options.text: Some parents worry that bright screens can tire children's eyes.

options.label: D
options.text: That is a fair counterpoint, but schools can easily require short screen breaks every twenty minutes.

questions.why: The survey result is the evidence that tablet users read more.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the author's claim in “Tablets Belong in Every Classroom”?
options: Parents should decide how long children may use screens.
Paper books are better for students than any tablet screen.
Village schools need bigger libraries than city schools.
Every student should be given a tablet to use for schoolwork.
questions.why: The author states the claim in the first sentence and supports it with reasons.

questions.stem: Under the heading “What the Numbers Show” in “Tablets Belong in Every Classroom,” which sentence tells the conclusion the author draws from the bar graph?

segments.text: In one survey of four hundred students, those who used tablets read nine more minutes each day.
This data suggests that tablets encourage reading.
Teachers can also send new lessons and practice activities to their classes in seconds.
Some parents worry that bright screens can tire children's eyes.

questions.why: The author uses the data to conclude that tablets encourage reading.

questions.stem: Under which heading of “Tablets Belong in Every Classroom” should a reader reread to find each detail?

rows.text: how many minutes students read each day
how a village student can read city books
a plan for short screen breaks

questions.why: Headings tell readers which section holds each kind of information.

questions.stem: Which details does the author of “Tablets Belong in Every Classroom” use as evidence for the claim? Choose two.
options: the price of a tablet compared with paper books
the worry that screens may tire children's eyes
the fact that one tablet can hold an entire library
the results of a survey of four hundred students
questions.why: Evidence supports the claim; the worry about eyes is the opposing view, and prices are never mentioned.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about research on devices to the key word it best shows.

pairs.left: Dr. Sara studied the survey results closely to find patterns.
Yusuf explained each step of thinking that led to his conclusion.
A new app helped the class move ahead in math.
Reem argued the opposite side to test her friend's idea.

questions.why: Each sentence describes the meaning of one key word.

questions.stem: After a careful ____ of the survey, the scientists found that most children used screens for less than two hours a day.
questions.why: An analysis is a close study of information.

questions.stem: Is each sentence about screen time an example of data or of reasoning?

rows.text: Sixty percent of the class owns a tablet.
Because most students own tablets, the school could send homework online.
In the survey, 250 families said they limit screen time.
Since outdoor play builds strong bodies, too much screen time may cause harm.

questions.why: Data are facts and numbers; reasoning explains what the facts mean.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about Maha's new laptop uses a key word incorrectly?
segments: and its drawbacks with two other models.
questions.why: Access is the right to use something, so it does not describe a feature to compare here.

questions.stem: In which sentence does the word advance mean “to move forward”?
options: Please buy your tickets in advance of the match on Friday.
The store asked for a small advance before ordering the laptop.
We were told about the change one week in advance of the trip.
Players advance to the next level after solving each puzzle.
questions.why: Players who advance move forward; in advance means beforehand.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the author respond to the counterpoint about video calls?

partA.stem: Part A: How does the author respond to the counterpoint about video calls?

options.label: A
options.text: The author argues that video calls with grandparents should be stopped completely.

options.label: B
options.text: The author ignores the counterpoint and moves straight on to the next heading.

options.label: C
options.text: The author agrees the calls matter but says one free evening still leaves room for them.

options.label: D
options.text: The author changes the claim and decides that devices have no drawbacks at all.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: However, a screen-free evening does not ban such calls; it simply protects one night for talking face to face.

options.label: B
options.text: Choose one evening, place every device in a basket, and let the conversation begin.

options.label: C
options.text: Families should switch off their devices for at least one evening each week.

options.label: D
options.text: Some people argue that video calls allow children to talk with grandparents who live far away.

questions.why: A strong argument admits what is true in a counterpoint and then explains why the claim still stands.

questions.stem: What does the line graph add to the author's argument?
options: It shows that families with more devices finish their dinner more quickly.
It shows that children mostly use their phones for school assignments.
It shows that grandparents prefer video calls to visiting their families.
It shows that conversation time drops as more devices come to the table.
questions.why: The graph's numbers fall from 40 to 19 minutes as devices increase.

questions.stem: In “Why Families Need Screen-Free Evenings,” which sentence shows the author using research to support the claim?

segments.text: A recent study by a children's health organization found that families who used phones during dinner talked to each other for only half as long.
This is true, and those calls are valuable.
Families should switch off their devices for at least one evening each week.
Choose one evening, place every device in a basket, and let the conversation begin.

questions.why: Citing a study gives the claim support from research.

questions.stem: The word disconnected under the heading “Less Talk at the Table” has the Latin prefix dis-, so it means ____.
questions.why: Dis- means not or apart, so disconnected means not connected.

questions.stem: Put the parts of the argument in “Why Families Need Screen-Free Evenings” in the order the author presents them.
sequence: the author's claim about switching off devices
research about how much families talk at dinner
a counterpoint about video calls with grandparents
a simple plan for families to get started
questions.why: The author states a claim, gives evidence, answers a counterpoint, and ends with a plan.

questions.stem: Which sentences cite a source to support an idea about screen time? Choose two.
options: Everyone knows that too much screen time is bad for young children.
I think tablets are the most useful invention of the last hundred years.
A 2022 survey by a university in Jeddah found that most students used apps to study.
The Ministry of Health advises that children need an hour of active play each day.
questions.why: To cite a source, a writer names who found or reported the information.

questions.stem: Faisal's essay claimed that games improve memory, so his sister offered a ____: many games reward fast clicking rather than careful thinking.
questions.why: A counterpoint is an argument against another idea.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about how scientists study sleep contains an error in word choice?
segments: understanding of how screens affect sleep.
questions.why: To advance understanding means to move it forward.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “Tablets are the most exciting tool a school can buy” is a claim supported by data.
questions.why: It is an opinion; it gives no facts or numbers as support.

questions.stem: The Latin prefix inter- means “between.” Why is interactive a good word for an app in which students and teachers send answers back and forth?
options: The app's actions happen between people who respond to each other.
The app works only after the teacher has checked every answer.
The app is used again and again until the answers are correct.
The app can be opened before school without an internet signal.
questions.why: Inter- means between, so interactive describes action going between people.

questions.stem: Match each key word about forming a nation to its meaning.

pairs.right: small groups chosen to do a special job
a plan offered for others to consider
a joining together of separate parts

questions.why: These words describe how groups of people work together to make decisions.

questions.stem: The class chose two ____ to speak for everyone at the student council meeting.
questions.why: Representatives are people chosen to speak or act for a group.

questions.stem: True or false: When two friends resolve a problem, they leave it without an answer.
questions.why: To resolve a problem is to settle or solve it.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “The students held a debate, arguing for and against a longer school day.” Which words are a context clue for debate?
questions.why: A debate is a discussion in which people argue for and against an idea.

questions.stem: Which kind of context clue explains the key word in each sentence about meetings and groups?

rows.text: A convention, or large formal meeting, was held in the city.
Committees for things like food, music, and games planned the fair.
The union, which means a joining of states, grew stronger.
Representatives, such as the mayor and two judges, spoke at the meeting.

questions.why: A definition clue tells the meaning; an example clue names examples.

questions.stem: Put the steps a class committee took to fix the broken water fountain in order.
sequence: The class noticed the water fountain was broken.
A committee met to talk about the problem.
The committee wrote a proposal to the principal.
The principal approved the plan, and the fountain was fixed.
questions.why: A problem is noticed first, then people plan and carry out a solution.

questions.stem: Is each sentence about the town park a problem or a solution?

rows.text: Trash piled up near the benches every weekend.
Volunteers placed three new bins by the gate.
There were too few swings for all the children.
The town council voted to build four more swings.

questions.why: A problem is something wrong; a solution is the action that fixes it.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “The situation grew worse; the river kept rising, and the roads were closed.” What does situation mean here?
options: the conditions happening at a certain time
a written plan that leaders make together
a meeting held to make an important choice
a quiet place where people go to rest
questions.why: The clues describe what is happening, so situation means the conditions at that time.

questions.stem: The two teams could not agree, so the coach asked them to ____ the argument by voting.
questions.why: To resolve an argument is to settle it.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about the flood uses the wrong word?
questions.why: A flood creates a dangerous situation, not a debate.

questions.stem: Part A: What problem did the Great Compromise solve?

partA.stem: Part A: What problem did the Great Compromise solve?

options.label: A
options.text: George Washington did not want to lead the meetings in Philadelphia.

options.label: B
options.text: Twelve states could not find a city large enough for their meeting.

options.label: C
options.text: Large and small states disagreed about how many votes each should have.

options.label: D
options.text: The national government could not collect taxes to pay its soldiers.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Under this plan, the national government could not collect taxes, so it had no money to pay its soldiers or its debts.

options.label: B
options.text: George Washington was chosen to lead the meetings.

options.label: C
options.text: Large states wanted more votes in Congress because they had more people, but small states feared that they would be ignored.

options.label: D
options.text: Congress would have two parts.

questions.why: The compromise settled the disagreement between large and small states.

questions.stem: In “A Plan for a Stronger Nation,” which sentence explains the problem with the first national government?

segments.text: Under this plan, the national government could not collect taxes, so it had no money to pay its soldiers or its debts.
George Washington was chosen to lead the meetings.
Congress would have two parts.
After the American Revolution, the thirteen states agreed to a plan called the Articles of Confederation.

questions.why: Without taxes, the government had no money, which was the problem.

questions.stem: Using the timeline in “A Plan for a Stronger Nation,” put the events in order.
sequence: The Articles of Confederation were approved.
The convention began in Philadelphia.
The Constitution was signed.
Enough states approved the Constitution.
questions.why: The timeline runs from 1781 to 1788.

questions.stem: What does the word delegates most likely mean as it is used under the heading “The Great Compromise”?
options: rules written down to settle a problem
people sent to act for their states
questions.why: The earlier mention of representatives from twelve states is a clue that delegates are people sent to act for their states.

questions.stem: Under which heading in “A Plan for a Stronger Nation” should a reader reread to find each fact?

rows.text: who led the meetings
how the Senate would be set up
why soldiers were not paid

questions.why: Headings show which section holds each fact.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about community decisions to the key word it describes.

pairs.left: The leaders met for three days to write new rules.
The class voted on Sara's plan for a school garden.
Ten small towns joined to form one city.
Groups of students planned the food, the games, and the decorations.

questions.why: Each sentence gives an example of one key word.

questions.stem: Before the vote, the two sides held a long ____ in which each speaker had three minutes to argue.
questions.why: A debate is a discussion where people argue different sides.

questions.stem: Which sentences use the word resolve correctly? Choose two.
options: The two countries asked a judge to help resolve their argument.
Please resolve the cake into eight equal pieces for the guests.
The neighbors met to resolve the problem of the noisy generator.
The children resolved loudly when the team scored a goal.
questions.why: Resolve means to settle or solve a problem.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about the town council contains an error?
segments: to sit on the town council
questions.why: Representatives are elected people; a situation is a set of conditions.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “The union of the two schools created one large school,” the word union means “a separation.”
questions.why: A union is a joining together, the opposite of a separation.

questions.stem: Part A: What was the main problem the emirates faced in 1968?

partA.stem: Part A: What was the main problem the emirates faced in 1968?

options.label: A
options.text: Each emirate was too small to protect itself and build services alone.

options.label: B
options.text: The rulers could not decide which city should become the capital.

options.label: C
options.text: Britain wanted the emirates to form a union before the next year.

options.label: D
options.text: Ras Al Khaimah refused to talk with any of the other emirates.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: On 2 December 1971, six emirates formed the United Arab Emirates, and Sheikh Zayed became its first president.

options.label: B
options.text: Ras Al Khaimah joined a few weeks later, in February 1972.

options.label: C
options.text: Each one was too small to protect itself and to build modern schools, hospitals, and roads alone.

options.label: D
options.text: They invited the other rulers to join them, and for nearly four years the leaders discussed how a union of the emirates could work fairly for everyone.

questions.why: The section titled “A Difficult Situation” explains the problem.

questions.stem: Which detail appears in the timeline of “Seven Emirates, One Nation” but is NOT stated in the paragraphs?
options: Abu Dhabi and Dubai agreed to unite in February 1968.
Ras Al Khaimah joined the new country in February 1972.
Britain said in 1968 that it would leave the Gulf region.
The United Arab Emirates was formed in December 1971.
questions.why: Rereading shows that only the timeline gives the month of the first agreement.

questions.stem: Which actions helped solve the problem described under the heading “A Difficult Situation”? Choose two.
options: Each emirate built its own army and hospitals.
The leaders spent years discussing a fair union.
Two rulers agreed to work together as partners.
Britain agreed to stay in the Gulf for longer.
questions.why: Working as partners and planning a fair union solved the problem.

questions.stem: Under the heading “Talking Together,” the clue “work as partners” helps a reader understand that a union is ____.
options: a joining of separate parts into one
a long meeting held to settle a quarrel
a person chosen to speak for a group
a written plan that leaders vote on
questions.why: Partners join together, so a union joins separate parts into one.

questions.stem: In “Seven Emirates, One Nation,” is each detail part of the problem or part of the solution?

rows.text: Britain announced it would leave the Gulf region.
Two rulers agreed to work as partners.
Each emirate was too small to build hospitals alone.
Six emirates formed one country in 1971.

questions.why: The problem comes first; the solution is how the leaders responded.

questions.stem: The mayor's ____ to build a footbridge over the highway was accepted after two committees studied its cost and safety.
questions.why: A proposal is a suggested plan that others consider.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Although the representatives argued for hours, they finally reached a resolution that satisfied both sides.” Using the meaning of resolve, what does resolution most likely mean?
options: a question that has no answer
a decision that settles a problem
a list of people at a large meeting
a speech that starts an argument
questions.why: To resolve is to settle, so a resolution is a decision that settles a problem.

questions.stem: Which sentence about the 1787 meeting in Philadelphia uses an appositive to define a key word?

segments.text: The convention, a formal meeting of state leaders, began in May.
The delegates argued about votes for many weeks.
Some states had far more people than others.
Washington listened carefully to every speaker.

questions.why: An appositive is a phrase set off by commas that renames or defines a word.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “The committees could not resolve the situation, so the representatives called for a new debate,” the problem is still not solved at the end of the sentence.
questions.why: The committees failed, so a new debate is needed.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about forming a stronger union contains an error?
questions.why: Both verbs must be in the past tense: debated and resolved.

questions.stem: Match each key word from the folktale unit to its meaning.

pairs.right: help or advice about what to do
the act of chasing or trying to get something

questions.why: These words often describe the hero's journey in a folktale.

questions.stem: Nadia showed her ____ by writing a thank-you card to the nurse who helped her.
questions.why: Gratitude is the feeling of being thankful.

questions.stem: True or false: Personification gives human actions or feelings to something that is not human, as in “The wind whispered through the palms.”
questions.why: Wind cannot really whisper, so the sentence uses personification.

questions.stem: Does each sentence about the desert storm use personification?

rows.text: The angry sand slapped the tent walls.
The sand blew across the road.
The tired moon rested on the dunes.
The camels walked slowly toward the oasis.

questions.why: Sand cannot be angry and the moon cannot be tired, so those are personification.

questions.stem: Which word means the opposite of previous?
questions.why: Previous means coming before, so its opposite is next.

questions.stem: Which phrases give human qualities to nature? Choose two.
options: the mountain was covered in snow
the river sang a gentle song
the river flowed past the village
the mountain frowned at the travelers
questions.why: Singing and frowning are human actions.

questions.stem: In the sentence “The fire greedily gobbled the dry logs,” the writer gives the fire the human quality of ____.
questions.why: Gobbling greedily is how a hungry person eats.

questions.stem: Read: “Dark clouds gathered, and the old fisherman pulled his boat higher onto the sand.” What will most likely happen next?
options: The sand will turn to gold.
Fish will jump into the boat.
questions.why: Dark clouds and the fisherman's action are clues that a storm is coming.

questions.stem: Put these events about Tariq's search for his lost falcon in order.
sequence: Tariq's falcon flew away during a sandstorm.
An old herder offered Tariq guidance.
Tariq crossed the dunes in pursuit of the bird.
Tariq found the falcon resting on a palm tree.
questions.why: The problem comes first, then help, the journey, and the ending.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about the weaver uses the wrong word?
questions.why: People thank others with gratitude, a feeling of being thankful.

questions.stem: Part A: Which theme does “The Lost Net of the Singing Sea” best express?

partA.stem: Part A: Which theme does “The Lost Net of the Singing Sea” best express?

options.label: A
options.text: The sea is far too dangerous for anyone to cross.

options.label: B
options.text: Courage and help from others can lead to success.

options.label: C
options.text: Old people always know more than young people.

options.label: D
options.text: It is wiser to stay home than to travel far away.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: One night a jealous wind snatched her finest net and carried it far across the water.

options.label: B
options.text: Hamad's arms ached, yet he remembered the old man's words.

options.label: C
options.text: Long ago, in a village where the sea sang softly to the shore each evening, there lived an old woman who made beautiful fishing nets.

options.label: D
options.text: Her son Hamad, determined to recover it, set out at dawn in his small wooden boat.

questions.why: Hamad keeps going because of his courage and the fisherman's advice.

questions.stem: Which sentences in “The Lost Net of the Singing Sea” use personification to describe the wind or the waves? Select two sentences.

segments.text: One night a jealous wind snatched her finest net and carried it far across the water.
Her son Hamad, determined to recover it, set out at dawn in his small wooden boat.
The waves grumbled and pushed against him, but he kept rowing.
Hamad thanked him and followed the gulls.

questions.why: A wind cannot be jealous and waves cannot grumble; those are human qualities.

questions.stem: Which detail helps a reader predict that Hamad's journey will be difficult?
options: The village sits beside a sea that sings each evening.
His mother makes beautiful nets in the village.
The fisherman warns that the sea will grow angry.
Hamad sets out at dawn in his own small boat.
questions.why: The warning hints that the sea will become dangerous.

questions.stem: In the sentence “At last he detected a flash of silver between two rocks,” the word detected means ____.
questions.why: Hamad noticed the shining net.

questions.stem: In “The Lost Net of the Singing Sea,” does each detail help Hamad or make his journey harder?

rows.text: the advice of the old fisherman
the grumbling waves
the gulls flying ahead
the black clouds and roaring sea

questions.why: The setting creates obstacles, while the fisherman and the gulls guide him.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about a journey to the key word it describes.

pairs.left: The judges announced which team had won the race.
The teacher gave tips on how to finish the project.
A green shoot pushed up out of the soil.
The guard noticed a small sound behind the door.

questions.why: Each sentence shows the meaning of one key word.

questions.stem: The mother kept ____ her nervous son that the long trip across the mountains would be safe.
questions.why: Assuring means telling someone something to make them feel sure and calm.

questions.stem: Which sentences use the word previous correctly? Choose two.
options: The previous chapter explained how the net was lost.
I hope the previous storm arrives tomorrow.
We will visit our previous cousins next summer.
Our previous teacher moved to Abha last year.
questions.why: Previous describes something that came before, not something in the future.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about the hunter's falcon contains a word-choice error?
segments: until it detected from the clouds.
questions.correction: until it emerged from the clouds.
questions.why: Emerged means came out; detected means noticed.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “Her pursuit of the gold medal took six years of training,” pursuit means “giving up on a goal.”
questions.why: A pursuit is an effort to reach or get something.

questions.stem: Part A: What will most likely happen next?

partA.stem: Part A: What will most likely happen next?

options.label: A
options.text: The old traveler will appear and climb the mountain himself.

options.label: B
options.text: Salma will return home because the climb was too difficult.

options.label: C
options.text: Salma will break the rock and free the water for her village.

options.label: D
options.text: An eagle will chase Salma away from the top of the mountain.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Long ago, a young weaver named Salma lived at the foot of a tall mountain whose stony face frowned down on her village.

options.label: B
options.text: She pressed her ear against it and heard water murmuring inside.

options.label: C
options.text: Every spring, the village well ran dry, and the people walked for hours to fetch water.

options.label: D
options.text: One morning, an old traveler stopped at Salma's door.

questions.why: Hearing water inside the rock and lifting her hammer suggest she will free the spring.

questions.stem: Which lessons does “The Mountain That Kept Its Secrets” teach? Choose two.
options: Strangers should never be trusted with family secrets.
Kindness to others can bring unexpected rewards.
Mountains are too dangerous for young people to climb.
People who keep trying after they fail can reach their goals.
questions.why: Salma's kindness earns the secret, and she keeps climbing after slipping.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Mountain That Kept Its Secrets” uses personification to show that the setting is warning Salma?

segments.text: As she climbed, the wind tugged at her scarf and tried to pull her backward, and loose stones whispered warnings under her feet.
Salma packed a rope and a small hammer and began the long, dangerous climb.
Near the summit, after many exhausting hours, she finally discovered the eagle's rock.
Salma lifted her hammer.

questions.why: Stones cannot really whisper warnings; the author gives them a human action.

questions.stem: How does the setting at the beginning of “The Mountain That Kept Its Secrets” create the problem?
options: The mountain blocks the traveler from reaching the village.
The eagles near the summit steal the villagers' bread.
The dry well forces villagers to walk far for water.
The spring wind ruins the cloth that Salma weaves.
questions.why: The village's dry well is the problem Salma sets out to solve.

questions.stem: Match each part of the setting in “The Mountain That Kept Its Secrets” to the human action the author gives it.
questions.why: Each phrase is personification: a human action given to nature.

questions.stem: Grateful for the stranger's ____, the boy followed the map exactly and reached the valley before nightfall.
questions.why: Guidance is helpful advice, which the map and directions gave him.

questions.stem: Read: “Each previous attempt to cross the icy river had failed, but this time Karim tied himself to a strong rope.” What outcome does the sentence lead a reader to predict?
options: Karim will probably wait until the river dries up.
Karim will probably cross the river safely this time.
Karim will probably give up and go back home today.
Karim will probably lose his rope in the icy water.
questions.why: The words but this time and the new rope suggest a different, successful outcome.

questions.stem: Is each sentence about a desert night an example of personification or of a simile?

rows.text: The emerging moon peeked shyly over the hills.
The emerging moon was as round as a silver plate.
The stars winked at the sleepy travelers.
The sand glowed like hot coals.

questions.why: A simile compares with like or as; personification gives human actions to things.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “She kept assuring the frightened children with a calm voice,” assuring means helping someone feel certain and safe.
questions.why: To assure someone is to make them feel sure and calm.

questions.stem: Put these events from a folktale about Mariam's pursuit of a stolen lamp in order.
sequence: A thief stole the family's golden lamp.
Mariam chased the thief into the dark forest.
A talking owl gave Mariam guidance.
Mariam brought the lamp home, full of gratitude.
questions.why: Folktale plots move from a problem, through a journey and help, to a happy outcome.

questions.stem: Match each key word from the poetry unit to its meaning.

pairs.right: having big goals and working hard to reach them
a pleased feeling after doing something well
shook suddenly from fear or cold

questions.why: These words describe characters and feelings in poems.

questions.stem: Lina ____ all twelve lines so she could recite them without looking at the page.
questions.why: To memorize is to learn something by heart.

questions.stem: True or false: Words that rhyme, such as light and night, end with the same sounds.
questions.why: Rhyming words share their ending sounds.

questions.stem: What does the homograph bat mean in each sentence?

rows.text: A bat flew out of the old cave at sunset.
Ahmed swung the bat and hit the ball.
The bat hung upside down from a branch.

columns.text: a stick for hitting a ball

questions.why: Homographs are spelled the same but have different meanings.

questions.stem: Which pair of words are homographs?
options: big (large in size) and huge (very large in size)
wind (moving air) and wind (to turn a key)
sea (a large ocean) and see (to look at something)
hot (very warm) and cold (not warm at all)
questions.why: Homographs have the same spelling but different meanings.

questions.stem: Which sentences use repetition to create a strong feeling? Choose two.
options: Run, run, run to the finish line!
The runner crossed the line and smiled.
We tried our very best in the final race.
We will try, and try, and try again.
questions.why: Repeating a word makes the feeling stronger.

questions.stem: A poem that tells a story with characters and events is called a ____ poem.
questions.why: A narrative poem tells a story.

questions.stem: Put the lines of this rhyming poem about a kite in order so that each pair of lines rhymes and makes sense.
sequence: My kite climbs high above the sand,
It tugs the string inside my hand,
It dances with the ocean breeze,
And floats above the swaying trees.
questions.why: Sand rhymes with hand, and breeze rhymes with trees.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about Sami's speech uses the wrong word?
questions.why: Satisfaction is the pleased feeling after doing something well.

questions.stem: True or false: Free verse is poetry that must rhyme at the end of every line.
questions.why: Free verse does not need rhyme or a regular rhythm.

questions.stem: Part A: Which theme does “The Boy Who Planted Shade” best express?

partA.stem: Part A: Which theme does “The Boy Who Planted Shade” best express?

options.label: A
