questions.stem: In a script, the lines that the characters speak are called the ____.
questions.why: Dialogue is the words characters say to each other.

questions.stem: Why do playwrights include stage directions such as “(astounded, dropping her book)”?
options: to show how a character feels and moves
to give the title of the next scene
to tell audience members when to clap
to list every character in the cast
questions.why: Stage directions tell actors and readers how characters feel and what they do.

questions.stem: How does Omar's perspective change during “The Tortoise Who Disappeared”?

partA.stem: How does Omar's perspective change during “The Tortoise Who Disappeared”?

options.label: A
options.text: He first wants to search but later decides to go home.

options.label: B
options.text: He first suspects Khalid but later sees that he was wrong.

options.label: C
options.text: He first feels calm but later becomes angry at Khalid.

options.label: D
options.text: He first blames Maryam but later blames the hot weather.

partB.stem: Which line from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I heard my name!

options.label: B
options.text: I suppose I should reconsider what I said.

options.label: C
options.text: I saw Khalid standing near the garden after school.

options.label: D
options.text: Look at this freshly dug soil under the lettuce.

questions.why: When Omar says he should reconsider, he shows that he has changed his mind.

questions.stem: What does Omar mean when he says, “Appearances can be deceiving”?
options: Things are not always what they first seem to be.
Looking neat matters more than being kind to others.
People should always trust the first thing they see.
Clues are useless when trying to solve a mystery.
questions.why: Omar learns that the situation looked bad for Khalid, but it was not what it seemed.

questions.stem: Which line from “The Tortoise Who Disappeared” shows that Maryam wants to use evidence before deciding what happened?

segments.text: We should interpret the clues before we blame anyone.
Our tortoise, Qamar, was inside this fence yesterday afternoon.
Here she is, concealed beneath the leaves and perfectly safe!
Maybe he took her home without asking.

questions.why: To interpret clues means to figure out what they show.

questions.stem: In the stage directions, the word perplexed shows that Maryam feels ____.
questions.why: Maryam cannot understand how the tortoise escaped, so she is perplexed.

questions.stem: Which two details from “The Tortoise Who Disappeared” help the reader visualize the setting? Choose two.
options: a pile of leafy lettuce that nobody has touched
I locked the gate when I left
Maybe he took her home without asking
a low wooden fence surrounds a patch of grass
questions.why: The setting description at the start of a scene paints a picture of the place.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about the detective club contains an error in word choice?
segments: Jana asked her brother to precise
questions.correction: Jana asked her brother to interpret
questions.why: To interpret is to explain the meaning of something; precise means exact.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word reconsider correctly?
options: He reconsidered the heavy ball all the way across the field to his teammate.
The frightened cat reconsidered under the bed until the loud storm ended.
We reconsidered our sandwiches at noon in the busy school cafeteria.
After hearing new evidence, the judge agreed to reconsider her decision.
questions.why: To reconsider means to think again about a decision or opinion.

questions.stem: True or false: The proverb “Still waters run deep” suggests that a quiet person may have deep thoughts and feelings.
questions.why: The proverb compares a quiet person to calm water that is deeper than it looks.

questions.stem: The young detectives were ____ by the empty terrarium: the lid was locked, the glass was unbroken, and yet the lizard was gone.
questions.why: The clues do not make sense together, so the detectives are confused, or perplexed.

questions.stem: Which three words could describe a character who studies every clue carefully and asks many questions? Choose three.
questions.why: A careful, curious detective is inquisitive, precise, and observant.

questions.stem: Which word names a group of lines that forms one section of a poem?
questions.why: A stanza is like a paragraph in a poem.

questions.stem: Match each poetry term from “How Do I Hold the Summer?” to its meaning.

pairs.right: repeating the same beginning sound in nearby words
a regular pattern of strong and weak beats
a short poem that expresses personal feelings
a way of showing a thought or feeling

questions.why: Knowing poetry terms helps you talk about how a poem is built.

questions.stem: The peacock spread its bright blue ____ to show off its beautiful tail feathers.
questions.why: Plumes are large, showy feathers.

questions.stem: True or false: Barren land is covered with thick, green plants and tall trees.
questions.why: Barren land has few or no plants growing on it.

questions.stem: Grandmother's old photograph is ____ to me because it reminds me of our happy trip to Abha.
questions.why: Something meaningful is important because of the feelings or memories it holds.

questions.stem: In the first stanza of “Keeping the Sea,” what does the poet compare the waves to?
questions.why: The line “The waves are silver ribbons” is a metaphor that compares waves to ribbons.

questions.stem: Decide whether each line from “Keeping the Sea” uses a simile or a metaphor.

rows.text: I hold the warm and golden afternoon like water in my hand.
The waves are silver ribbons that unravel on the sand;
and all the fishing boats are sleepy whales that drift nearby.

questions.why: A simile uses like or as; a metaphor says one thing is another.

questions.stem: Which line from “Keeping the Sea” best shows the theme that we can hold on to happy memories?

segments.text: I fill a jar with memories, with laughter, salt, and light,
The seagulls are writing messages in circles on the sky,
collecting every shining shell the tide delivered here before.
and all the fishing boats are sleepy whales that drift nearby.

questions.why: Filling a jar with memories shows the speaker saving the joy of summer.

questions.stem: True or false: “Keeping the Sea” has two stanzas, and each stanza has four lines.
questions.why: A blank line separates the two four-line stanzas.

questions.stem: “Keeping the Sea” is a lyric poem because it ____.
questions.why: A lyric poem shares a speaker's own thoughts and emotions.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about a summer day uses a simile or a metaphor.

rows.text: The sun was a golden coin in the sky.
The sand felt as hot as an oven.
Summer is a book I never want to close.
The waves ran like children to the shore.

questions.why: Look for like or as to spot a simile.

questions.stem: Which two lines use alliteration? Choose two.
options: The moon is round and white.
We laughed beneath the palm tree.
questions.why: Alliteration repeats the same first sound in words that are close together.

questions.stem: In the line “My memory is a treasure chest,” the poet uses a ____ to compare memory to a treasure chest without using like or as.
questions.why: A metaphor makes a direct comparison without like or as.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence explaining similes contains an error?
questions.why: A simile always uses like or as; a metaphor does not.

questions.stem: Which sentence best explains the metaphor “Her laugh was music on a sad day”?
options: She played music on the radio every afternoon.
Her laugh was loud and hurt other people's ears.
She liked to sing songs whenever she felt sad.
Her laugh was pleasant and made a sad day feel better.
questions.why: The metaphor compares the laugh to music to show that it was pleasant and comforting.

questions.stem: Read the lines: “The SUN is UP, the DAY is BRIGHT, / The BIRDS are SINGing IN the LIGHT.” Which statement best describes the meter of these lines?

partA.stem: Read the lines: “The SUN is UP, the DAY is BRIGHT, / The BIRDS are SINGing IN the LIGHT.” Which statement best describes the meter of these lines?

options.label: A
options.text: Each line has a steady pattern of four strong beats.

options.label: B
options.text: Each line has exactly two strong beats.

options.label: C
options.text: Only the first line has strong beats.

options.label: D
options.text: The lines have no pattern of beats at all.

partB.stem: Which feature of the lines best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The second line begins with the word The.

options.label: B
options.text: The lines describe a bright morning.

options.label: C
options.text: Both lines describe things found in nature.

options.label: D
options.text: Weak and strong syllables take turns in a regular pattern.

questions.why: Meter is the regular pattern of strong and weak beats in a line of poetry.

questions.stem: Sort each feature: does it describe a rhymed poem with regular meter or a poem written in free verse?

rows.text: Lines follow a steady beat.
Lines can be any length.
Ending sounds repeat in a pattern.
Lines sound like natural speech.

questions.why: Free verse has no set rhyme or meter, so it often sounds like everyday speech.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states a theme a reader might find in a lyric poem about saving seashells at the end of summer?
options: Small objects can keep precious memories alive.
Summer is the hottest season of the whole year.
Seashells are found on many beaches in the world.
Collecting seashells can be dangerous for children.
questions.why: A theme is a message about life, not a fact about the topic.

questions.stem: Put these steps for finding the theme of a lyric poem in a logical order.
sequence: Read the poem and notice the speaker's feelings.
Look for images and words that repeat.
Ask what the speaker learns or realizes.
State the lesson in a complete sentence.
questions.why: Finding a theme starts with noticing details and ends with stating a message.

questions.stem: A poet's choice of strong, colorful words is a form of personal ____, a way of showing feelings to readers.
questions.why: Expression is the way a person shows thoughts and feelings.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the theme of “After the Rain in the Desert”?

partA.stem: Which statement best expresses the theme of “After the Rain in the Desert”?

options.label: A
options.text: Desert storms are dangerous and should be avoided.

options.label: B
options.text: Wind is the most powerful force found in the desert.

options.label: C
options.text: Something that seems empty may be quietly waiting to grow.

options.label: D
options.text: Bees travel long distances to find flowers in spring.

partB.stem: Which line from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: and the bees were humming, busy as merchants in a crowded market.

options.label: B
options.text: Then one evening the heavy clouds arrived,

options.label: C
options.text: The land had not been empty after all.

options.label: D
options.text: For months the valley was barren and brown,

questions.why: The speaker realizes that the barren land was only waiting, which reveals the theme.

questions.stem: Classify each line from “After the Rain in the Desert” as a simile or a metaphor.

rows.text: a dusty page that nobody wanted to open or read
Purple flowers opened like delicate umbrellas
busy as merchants in a crowded market
tiny green fingers were reaching upward everywhere

questions.why: Similes use like or as; metaphors call one thing another.

questions.stem: Which two features show that “After the Rain in the Desert” is written in free verse? Choose two.
options: The lines have different lengths and no steady meter.
Each line ends with a word that rhymes.
The lines do not follow a regular rhyme pattern.
Every stanza has exactly two short lines.
questions.why: Free verse does not use a fixed rhyme scheme or meter.

questions.stem: In the second stanza, what does the phrase “gray plumes of feathers” suggest about the clouds?
options: They are soft and light, drifting like feathers.
They are birds flying together in a large flock.
They are sharp, hard, and about to break apart.
They are thin lines of smoke from a small fire.
questions.why: Plumes are soft feathers, so the image makes the clouds seem light and soft.

questions.stem: The word barren in the first stanza most likely means ____.
options: empty and unable to grow plants
wet and full of rich soil
questions.why: Before the rain, the valley is brown and dusty, so it is barren.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about a poetry lesson uses a key word incorrectly?
questions.why: A group of lines followed by a blank space is a stanza; alliteration is a sound device.

questions.stem: Match each line of poetry to the device it uses: alliteration, simile, metaphor, or personification.

pairs.left: The moon is a lantern in the night.
The river ran like a racing horse.
The old door groaned and complained.

questions.why: Each device creates a different effect: sound, comparison, or human qualities.

questions.stem: Which line uses a metaphor to describe a barren place?
options: The empty field stretched far and wide.
The empty field was a forgotten page.
The empty field was quiet like a library.
The empty field felt as dry as old bread.
questions.why: Only the first line says the field is something else without using like or as.

questions.stem: True or false: In free verse, a poet must keep exactly the same meter in every line.
questions.why: Free verse does not follow a set meter.

questions.stem: A poem describes a barren tree that blooms again every spring. Which two statements could be its theme? Choose two.
options: Spring is the shortest season of the year.
Hard times do not last forever.
Trees need water in order to grow tall.
Hope can return after a difficult period.
questions.why: A theme is a lesson about life that the poem's images suggest.

questions.stem: Match each word about space science with its meaning: orbit, diameter, spheres, approximately.

pairs.right: the curved path one object follows around another in space
the distance straight across a circle through its center
close to an exact amount, but not exact

questions.why: Knowing these words helps you read about planets and their movements.

questions.stem: The Moon takes ____ 27 days to travel once around Earth, so the number is close but not exact.
questions.why: Approximately means about or nearly, which fits a number that is close but not exact.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “Earth's orbit around the Sun takes one year,” the word orbit means a curved path around an object in space.
questions.why: An orbit is the path a planet or moon follows around another body.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word spheres correctly?
options: The spheres of the box had four sharp, pointed corners.
The Sun, the Moon, and Earth are all huge spheres.
Sara folded the paper into two flat, square spheres.
Ahmed drew a straight spheres from one side to the other.
questions.why: A sphere is round like a ball, so planets and moons are spheres.

questions.stem: Each word below comes from a Greek root. Tell which root meaning each word uses: astronomical, geology, thermometer, asteroid, diameter.

rows.text: astronomical
geology
thermometer
asteroid
diameter

questions.why: Greek roots such as astro, geo, and meter give clues to the meanings of many science words.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of “Al-Biruni Measures Earth”?
options: Al-Biruni used a mountain, an angle, and math to find Earth's size.
Al-Biruni proved that earlier thinkers were wrong about the shape of Earth.
Al-Biruni traveled across many deserts to measure the distance between towns.
Al-Biruni climbed mountains because he enjoyed the view of the horizon.
questions.why: The central idea tells what the whole passage is mostly about: how Al-Biruni measured Earth.

questions.stem: Part A: According to the diagram, what did Al-Biruni measure from the mountaintop?

partA.stem: Part A: According to the diagram, what did Al-Biruni measure from the mountaintop?

options.label: A
options.text: the angle of dip toward the horizon

options.label: B
options.text: the length of the mountain's shadow

options.label: C
options.text: the distance back to the town

options.label: D
options.text: the height of the clouds above him

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: He measured how far the horizon dipped below a level line.

options.label: B
options.text: Al-Biruni found a simpler way.

options.label: C
options.text: Other thinkers had tried before, but their methods needed long trips across deserts.

options.label: D
options.text: First, he measured the height of a mountain near the town of Nandana.

questions.why: The diagram's label “angle of dip” matches the sentence about how far the horizon dipped.

questions.stem: Put the steps Al-Biruni followed to measure Earth in order.
sequence: He measured the height of a mountain near Nandana.
He climbed to the top and looked at the horizon.
He measured how far the horizon dipped below a level line.
He used a calculation to work out the size of Earth.
questions.why: Signal words such as first, next, and with these two numbers show the order of the steps.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Al-Biruni Measures Earth” answers the question “How close was Al-Biruni's answer to the answer used today?”

segments.text: Al-Biruni found a simpler way.
He measured how far the horizon dipped below a level line.
His answer was approximately the same as the one scientists use today.
He showed that a clever idea can be as useful as a long and difficult journey.

questions.why: The sentence with approximately the same answers the question directly.

questions.stem: Which two details support the idea that Al-Biruni's method was simpler than earlier methods? Choose two.
options: He measured the height of clouds over Nandana.
He asked other scholars to travel for him.
He did not need to make long trips across deserts.
He needed only a mountain height and one angle.
questions.why: Relevant details explain why his method was simpler: no long trips and only two numbers.

questions.stem: Which two words share a Greek root meaning “star”? Choose two.
questions.why: Astro and aster both mean star, as in astronomical and asterisk (a star-shaped mark).

questions.stem: Find and fix the error: “The astronomers set clear criteria to evaluation which comet photos were the sharpest.”
questions.why: After to, use the verb evaluate, which means to judge carefully.

questions.stem: Before choosing a telescope, the astronomy club listed its ____: it had to be light, sturdy, and affordable.
questions.why: Criteria are the rules or standards used to make a choice.

questions.stem: The Greek root photo means “light” and graph means “write” or “record.” What does photograph most likely mean?
options: a letter written about the sky
a drawing made with a pencil
a map of light in the stars
questions.why: Putting the roots together gives an image recorded with light.

questions.stem: Match each Greek root found in astronomy words with its meaning: tele, scope, meter, geo.
questions.why: A telescope lets you look at far things; a meter measures; geo means earth.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does a weather balloon burst high in the sky?

partA.stem: Part A: Why does a weather balloon burst high in the sky?

options.label: A
options.text: The parachute opens and tears the side of the balloon.

options.label: B
options.text: The radiosonde becomes too heavy for the string to hold.

options.label: C
options.text: The air pressure around it drops, so it swells too much.

options.label: D
options.text: The helium freezes into ice once it is very cold.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Forecasters use the data to predict storms and plan safe flights.

options.label: B
options.text: It sends this data back to the ground by radio every few seconds.

options.label: C
options.text: Each balloon carries a small box of instruments called a radiosonde.

options.label: D
options.text: The air pressure gets lower as the balloon climbs higher.

questions.why: Lower pressure lets the balloon swell until it bursts.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Weather Balloons” answers the question “What does a radiosonde measure?”

segments.text: Each balloon carries a small box of instruments called a radiosonde.
As the balloon rises, the radiosonde measures temperature, air pressure, and moisture.
The parachute then opens, and the radiosonde drifts gently back to Earth.
At about 30 kilometers high, it finally bursts.

questions.why: The sentence that lists temperature, air pressure, and moisture answers the question.

questions.stem: Tell whether each fact about weather balloons is shown in the diagram of “Weather Balloons” or is stated only in the paragraphs.

rows.text: The balloon is filled with helium.
A parachute hangs below the balloon.
The balloon bursts about 30 kilometers up.
Data is sent by radio every few seconds.

questions.why: A diagram shows parts and labels; the paragraphs give facts such as heights and times.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of “Weather Balloons”?
options: Weather balloons burst at about thirty kilometers above the ground.
Weather balloons carry instruments that collect data used for forecasts.
Weather balloons are filled with helium and tied to small parachutes.
Weather stations around the world are built in hundreds of places.
questions.why: The central idea covers the whole passage: balloons collect data that forecasters use.

questions.stem: Which two details are most relevant to the central idea of “Weather Balloons”? Choose two.
options: The parachute drifts gently back to Earth.
The radiosonde measures temperature, air pressure, and moisture.
Forecasters use the data to predict storms.
The balloon is filled with helium.
questions.why: Relevant details support the idea that balloons collect useful weather data.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The cost of the new space telescope was astronomical, so twelve nations agreed to share it.” What does astronomical mean in this sentence?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The cost of the new space telescope was astronomical, so twelve nations agreed to share it.” What does astronomical mean in this sentence?

options.label: A
options.text: related to stars

options.label: B
options.text: hard to see

options.label: C
options.text: extremely large

options.label: D
options.text: very bright

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase from the sentence best helps the reader understand astronomical?

options.label: A
options.text: The cost of

options.label: B
options.text: so twelve nations agreed to share it

options.label: C
options.text: the new space telescope

options.label: D
options.text: agreed to

questions.why: Astronomical can mean huge; the cost needed twelve nations to share it.

questions.stem: Tell whether each word contains the Greek root sphere (“ball”) or meter (“measure”): atmosphere, hemisphere, perimeter, diameter, spheres.

rows.text: atmosphere
hemisphere
perimeter
diameter
spheres

questions.why: Sphere words name round shapes; meter words name measurements.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error: “Each planet follow its own orbit, which is approximately an oval shape.”
questions.why: A singular subject such as each planet needs the verb follows.

questions.stem: Which two sentences use the word evaluate correctly? Choose two.
options: The rocket will evaluate into space at noon.
Scientists evaluate new data before they publish their results.
Please evaluate the cookies on the top shelf.
The judges will evaluate each science project using a checklist.
questions.why: Evaluate means to judge or check the value of something carefully.

questions.stem: Put the steps a student follows to find the diameter of a ball by calculation in order.
sequence: Wrap a string once around the widest part of the ball.
Measure the length of the string with a ruler.
Divide that length by approximately 3.14.
Record the answer as the ball's diameter.
questions.why: A calculation follows clear steps: measure, then divide, then record.

questions.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses the central idea of “Watching Earth from Space”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses the central idea of “Watching Earth from Space”?

options.label: A
options.text: Satellites let scientists study Earth as one whole, connected system.

options.label: B
options.text: Dust storms travel across oceans for thousands of kilometers.

options.label: C
options.text: The first satellite was small, but it carried many instruments.

options.label: D
options.text: Thermometers on rooftops were the best tools for studying weather.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Today, satellites give scientists a view of Earth as one connected system rather than a collection of separate places.

options.label: B
options.text: The first satellite, launched in 1957, was about the size of a beach ball.

options.label: C
options.text: A thermometer on a rooftop recorded the temperature of one city, and a ship could measure the waves of one patch of sea.

options.label: D
options.text: Satellites changed that.

questions.why: The final paragraph sums up the central idea: satellites show Earth as one system.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Watching Earth from Space” that are relevant details showing what satellites help scientists observe.

segments.text: Before the space age, scientists could study only small pieces of Earth at a time.
Circling high above the surface, these machines photograph clouds, oceans, forests, and ice every day.
The first satellite, launched in 1957, was about the size of a beach ball.
Researchers have watched sea ice shrink, deserts spread, and enormous dust storms travel thousands of kilometers across oceans.

questions.why: These two sentences give details about what satellites let scientists see.

questions.stem: The Greek root atmos means “vapor,” and sphaira means “ball.” What does atmosphere most likely mean as it is used in paragraph 2?
options: the layer of air that surrounds the planet
the deep water that covers most of Earth
the hot rock found deep inside Earth
the round metal body of a satellite
questions.why: Atmos plus sphere suggests a ball of gas: the air around Earth.

questions.stem: Decide whether each detail from “Watching Earth from Space” is important to the central idea or is interesting but less important.

rows.text: Satellites photograph clouds, oceans, and ice every day.
The first satellite was about the size of a beach ball.
Satellite data revealed patterns that were once invisible.
A ship could measure the waves of one patch of sea.

questions.why: Important details support the central idea; others are interesting facts that do not.

questions.stem: Put the ideas of “Watching Earth from Space” in the order the author presents them.
sequence: Scientists once studied only small pieces of Earth.
Satellites began photographing the whole planet every day.
Satellite data revealed patterns such as shrinking sea ice.
Scientists now see Earth as one connected system.
questions.why: The author moves from the past, to satellites, to discoveries, to a conclusion.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: rely, nominate, sympathy, weakling.

pairs.right: to depend on someone or something
to suggest someone for a job or honor
a feeling of sorrow for another person's trouble
a person who is not strong

questions.why: Learning exact meanings helps you use each word correctly.

questions.stem: The coach could ____ on Hamad to arrive early, because he was never late to practice.
questions.why: Only rely is used with on to mean depend on.

questions.stem: True or false: A supportive friend is someone who encourages you when you are having a hard time.
questions.why: Supportive means giving help and encouragement.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error: “Our class decided to nominated Sara as team captain.”
questions.why: After to, use the base form of the verb: nominate.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word obviously correctly?
options: The floor was wet and muddy, so obviously someone had come in from the rain.
Obviously, I have no idea at all where my sister went this afternoon.
The teacher whispered obviously so that no one in the room could hear.
We obviously hid the gift where nobody would ever be able to find it.
questions.why: Obviously means in a way that is easy to see or understand.

questions.stem: Part A: What does Ruth's action at the end of “The Soup Pot, 1932” show about her?

partA.stem: Part A: What does Ruth's action at the end of “The Soup Pot, 1932” show about her?

options.label: A
options.text: She is generous even when she has little.

options.label: B
options.text: She wants to leave home and find work.

options.label: C
options.text: She does not like the taste of the soup.

options.label: D
options.text: She is angry that Mama said no to her.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Ruth did not argue.

options.label: B
options.text: In the winter of 1932, Papa lost his job at the shoe factory, and the family's small savings disappeared within a few months.

options.label: C
options.text: She simply poured half of her own bowl into a glass jar and wrapped it carefully in a towel to keep it warm.

options.label: D
options.text: Mama started making soup from whatever was left in the cupboard.

questions.why: Giving away half of her own food shows Ruth is generous.

questions.stem: Based on the end of “The Soup Pot, 1932,” what will Ruth most likely do next?
options: Eat the soup in the hallway so Mama will not see her.
Ask her little brother to carry the jar to the factory.
Take the jar of soup to Mr. Kaplan's door.
Pour the soup back into the pot because Mama said no.
questions.why: Ruth wrapped her food and stepped into the hallway toward her neighbor's home.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Soup Pot, 1932” best helps the reader predict where Ruth is going?

segments.text: Some nights it was only potatoes and water with a little salt.
One evening, Ruth noticed that old Mr. Kaplan next door had not lit his stove for several days.
Mama sighed and rubbed her tired eyes.
Ruth did not argue.

questions.why: Ruth noticed her neighbor had no fire, a clue that she will bring him food.

questions.stem: Tell whether each detail about the family in “The Soup Pot, 1932” shows a problem or a character's response to the problem.

rows.text: Papa lost his job at the shoe factory.
Some nights the soup was only potatoes and water.
Mama made soup from whatever was left.
Ruth poured half of her bowl into a jar.

questions.why: Characters show who they are by how they respond to problems.

questions.stem: Which two words best describe Mama in “The Soup Pot, 1932”? Choose two.
questions.why: Mama sighs, looks tired, and thinks carefully about how much food the family has.

questions.stem: Match each idiom about hard times with its meaning: in the same boat, tighten our belts, keep your chin up, make ends meet.

pairs.right: have just enough money for needs

questions.why: An idiom means something different from its exact words.

questions.stem: Obviously worried, Uncle Faisal told us, “The shop has closed, so we will have to ____ until I find new work.”
questions.why: Tighten our belts means spend less money, which fits losing a job.

questions.stem: Tell whether the key word in each sentence is used correctly or incorrectly: assume, sympathy, weakling, nominate.

rows.text: I assume the bus is late because it has not arrived yet.
Her sympathy for the lost kitten made her search for its owner.
The weakling lifted the heavy piano all by himself.
We nominate the weather to be sunny tomorrow.

questions.why: A weakling is not strong, and people, not weather, are nominated.

questions.stem: Which two sentences contain an idiom? Choose two.
options: The clouds moved slowly across the evening sky.
My little sister was on cloud nine after the school show.
Let's not beat around the bush; just tell me the news.
We walked around the bush in my uncle's garden.
questions.why: On cloud nine means very happy; beat around the bush means avoid the main point.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Grandpa said the old radio cost an arm and a leg,” the idiom means the radio was very expensive.
questions.why: Cost an arm and a leg is an idiom meaning very expensive.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the main conflict in “Leo's Plan”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the main conflict in “Leo's Plan”?

options.label: A
options.text: Leo and Pa argue about who should sell newspapers on the corner.

options.label: B
options.text: Leo wants to quit arithmetic, but his teacher will not allow it.

options.label: C
options.text: Leo wants to earn money, but Pa wants him to stay in school.

options.label: D
options.text: Leo cannot find a corner where he is allowed to sell newspapers.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Each morning Pa left before sunrise, and each evening he came home with empty hands and a tired smile.

options.label: B
options.text: He felt caught between two things he cared about.

options.label: C
options.text: In the morning, he explained his plan carefully.

options.label: D
options.text: Leo pushed his beans around his plate.

pairs.left: Small fish swim toward the anglerfish's lure.
A shrimp sprays a glowing cloud.
Sunlight cannot reach the deep ocean.
pairs.right: The water below 1,000 meters is dark.

questions.why: A cause is why something happens; an effect is what happens.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Lights in the Deep” is a context clue that helps explain the word lure?

segments.text: Below about 1,000 meters, the water is completely dark.
Small fish swim toward the light, and the anglerfish quickly snaps them up.
Some shrimp spray a cloud of glowing liquid when a predator comes near.
Light can also help animals find each other in the endless dark.

questions.why: Fish swim toward the lure and get caught, so a lure is something that attracts prey.

questions.stem: Which question is answered in paragraph 2 of “Lights in the Deep”?
options: How does the anglerfish catch its food?
How do fish find each other in the dark?
How cold is the water in the deep sea?
How deep can sunlight travel in the sea?
questions.why: Paragraph 2 explains the anglerfish's glowing lure.

questions.stem: Which two animals in “Lights in the Deep” use light to hunt or to escape? Choose two.
questions.why: The anglerfish hunts with light, and the shrimp escapes with it.

questions.stem: The ____ squirrel leaped from branch to branch without ever slipping.
questions.why: The clue leaped without slipping shows the squirrel moves quickly and easily.

questions.stem: Read: “The volcano had been dormant for centuries; it was quiet, and no lava had flowed.” Which two clues help explain dormant? Choose two.
questions.why: The clues after the semicolon describe something inactive.

questions.stem: Tell which type of context clue explains the key word in each sentence about animals.

rows.text: The jay hid a cache, or secret store, of acorns.
Some animals hibernate, such as bears, bats, and groundhogs.
Unlike the frigid north, the tropics are warm all year.
Seals forage, or search for food, under the ice.

questions.why: Clue words such as or, such as, and unlike signal different kinds of context clues.

questions.stem: Match each ocean science word with its meaning: pressure, predator, prey, current.

pairs.right: the force of something pressing down

questions.why: These words help you read about life in the ocean.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Fur insulates the fox, so it stays warm in the snow,” the clue “stays warm” helps explain insulates.
questions.why: Stays warm tells what insulating fur does.

questions.stem: Part A: According to the map in “Hot Springs on the Ocean Floor,” where are the vent sites found?

partA.stem: Part A: According to the map in “Hot Springs on the Ocean Floor,” where are the vent sites found?

options.label: A
options.text: along a ridge on the sea floor

options.label: B
options.text: near the surface of the ocean

options.label: C
options.text: on the beaches of the islands

options.label: D
options.text: in the middle of a calm bay

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: These openings are called hydrothermal vents.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the water carries chemicals, tiny bacteria can turn them into food.

options.label: C
options.text: As a result, tubeworms, crabs, and clams live near the vents even though sunlight never reaches them.

options.label: D
options.text: Vents form where the plates of Earth's crust slowly pull apart.

questions.why: Plates pull apart at ridges, which is where the map shows the stars.

questions.stem: Put the steps that create a hydrothermal vent, as described in “Hot Springs on the Ocean Floor,” in order.
sequence: Plates of Earth's crust pull apart and form cracks.
Seawater sinks into the cracks.
Melted rock below heats the water.
Hot water shoots back up through the vent.
questions.why: Cause-and-effect steps follow one another in order.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Hot Springs on the Ocean Floor” explains why animals can live near the vents without sunlight?

segments.text: In 1977, scientists in a small submarine called Alvin made a surprising discovery near the Galápagos Islands.
These openings are called hydrothermal vents.
Because the water carries chemicals, tiny bacteria can turn them into food.
Seawater sinks into the cracks, is heated by melted rock below, and then shoots back up.

questions.why: Bacteria make food from chemicals, so animals can eat without sunlight.

questions.stem: Tell whether each question about hydrothermal vents can be answered with the map or with the paragraphs of “Hot Springs on the Ocean Floor.”

rows.text: Where are the vent sites located?
Which islands are near a vent site?
In what year were the vents discovered?
Which animals live near the vents?

questions.why: Maps show where things are; paragraphs explain when, how, and why.

questions.stem: What does the word vents most likely mean as it is used in paragraph 1 of “Hot Springs on the Ocean Floor”?
options: large rocks on the ocean floor
deep holes that fill with sand
small animals that live in cracks
questions.why: The clue These openings are called hydrothermal vents defines the word.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “Arctic foxes cache extra food in summer; they bury lemmings and eggs to eat when the frigid winter arrives.” What does cache mean in this sentence?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “Arctic foxes cache extra food in summer; they bury lemmings and eggs to eat when the frigid winter arrives.” What does cache mean in this sentence?

options.label: A
options.text: share something with others

options.label: B
options.text: cook something over a fire

options.label: C
options.text: catch something very quickly

options.label: D
options.text: store something in a hidden place

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase from the sentence best helps the reader understand cache?

options.label: A
options.text: when the frigid winter arrives

options.label: B
options.text: Arctic foxes

options.label: C
options.text: extra food in summer

options.label: D
options.text: they bury lemmings and eggs to eat

questions.why: Burying food to eat later shows that cache means hide and store.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error: “Because the water is so frigid, the walrus rely on thick blubber, which insulates its body.”
questions.why: The walrus is singular, so the verb is relies.

questions.stem: Put the events in the cause-and-effect chain of a ground squirrel's winter in order.
sequence: The days grow short and cold.
Food becomes hard to find.
The squirrel enters its burrow to hibernate.
Its body stays dormant until spring.
questions.why: Each event causes the next one.

questions.stem: Which three sentences describe an animal adaptation? Choose three.
options: A boat carries a lamp to see underwater.
A diver wears a wetsuit in cold water.
An agile octopus squeezes through tiny cracks to escape.
A deep-sea fish has huge eyes that collect faint light.
A polar bear's thick fur insulates it from the cold.
questions.why: Adaptations are features of living things, not tools people use.

questions.stem: Tell whether the first part of each sentence about animals in harsh places is a cause or an effect.

rows.text: Because food is scarce in the deep sea, fish forage over long distances.
Whales grow thick blubber since the water is frigid.
The squid is agile, so it escapes most hunters.
The seeds stayed dormant because the soil was dry.

questions.why: Because, since, and so signal cause-and-effect relationships.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the main cause of the Red Sea's warm deep water?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the main cause of the Red Sea's warm deep water?

options.label: A
options.text: Deep-sea animals warm the water as they swim.

options.label: B
options.text: A shallow entrance blocks cold deep currents.

options.label: C
options.text: Rivers bring warm water from the deserts.

options.label: D
options.text: Hot springs on the sea floor heat the water.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Bab el-Mandeb is shallow, so the icy deep currents of the Indian Ocean cannot flow over it.

options.label: B
options.text: The Red Sea is a remarkable exception.

options.label: C
options.text: This unusual warmth has consequences.

options.label: D
options.text: Most of the deep ocean is frigid, with temperatures barely above freezing.

questions.why: Cold currents cannot enter, so the deep water stays warm.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “The Warm Deep of the Red Sea” that describe effects of the deep water's warmth.

segments.text: Most of the deep ocean is frigid, with temperatures barely above freezing.
The answer lies at the southern entrance.
Many deep-sea animals from the Indian Ocean need cold water, so they cannot survive in the Red Sea's depths.
As a result, its deep waters hold fewer species, yet several of them are found nowhere else.

questions.why: These sentences tell what happens because the water is warm.

questions.stem: What does the word basin most likely mean as it is used in the paragraph that begins “Why is the deep water so warm?”
options: a strong current that moves quickly
a layer of salt on the ocean floor
a large, low area that holds water
a narrow passage between two seas
questions.why: The water sinks and fills the basin, so a basin is a low area that holds water.

questions.stem: Tell whether each fact about the Red Sea is shown on the map in “The Warm Deep of the Red Sea” or is given only in the paragraphs.

rows.text: Bab el-Mandeb is at the southern end of the sea.
The Red Sea lies between Africa and Arabia.
The deep water is about 21 degrees Celsius.
Fewer species live in the deep water.

questions.why: Maps show places and connections; paragraphs give facts and explanations.

questions.stem: Which two questions are answered in “The Warm Deep of the Red Sea”? Choose two.
options: What connects the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean?
Why does surface water in the Red Sea sink?
When was the Red Sea first explored by submarine?
How do Red Sea fish find food in the dark?
questions.why: Asking questions and finding answers helps check understanding.

questions.stem: Match each word about travel and meeting people with its meaning: blares, errand, exchange, connection.

pairs.right: makes a very loud, harsh sound
a short trip to do a small job
giving one thing and getting another back
a link or friendship between people or things

questions.why: These words help you talk about journeys, trades, and friendships.

questions.stem: Every morning the old bus horn ____ outside our school gate, and everyone covers their ears.
questions.why: Blares means makes a loud, harsh sound, which is why everyone covers their ears.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “Mom sent me on an errand to buy bread,” an errand is a short trip to do a small job.
questions.why: An errand is a small task, such as buying something from a shop.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses personification?
options: The kettle on the stove was made of steel.
The kettle boiled water for the family's tea.
The tired kettle sighed on the stove.
The kettle was as hot as the desert sun.
questions.why: Personification gives a human action, like sighing, to a thing that is not human.

questions.stem: Tell whether each sentence about packing for a trip uses personification or not.

rows.text: The suitcase yawned open on the bed.
The train left the station at noon.
The waves waved goodbye to our boat.
We packed water and dates for the road.

questions.why: A suitcase cannot yawn and waves cannot wave goodbye, so those sentences use personification.

questions.stem: Tell whether each line repeats a vowel sound (assonance) or a consonant sound (consonance).

rows.text: Blue moons glow over the dunes.
Tick, tock, the black clock clicks.
The rain stayed away all day.
The dog dug deep under the red sand.

questions.why: Assonance repeats vowel sounds (oo, long a); consonance repeats consonant sounds (k, d).

questions.stem: A poem that tells a story with characters, a setting, and events is called a ____ poem.
questions.why: A narrative poem tells a story; a lyric poem shares feelings.

questions.stem: True or false: A lyric poem mainly shares the speaker's thoughts and feelings instead of telling a long story.
questions.why: Lyric poems focus on emotions and personal thoughts.

questions.stem: Which two lines use assonance, the repeating of a vowel sound? Choose two.
options: Go slow on the road back home.
The light of the white kite climbs high.
Pick up the cookie and the cup.
questions.why: The long i in light, white, kite and the long o in go, slow, road, home are repeated vowel sounds.

questions.stem: In the line “The radio blares a song across the busy market,” what does blares mean?
options: shines with a bright, sudden light
questions.why: Something that blares is very loud, like a radio turned all the way up.

questions.stem: Which line from “The Library Door” uses personification to describe the library door?

segments.text: Every afternoon the library door opens its patient arms and invites me inside,
I choose a heavy atlas, and the pages flutter like eager birds beneath my fingers.
Suddenly I am standing in a crowded market in Morocco, where copper lanterns glow,
When the clock on the wall announces closing time, I return the atlas to its shelf,

questions.why: A door does not have arms and cannot invite anyone, so the poet gives it human traits.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the speaker's point of view about reading?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the speaker's point of view about reading?

options.label: A
options.text: Reading lets a person explore the world without leaving home.

options.label: B
options.text: Reading an atlas is useful only for finishing school projects.

options.label: C
options.text: Reading is much less exciting than taking a real journey.

options.label: D
options.text: Reading in a library is difficult because it is so noisy.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Then I am sailing across the cold green sea toward the islands of Norway,

options.label: B
options.text: I have never needed a ticket or a suitcase to discover the wonderful world.

options.label: C
options.text: When the clock on the wall announces closing time, I return the atlas to its shelf,

options.label: D
options.text: I choose a heavy atlas, and the pages flutter like eager birds beneath my fingers.

questions.why: The speaker says books let her discover the world without a ticket or suitcase.

questions.stem: Which two phrases from “The Library Door” use imagery that appeals to the sense of hearing? Choose two.
options: the wind sings a long, low song
the waves slap the sides of the wooden boat
questions.why: Singing wind and slapping waves are sounds; glowing lanterns are sight and tea is taste.

questions.stem: In the line “a merchant offers me sweet mint tea in exchange for a friendly conversation,” the word exchange means ____.
options: a gift given without expecting anything back
a long and tiring journey to a distant city
giving one thing and receiving another in return
a loud argument between two busy sellers
questions.why: In an exchange, each person gives something and gets something back.

questions.stem: Why is “The Library Door” best described as a lyric poem?
options: It tells a long story about a sailor's trip to Norway.
It shares the speaker's feelings about the joy of reading.
It follows several characters through a dangerous adventure.
It explains the rules for borrowing books from a library.
questions.why: A lyric poem expresses a speaker's emotions, like the delight of traveling through books.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error in this sentence about a busy street.
questions.why: The singular subject siren needs the verb blares.

questions.stem: Match each line about a desert journey with the device it shows: personification, metaphor, assonance, simile.

pairs.left: The lazy river yawned beneath the bridge.
The road was a gray ribbon across the sand.
I sleep deep and dream of green streets.
The sand was as hot as an oven.

questions.why: Each device works differently: human actions, direct comparison, repeated vowels, or a comparison with like/as.

questions.stem: These lines come from a short narrative poem about an errand to the market. Put them in story order.
sequence: Grandma handed me a coin and a list for the market.
I raced past the bakery as the street horn blared.
The fruit seller wrapped six oranges in paper.
I hurried home and placed the oranges in Grandma's hands.
questions.why: A narrative poem follows events from beginning to end, like a story.

questions.stem: Which sentence about a desert trip is written from a first-person point of view?
options: They watched the camels cross the dunes at sunset.
The guides watched camels cross the dunes at sunset.
I watched the camels cross the dunes at sunset.
She watched the camels cross the dunes at sunset.
questions.why: First-person point of view uses words like I, me, and my.

questions.stem: True or false: The phrase “a cool, smooth pool of blue” is an example of imagery because it helps the reader picture and feel a scene.
questions.why: Imagery uses words that appeal to the senses, such as sight and touch.

questions.stem: The line “Spices sting my nose, drums thunder in my chest, and silk slides cool across my hand” uses imagery. Which three senses does it appeal to? Choose three.
questions.why: Spices are smelled, drums are heard, and silk is felt.

questions.stem: The poet repeats the s and l sounds in “silk slides slowly” to create ____, a sound device that makes the line feel smooth.
questions.why: Consonance is the repeating of consonant sounds, such as s and l.

questions.stem: Tell whether each description fits a lyric poem or a narrative poem.

rows.text: It follows a boy's errand from start to finish.
It expresses the speaker's joy at seeing the sea.
It has characters, a setting, and a plot.
It focuses on one feeling or one moment.

questions.why: Narrative poems tell stories; lyric poems focus on feelings.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the lines: “My cousin from Jakarta taught me a song, / and I taught her a game from Riyadh; / now each of us carries a piece of the other's home.” What is the speaker's perspective on this cultural exchange?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the lines: “My cousin from Jakarta taught me a song, / and I taught her a game from Riyadh; / now each of us carries a piece of the other's home.” What is the speaker's perspective on this cultural exchange?

options.label: A
options.text: Learning a new game is harder than learning a song.

options.label: B
options.text: Visiting relatives is tiring and not very useful.

options.label: C
options.text: People should keep their own traditions to themselves.

options.label: D
options.text: Sharing traditions brings people closer together.

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase from the lines best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: carries a piece of the other's home

options.label: B
options.text: a game from Riyadh

options.label: C
options.text: My cousin from Jakarta

options.label: D
options.text: taught me a song

questions.why: Carrying a piece of each other's home shows the speaker values what they shared.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Through letters, the two pen pals built a strong connection across three oceans.” What does connection mean?
options: a fee paid for sending a letter
a bond that links people together
a long road that joins two cities
a quarrel that keeps people apart
questions.why: A connection is a link or relationship between people.

questions.stem: Part A: What does Grandfather believe about the meeting between Layla and the sailor?

partA.stem: Part A: What does Grandfather believe about the meeting between Layla and the sailor?

options.label: A
options.text: A small trade can connect people from different places.

options.label: B
options.text: Layla should not have stayed so long on the busy dock.

options.label: C
options.text: Seashells are worth much more than a basket of dates.

options.label: D
options.text: Strangers at the harbor should never be offered gifts.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “Sometimes,” he says, “a simple exchange becomes a bridge between two different worlds.”

options.label: B
options.text: On the crowded dock, a tired sailor from a distant island rests beside his heavy bag.

options.label: C
options.text: Grandfather hands Layla a basket of dates and sends her on an errand to the harbor.

options.label: D
options.text: She carries the seashells home, and Grandfather listens as she describes the stranger.

questions.why: Grandfather calls the exchange a bridge between two worlds, which shows his perspective.

questions.stem: Select two lines from “The Errand to the Harbor” that use personification.

segments.text: Grandfather hands Layla a basket of dates and sends her on an errand to the harbor.
The morning sun stretches its golden fingers across the sleepy rooftops of the town,
Layla offers him the sweetest dates, and he smiles and opens a small wooden box.
Layla places the shells on her windowsill, where they whisper of the open ocean every evening.

questions.why: The sun cannot stretch fingers and shells cannot whisper; these are human actions.

questions.stem: Why is “The Errand to the Harbor” a narrative poem rather than a lyric poem?
options: It tells a story with characters, events, and an ending.
It shares only the speaker's private feelings about the sea.
It repeats the same vowel sound at the end of every line.
It describes one single moment without any characters at all.
questions.why: A narrative poem tells a story with characters and events.

questions.stem: In the line “far away the ferry horn blares twice,” the verb blares is imagery that helps the reader ____.
options: taste the sweet dates in the basket
hear a loud, sudden sound at the harbor
see the bright colors of the busy dock
feel the smooth shells in Layla's hand
questions.why: Blares describes a loud sound, so it appeals to hearing.

questions.stem: Put the events of “The Errand to the Harbor” in order.
sequence: Grandfather sends Layla to the harbor with dates.
Layla gives the sailor some of the sweetest dates.
The sailor shares seashells from a wooden box.
Grandfather explains the meaning of the exchange.
questions.why: The narrative poem moves from the errand, to the trade, to Grandfather's lesson.

questions.stem: Match each word about friendship and competition with its meaning: rival, loyalty, perpetual, evade.

pairs.right: a person competing for the same goal
faithful support for a friend or group

questions.why: These words describe how people compete and stay faithful to each other.

questions.stem: The small fox darted behind a rock to ____ the hungry eagle circling above.
questions.why: To evade is to escape or avoid, which is what the fox wants to do.

questions.stem: True or false: A pensive person is someone who is laughing loudly and acting carelessly.
questions.why: Pensive means deeply and quietly thoughtful, often a little sad.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word barrage correctly?
options: Sara slowly opened the barrage to let the cat into the yard.
The barrage of the house was painted a soft shade of green.
The reporters fired a barrage of questions at the coach.
Ali drank a cool barrage of juice after the long match.
questions.why: A barrage is a large number of things coming quickly, such as many questions at once.

questions.stem: Tell whether each phrase about two competing friends has a positive or a negative connotation.

rows.text: deep loyalty
a devastating loss
a barrage of complaints
dispel the children's fears

questions.why: Loyalty and calming fears feel good; a devastating loss and many complaints feel bad.

questions.stem: Which two statements are themes rather than topics? Choose two.
options: True friends stay loyal even when they must compete.
Doing your best matters more than winning.
a boxing match between two friends
questions.why: A theme is a complete message about life; a topic is just a subject.

questions.stem: A theme is ____ that a story expresses about life or people.
questions.why: Theme is the big idea or lesson the reader takes away.

questions.stem: True or false: An author usually states the theme of a realistic fiction story directly in the first sentence.
questions.why: Readers usually infer the theme from what characters do, say, and learn.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Even after losing the final, Samir's loyalty to his teammate never wavered.” Which theme does this detail most support?
options: Practice is the only way to win a final.
Teams should always change their players.
Losing makes people forget their friends.
questions.why: Samir stays loyal after losing, which shows friendship lasting through disappointment.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error in this sentence about a runner before a race.
questions.why: The sentence is in the past tense, so sit must be sat.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states a theme of “The Final Round”?
options: Strong friends can compete hard and still respect each other.
Friends should never enter the same tournament together.
Chess is a game that only patient players can ever master.
Winning a trophy is the best way to prove you are smart.
questions.why: The boys play their best and stay friends, which shows respect in competition.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does Karim decide to play his best against Yusuf?

partA.stem: Part A: Why does Karim decide to play his best against Yusuf?

options.label: A
options.text: He thinks holding back would disrespect his friend.

options.label: B
options.text: He wants to end his friendship with Yusuf.

options.label: C
options.text: He believes Yusuf is a much weaker player.

options.label: D
options.text: He was told to win by the tournament judges.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: After two exhausting hours, Yusuf won by a single pawn.

options.label: B
options.text: Karim felt the same way, but he also knew that holding back would be a kind of insult.

options.label: C
options.text: Now both boys had reached the final round of the city tournament, and only one of them could win the trophy.

options.label: D
options.text: He worried that beating Karim might damage their friendship.

questions.why: Karim sees holding back as an insult, so playing his best is a sign of respect.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Final Round” best shows that the friendship survives the competition?

segments.text: The night before the match, Yusuf sat at his desk, pensive and silent.
Karim launched a barrage of attacks, and Yusuf defended calmly, move after move.
After two exhausting hours, Yusuf won by a single pawn.
Both boys laughed, and they walked home together, just as they always had.

questions.why: Walking home together as always shows the friendship is unchanged.

questions.stem: In paragraph 3, the phrase “a barrage of attacks” suggests that Karim ____.
options: gave up quickly after his first mistake
made many strong moves one after another
waited quietly for Yusuf to make errors
asked the judges to stop the long game
questions.why: A barrage is a rapid series, so Karim attacked again and again.

questions.stem: Which two details from “The Final Round” show that Yusuf was worried before the match? Choose two.
options: He defended calmly, move after move.
He feared beating Karim could harm their friendship.
He sat at his desk, pensive and silent.
He won by a single pawn.
questions.why: Being pensive and fearing for the friendship show worry before the game.

questions.stem: Read the claim “Lina is a loyal friend.” Tell whether each detail about Lina supports the claim or does not support it.

rows.text: She defended her friend when others teased him.
She likes to read adventure books.
She visited her sick friend every day.
She lives near the school gate.

questions.why: Strong evidence must connect directly to loyalty.

questions.stem: Put the steps for answering a theme question about a realistic fiction story with text evidence in order.
sequence: Read the question and decide what it asks.
Reread to find details about what characters do and learn.
Choose the detail that best supports your answer.
Explain how the detail shows the theme.
questions.why: Good answers move from understanding the question to explaining the evidence.

questions.stem: Match each word with the sentence that shows its meaning: perpetual, dispel, devastating, rival.

pairs.right: The fountain's water never stopped flowing.
The teacher's smile made our nervousness disappear.
The storm destroyed almost every house on the coast.
Two schools competed for the same science prize.

questions.why: Each sentence describes the meaning of the word without using it.

questions.stem: Which sentence would be the strongest evidence that Huda is a hardworking athlete?
options: Huda has two older brothers who also enjoy sports.
Huda owns a pair of bright blue running shoes.
Huda trains on the track every morning before school.
Huda once watched a race on television with friends.
questions.why: Training every morning shows hard work; the others are unrelated details.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “The coach's kind words helped dispel the team's fear,” dispel means to make a feeling go away.
questions.why: To dispel is to drive away a feeling or belief.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error in this sentence about a noisy street.
questions.why: The subject noise is singular, so the verb must be was.

questions.stem: After the ____ flood destroyed the farm's crops, the whole village came together to help rebuild.
questions.why: Devastating means causing great damage, which fits a destructive flood.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: “Omar and Bilal were rivals on the track, but every evening they trained together. When Bilal twisted his ankle, Omar walked him home and carried his bag.” Which two themes are best supported by these sentences? Choose two.
options: Competition does not have to destroy friendship.
People should avoid sports that cause injuries.
Winning a race is the most important goal.
Real friends show kindness even to their rivals.
questions.why: Omar competes with Bilal yet helps him, showing kindness and friendship.

questions.stem: Read: “The spokesperson tried to evade the reporter's difficult question.” Which word is closest in meaning to evade?
questions.why: To evade a question is to avoid answering it.

questions.stem: True or false: The best text evidence for a theme is any sentence that mentions the main character's name.
questions.why: Evidence must show what the character does, says, or learns that connects to the theme.

questions.stem: Part A: Which theme does the author develop through Dana's choice during tryouts?

partA.stem: Part A: Which theme does the author develop through Dana's choice during tryouts?

options.label: A
options.text: Friends should never try out for the same team.

options.label: B
options.text: Injuries are a normal part of every sport.

options.label: C
options.text: Loyalty to a friend matters more than an easy win.

options.label: D
options.text: Coaches always choose the most talented player.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Finally, Reem knocked on Dana's door holding two pairs of gloves.

options.label: B
options.text: Eventually, the coach selected Dana for the position, explaining that her reflexes were remarkably quick.

options.label: C
options.text: “You chose my health over an easy victory, and I won't forget that.”

options.label: D
options.text: Then the coach announced that the school team needed only one goalkeeper, and the two friends became rivals overnight.

questions.why: Reem's words show that Dana put her friend before winning.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Two Gloves, One Goal” shows that Dana faced a difficult choice?

segments.text: Dana could have stayed silent, since an injured rival would make her own victory almost certain.
Eventually, the coach selected Dana for the position, explaining that her reflexes were remarkably quick.
Reem was disappointed, and for a few days the silence between them felt devastating.
Then she grinned and offered to help her friend practice every afternoon before the championship season.

questions.why: Dana had to choose between an easy victory and helping her friend.

questions.stem: Put the events of “Two Gloves, One Goal” in order.
sequence: The coach says the team needs only one goalkeeper.
Dana tells the coach about Reem's wrist.
The coach chooses Dana for the position.
Reem visits Dana with two pairs of gloves.
questions.why: The events move from the competition, to Dana's choice, to the friends making peace.

questions.stem: Tell whether each statement about Reem and Dana in “Two Gloves, One Goal” is stated directly or must be inferred.

rows.text: The team needed only one goalkeeper.
Dana values her friend more than an easy win.
Reem brought two pairs of gloves to Dana's door.
Reem has accepted the result and values Dana's friendship.

questions.why: Inferences combine text evidence with what the reader already knows.

questions.stem: How does the word devastating in paragraph 3 help develop the theme?
options: It shows that Reem's wrist injury was extremely serious.
It shows that the coach regretted choosing a goalkeeper.
It shows how painful the distance between the friends felt.
It shows that the football team lost every one of its games.
questions.why: The strong word shows how much the friendship matters to both girls.

questions.stem: Match each word about young changemakers with its meaning: activist, advocate, initiative, impact.

pairs.right: a person who works hard for social or environmental change
a person who speaks up in support of a cause
the energy to start something without being told
a strong effect on someone or something

questions.why: These words describe people who make a difference and the results of their work.

questions.stem: Nora showed ____ when she started a recycling club without waiting for a teacher to ask.
questions.why: Initiative means taking action on your own.

questions.stem: True or false: To persevere means to give up quickly when a task becomes difficult.
questions.why: To persevere is to keep trying even when something is hard.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word contribute correctly?
options: Faisal decided to contribute his bike in the garage.
The tired puppy wanted to contribute on the soft rug.
The heavy rain will contribute the roads very slippery.
Every student can contribute an idea to the class garden.
questions.why: To contribute is to give or add something to help a shared goal.

questions.stem: Tell whether advocate, impact, or inspire in each sentence is used as a noun or a verb.

rows.text: She is an advocate for clean water.
He advocates for safer bike lanes.
The new park had a big impact on the town.
Her speech will inspire many students.

questions.why: A noun names a person or thing; a verb shows an action.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph: “Mariam wanted children in hospitals to have books. She collected donations from neighbors, sorted hundreds of books, and delivered them herself. She also wrote to local shops asking them to help.” Which two details support the idea that Mariam took action for others? Choose two.
options: She lives in a large city.
She sorted and delivered hundreds of books.
She asked local shops to help.
questions.why: Supporting details must connect to the central idea of taking action.

questions.stem: The ____ of a biography is the most important point the author makes about the person's life.
questions.why: The central idea is what the whole text is mostly about.

questions.stem: Put the sentences of a short biography of a young activist named Sami in a logical order.
sequence: At age twelve, Sami noticed plastic bags piling up on the beach near his home.
He started a weekend cleanup club and invited his classmates.
Within a year, more than two hundred volunteers had joined him.
Today, the city credits his initiative with cleaner beaches.
questions.why: Biographies often use time order, from the problem to the results.

questions.stem: True or false: A central idea is usually supported by several key details, not just one.
questions.why: Authors build a central idea with many details and examples.

questions.stem: Read: “Young people around the world are solving real problems. One teen built a low-cost water filter. Another designed an app that helps farmers.” Which sentence best states the central idea?
options: Farmers use many different apps on their phones.
Water filters are cheaper than they used to be.
Young people are finding ways to solve real problems.
Teenagers enjoy designing new apps in their free time.
questions.why: The first sentence is the central idea; the others are examples.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of “The Boy Who Gave Books Fingertips”?
options: Schools in Paris used very large books with heavy raised letters.
Louis Braille injured his eye while playing in his father's workshop.
Charles Barbier was a soldier who invented a way to read at night.
As a teenager, Louis Braille created a reading system that still helps people.
questions.why: The whole biography explains how young Louis created braille and why it matters.

questions.stem: Part A: What problem did Louis Braille's code solve?

partA.stem: Part A: What problem did Louis Braille's code solve?

options.label: A
options.text: Teachers in Paris did not have enough classrooms.

options.label: B
options.text: Books for blind children were too expensive to print.

options.label: C
options.text: Soldiers could not send messages during the night.

options.label: D
options.text: Blind readers had no quick, easy way to read by touch.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The school's few books used huge raised letters that were slow and difficult to read by touch.

options.label: B
options.text: At ten, Louis entered a school for blind children in Paris.

options.label: C
options.text: Louis later became a teacher and continued improving his code.

options.label: D
options.text: Louis Braille was born in a small French village in 1809.

questions.why: The raised-letter books were slow and difficult, which is the problem braille solved.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Boy Who Gave Books Fingertips” shows the impact Braille's work still has today?

segments.text: Barbier's system was complicated, but Louis recognized its possibilities.
By 1824, when he was only fifteen, his new alphabet was ready.
Louis later became a teacher and continued improving his code.
Today, braille is used around the world, and millions of blind readers can enjoy books independently because of a teenager's persistence.

questions.why: The last sentence tells the effect of his work on millions of readers today.

questions.stem: Put the events of Louis Braille's life in order.
sequence: Louis is injured in his father's workshop.
Louis enters a school for blind children in Paris.
Charles Barbier shares his night-reading code.
Louis completes his six-dot alphabet at fifteen.
questions.why: Biographies are often told in time order.

questions.stem: Which two details best support the idea that Louis showed determination? Choose two.
options: He was born in a small French village.
A soldier visited his school in Paris.
He kept improving his code as a teacher.
He simplified a complicated code into six dots.
questions.why: Simplifying and continually improving the code show he did not give up.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error in this sentence about young changemakers.
questions.why: The plural subject activists needs the verb have.

questions.stem: Match each claim about a young inventor named Rana with the evidence that best supports it.

pairs.right: She tested her design forty times before it worked.
Her water filter now serves three villages.
She started the project without waiting for help.
Dozens of students later began projects of their own.

questions.why: Good evidence matches the exact idea in each claim.

questions.stem: For the claim “Hana is a dedicated advocate for animals,” tell whether each detail is strong evidence or weak evidence.

rows.text: She volunteers at the animal shelter every Saturday.
She likes the color blue.
She wrote letters asking the city for a dog park.
Her brother is older than she is.

questions.why: Strong evidence connects directly to the claim about helping animals.

questions.stem: Although his first three designs failed, Daniel continued to ____ until his solar oven finally worked.
questions.why: To persevere is to keep going despite failure.

questions.stem: Which sentence would best support the claim “Young people can contribute to their communities”?
options: Some students prefer science classes to art classes.
A group of teens repaired benches in the town park.
Many teenagers enjoy listening to music after school.
A new phone model was released for young buyers.
questions.why: Repairing benches is a clear example of contributing to a community.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “The teacher's story inspired Khalid to start a reading club,” inspired means filled someone with the desire to do something.
questions.why: To inspire is to give someone the wish and energy to act.

questions.stem: Which three words or phrases are synonyms for persevere? Choose three.
questions.why: Persist, keep going, and endure all mean continuing despite difficulty.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error in this sentence about planting trees.
questions.why: The subject initiative is singular, so the verb is has had.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: “(1) Amal began a tutoring program for younger students. (2) She trained ten volunteers to help. (3) Her school has a red front door. (4) Test scores rose the next year.” Which sentence is least relevant to the central idea?
questions.why: The color of the door does not support the idea of Amal's tutoring program.

questions.stem: An ____ often gives speeches, writes letters, and organizes events to support a cause such as protecting coral reefs.
questions.why: An activist works actively for a cause.

questions.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses the central idea of “The Windmill Builder”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses the central idea of “The Windmill Builder”?

options.label: A
options.text: Malawi suffered a terrible drought at the start of the century.

options.label: B
options.text: Building a windmill requires costly tools and expert training.

options.label: C
options.text: Libraries in small villages often have very few science books.

options.label: D
options.text: Curiosity and hard work helped a teenager solve a serious problem.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: There he discovered a science book with a picture of windmills on its cover.

options.label: B
options.text: Neighbors laughed as William collected scrap metal, an old bicycle frame, and plastic pipes from a junkyard.

options.label: C
options.text: In 2001, a severe drought struck Malawi, and William Kamkwamba's family, like many farming families, could barely find enough food.

options.label: D
options.text: His story shows that curiosity and persistence can contribute more to success than expensive equipment.

questions.why: The last sentence sums up the central idea of the biography.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “The Windmill Builder” that show how William persevered despite obstacles.

segments.text: Unable to pay school fees, fourteen-year-old William had to leave school.
Instead of giving up on learning, he visited a small village library.
Although his English was limited, he studied the diagrams carefully and imagined building one himself.
Later, he built a larger windmill to pump water for crops.

questions.why: He kept learning after leaving school and studied hard despite limited English.

questions.stem: Tell whether each detail from “The Windmill Builder” is an obstacle William faced or an action William took.

rows.text: A drought left his family short of food.
He studied diagrams in a library book.
His neighbors laughed at him.
He collected scrap from a junkyard.

questions.why: Sorting obstacles and actions shows how William overcame challenges.

questions.stem: The author includes the detail that neighbors laughed at William in order to ____.
options: show the doubts he had to overcome
prove that his neighbors were scientists
questions.why: The detail shows that William kept going even when others doubted him.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the impact of William's windmills?
options: They brought light to his home and water to crops.
They replaced the library that had closed in 2001.
They made his neighbors stop farming completely.
They allowed his family to move to a large city.
