questions.stem: Put the events of “Dana in the Deep End” in order.
sequence: Dana slips off her float into the deep end.
The narrator sees small hands splashing.
The narrator pushes the pool hook toward Dana.
The uncle shakes the narrator's hand.
questions.why: Personal narratives usually tell events in time order.

questions.stem: Which two details from “Dana in the Deep End” support the idea that the narrator stayed calm? Choose two.
options: the aunt wrapping Dana in a towel
using the pool hook instead of jumping in
the swimming trip at the farm
questions.why: Clear thinking shows in remembering advice and choosing a safe tool.

questions.stem: Find the word that is used incorrectly in this sentence about the nurse's message.
questions.why: Something urgent must be dealt with right away.

questions.stem: Although the crowd around the injured runner was shouting, the coach kept her ____ and gave clear directions.
questions.why: Keeping your composure means staying calm under pressure.

questions.stem: Which phrase is closest in meaning to “frantic” in “Omar made a frantic search for his inhaler as his breathing grew worse”?
questions.why: A frantic search is rushed and desperate.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Her first instinct was to pull her hand away from the hot pan,” the word “instinct” means a reaction that happens naturally, without planning.
questions.why: An instinct is an automatic reaction.

questions.stem: Does each sentence use a form of the word “respond” correctly?

rows.text: Paramedics respond to calls within minutes.
Please respond to the invitation by Thursday.
The respond of the crowd was loud cheering.
He responded the ball into the goal.

questions.why: Respond is a verb meaning to answer or react; the noun is response.

questions.stem: How does the narrator's point of view about fire drills change in “The Smell of Smoke”?

partA.stem: How does the narrator's point of view about fire drills change in “The Smell of Smoke”?

options.label: A
options.text: from fearing them to laughing at them with friends

options.label: B
options.text: from trusting them to doubting that they work at all

options.label: C
options.text: from thinking they are pointless to believing they are valuable

options.label: D
options.text: from enjoying them to finding them dull and very tiring

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The fire had started in our kitchen, and the firefighters extinguished it before it spread.

options.label: B
options.text: Gray smoke was drifting under my bedroom door, and for a second I felt panic rise in my chest.

options.label: C
options.text: Now, whenever my classmates grumble during a practice evacuation, I describe that terrifying night to them.

options.label: D
options.text: We would line up, march outside, and stand in the blazing sun while the teachers counted us again and again.

questions.why: The narrator now defends drills to classmates who complain.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “The Smell of Smoke” that show the narrator used what was learned in the drills.

segments.text: I touched the door, and because it felt hot, I did not open it.
Instead, I opened my window, shouted for my father, and woke my younger brother, who was sleeping beside me.
I complained loudly about those drills to anyone who would listen.
Then, one night in January, I woke up to a strange, bitter smell.
Gray smoke was drifting under my bedroom door, and for a second I felt panic rise in my chest.

questions.why: Checking the door and using the window are safety steps learned in drills.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea of “The Smell of Smoke”?
options: Firefighters visit homes to teach children about fire safety rules.
Kitchens are the most common place in any home for a dangerous fire to begin.
Practice that seems boring can prepare people to act wisely in danger.
Students should be allowed to skip drills that happen too often.
questions.why: The whole narrative shows boring drills paying off in a real emergency.

questions.stem: In “The Smell of Smoke,” is each statement a fact the narrator reports or an opinion?

rows.text: The fire started in the kitchen.
Fire drills are a waste of time.
A firefighter checked the house.
Every student should take fire drills seriously.

questions.why: Facts can be checked; opinions tell what someone believes.

questions.stem: In “The Smell of Smoke,” the words “I felt panic rise in my chest” show that the narrator's first reaction was ____.
questions.why: Panic is a sudden rush of fear.

questions.stem: Which two sentences use the word “composure” correctly? Choose two.
options: The pilot's composure during the storm calmed the nervous passengers.
Even when the judges frowned, the young singer kept her composure.
He wrote a beautiful composure for the school orchestra concert.
The composure of the soup was too salty for most of the guests.
questions.why: Composure means calmness; do not confuse it with composition.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the word that fits its blank: “emergency,” “urgent,” “relief,” or “respond.”

pairs.left: The flood was an ____ that required rescue boats.
Doctors marked her case ____ and treated her first.
A wave of ____ swept over the family when the boy was found.
Rescue teams must ____ quickly when a call comes in.

questions.why: Use the meaning of each sentence and the part of speech needed to choose the word.

questions.stem: In which sentence does “instinct” mean a natural talent rather than an automatic reaction?
options: Laila has an instinct for finding good routes through markets.
When the ball flew at his face, his instinct was to duck.
A newborn sea turtle's instinct sends it crawling toward the water.
My first instinct was to scream when the lights went out suddenly.
questions.why: Instinct can also mean a natural ability, like a talent for finding routes.

questions.stem: Find the part of this sentence about a frantic mother that does not make sense.
questions.why: Frantic and calmly have opposite meanings, so they cannot describe the same moment.

questions.stem: True or false: The words “panic” and “composure” have nearly opposite meanings.
questions.why: Panic is sudden fear; composure is calm control.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the author's point of view about heroes in “Five Minutes on Platform Two”?

partA.stem: Which statement best expresses the author's point of view about heroes in “Five Minutes on Platform Two”?

options.label: A
options.text: Heroes are people who never feel afraid.

options.label: B
options.text: Heroes act alone without help from others.

options.label: C
options.text: Heroes feel fear but act anyway.

options.label: D
options.text: Heroes are mostly trained adults like paramedics.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Later, the man's son found our family and thanked me.

options.label: B
options.text: Several passengers stared, unsure what to do.

options.label: C
options.text: Within minutes, paramedics arrived and took over.

options.label: D
options.text: It is choosing to act while you are afraid.

questions.why: The author ends by defining courage as acting while afraid.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Five Minutes on Platform Two” most clearly shows the narrator's emotions during the emergency?

segments.text: My hands were shaking, and every instinct told me to step back and let an adult handle it.
I was waiting for the train with my older sister when an elderly man nearby suddenly clutched his chest and sank onto a bench.
The worker placed the pads, and the machine gave clear spoken instructions.
Within minutes, paramedics arrived and took over.

questions.why: Shaking hands and the urge to step back reveal the narrator's fear.

questions.stem: Which three details from “Five Minutes on Platform Two” support the idea that preparation helped the narrator respond? Choose three.
options: telling a worker to bring the defibrillator
passengers staring at the elderly man
the son thanking the family later
questions.why: These actions come from what the narrator learned in the course.

questions.stem: How does the opening sentence of “Five Minutes on Platform Two” contribute to the narrative?
options: It presents a common belief that the narrator's experience will challenge.
It describes the busy setting of the metro station in careful, vivid detail.
It introduces the narrator's sister as the true hero of the event.
It explains the medical reasons why the elderly man fell ill.
questions.why: The narrator states what people believe, then shows it is not true.

questions.stem: Put the narrator's actions in “Five Minutes on Platform Two” in order.
sequence: notices the man sink onto a bench
remembers the first-aid course
asks the sister to call 997
is thanked by the man's son
questions.why: Following the sequence shows how the narrator moved from fear to action.

questions.stem: The lost hikers had to ____ two cold nights in the mountains before rescuers found them.
questions.why: To endure is to live through something difficult.

questions.stem: Which person shows courage?
options: a child who hides the broken vase so that no one will blame him
a boy who stays home because he is afraid to try out for the team
a girl who speaks up to stop classmates from teasing a new student
a student who copies a friend's homework to avoid a bad grade
questions.why: Courage means doing the right thing even when it is hard or scary.

questions.stem: True or false: A hostile crowd is friendly and welcoming to visitors.
questions.why: Hostile means unfriendly or showing anger.

questions.stem: Match each word (“courage,” “dignity,” “intimidate,” “resilient”) with its meaning.

pairs.right: bravery when facing danger or fear
a sense of self-respect and worth
to frighten someone in order to control them
able to recover quickly from difficulty

questions.why: These words describe how people face and react to hard times.

questions.stem: Does each sentence show perseverance or giving up?

rows.text: Ahmed practiced the hard piano piece every day for three months.
Reem quit the puzzle after the first two pieces did not fit.
The team kept training after losing their first five matches.
Fahad stopped studying calligraphy after one difficult lesson.

questions.why: Perseverance means continuing to try even when progress is slow.

questions.stem: What does the word “dignity” most likely mean as it is used in paragraph 2 of “The New Accent”?
questions.why: The mother's words “Hold your head up” are a clue that dignity means self-respect.

questions.stem: What is a theme of “The New Accent”?

partA.stem: What is a theme of “The New Accent”?

options.label: A
options.text: Students should hide their accents to fit in.

options.label: B
options.text: A science club is the best place to make friends.

options.label: C
options.text: Moving to a new city is always a sad experience.

options.label: D
options.text: Steady kindness can change how others treat you.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I also joined the science club, where nobody cared about my accent and everybody cared about experiments.

options.label: B
options.text: On the first morning, a group of boys laughed at my accent whenever I answered a question, and one of them whispered that I should return to wherever I had come from.

options.label: C
options.text: For days afterward, I seriously considered remaining silent for the rest of the year.

options.label: D
options.text: I learned that patient kindness can change people far more effectively than anger can.

questions.why: The narrator states the lesson directly at the end.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The New Accent” shows that the narrator decided not to give up?

segments.text: So I kept raising my hand, even when my voice trembled.
For days afterward, I seriously considered remaining silent for the rest of the year.
But my mother reminded me that our family had always faced difficult times with dignity.
When my family moved from Cairo to a new city, I was the only new student in my sixth-grade class.

questions.why: Raising a hand again shows the narrator kept participating.

questions.stem: Put the events of “The New Accent” in order.
sequence: The boys laugh at the narrator's accent.
The mother tells the narrator to hold up their head.
The narrator joins the science club.
Two of the boys ask the narrator for help.
questions.why: A memoir often moves from a problem to a change in the writer.

questions.stem: Which two words best describe the narrator by the end of “The New Accent”? Choose two.
questions.why: The narrator recovers from the teasing and keeps taking part.

questions.stem: Find the part of this sentence about a determined climber that does not make sense.
segments: and kept pushing through the snow
questions.why: A determined person keeps going rather than giving up.

questions.stem: The large dog barked at the gate to ____ strangers, but it wagged its tail at the family.
questions.why: To intimidate is to frighten someone so they stay away or obey.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word “resilient” correctly?
options: The resilient student gave up completely the very first time she failed a quiz.
The resilient palm trees bent in the storm but stood tall again the next day.
The resilient glass shattered into pieces the moment it hit the floor.
The resilient plant died after one day without any water.
questions.why: Something resilient bounces back after being bent or hurt.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The old man spoke with dignity even when the guards were rude to him,” the man lost his self-respect.
questions.why: Speaking with dignity shows that he kept his self-respect.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “determined”?

rows.text: resolved
unsure
persistent
hesitant

questions.why: Synonyms share a meaning; antonyms have opposite meanings.

questions.stem: What does the phrase “hiding in the back row like a turtle in its shell” suggest about the narrator in fifth grade?
options: The narrator tried to stay out of sight to feel protected.
The narrator preferred a seat far from the board to daydream.
The narrator brought a small pet turtle into the classroom.
The narrator moved very slowly and carefully between classes each day.
questions.why: A turtle pulls into its shell for protection, just as the narrator hid from others.

questions.stem: What does the word “endured” mean as it is used in paragraph 3 of “Finding My Voice”?

options.label: B
options.text: quickly forgot something

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Finding My Voice” best reveals the author's point of view about speaking up?

segments.text: Yet a stubborn voice inside me said that silence was not the same as safety.
Then our teacher announced a public speaking contest for the entire grade.
For as long as I can remember, I have struggled with a stutter.
On contest day, I stuttered twice during my speech.

questions.why: The author believes staying silent is not a real way to be safe.

questions.stem: In “Finding My Voice,” does each phrase show the narrator's fear or the narrator's courage?

rows.text: hiding in the back row
signed up before I could change my mind
avoided speaking whenever I could
practiced every evening in front of the mirror

questions.why: The narrator moves from hiding to acting bravely.

questions.stem: Which two statements express themes of “Finding My Voice”? Choose two.
options: People who stutter should avoid speaking contests.
Perseverance can matter more than winning a prize.
Audiences usually judge speakers harshly for mistakes.
Courage means acting even when success is not certain.
questions.why: The narrator did not win but gained something more important by trying.

questions.stem: Which two words are closest in meaning to “perseverance”? Choose two.
questions.why: Perseverance is steady effort over time.

questions.stem: Instead of letting the ____ shouts of the opposing fans upset him, the goalkeeper smiled and focused on the game.
questions.why: Hostile shouts are angry and unfriendly.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the word it illustrates: “endure,” “intimidate,” “resilient,” or “courage.”

pairs.left: The camel walked for days across hot sand without water.
The bully cracked his knuckles to frighten the younger boys.
After the flood, the town rebuilt its market in one year.
The firefighter ran into the smoking building to save a child.

questions.why: Look for the action in each sentence that shows the word's meaning.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Though reporters shouted questions and cameras flashed in her face, the athlete answered each one with quiet dignity.” What is the effect of the phrase “quiet dignity”?
options: It shows that she is too shy to answer the reporters at all.
It shows that she is angry but hides it behind a forced smile.
It shows that she does not understand any of the questions asked.
It shows that she stays calm and respectful despite the pressure.
questions.why: Quiet dignity suggests calm self-respect even in a stressful moment.

questions.stem: Find the part of this sentence about a resilient team that does not make sense.
segments: and began training the next morning.
questions.why: A resilient team bounces back instead of quitting.

questions.stem: What does “agonizingly” most likely mean as it is used in paragraph 3 of “Learning to Run Again”?

options.label: A
options.text: in a very painful way

options.label: B
options.text: in a surprisingly fast way

options.label: C
options.text: in a calm and easy way

options.label: D
options.text: in a careless way

options.label: B
options.text: I was not fast, but I was running.

options.label: C

questions.stem: Why does the author describe Ms. Hessa's expectations as “almost hostile at first”?

to prove that Ms. Hessa truly disliked working with young, complaining patients
to show how the narrator misjudged her before understanding her purpose
questions.why: “Only later did I realize” shows that the narrator's first view was wrong.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Learning to Run Again” that best show the author's changed perspective.

However, I gradually discovered that each small victory gave me the strength to attempt the next one.
For weeks, I lay in a hospital bed in Dammam, staring at the ceiling and feeling sorry for myself.
The doctors cautiously warned my parents that I might never run again.
I was eleven, and a car accident had shattered my left leg in three places.

questions.why: “Only later did I realize” and “I gradually discovered” signal new understanding.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the theme of “Learning to Run Again”?
options: Small, steady efforts can build the resilience needed to overcome setbacks.
Strict teachers and therapists are rarely as kind as gentle ones are.
Winning a race is the best way to prove that someone has fully healed.
Doctors are usually wrong whenever they try to predict how a young patient will recover.
questions.why: Each small victory built the strength for the next until the narrator ran again.

questions.stem: In “Learning to Run Again,” does each detail describe the narrator early or late in recovery?

rows.text: staring at the ceiling and feeling sorry for myself
crossing the finish line of a charity race
trying to stand for ten seconds
using each small victory as strength for the next

questions.why: Tracking details over time shows how the narrator changed.

questions.stem: The children were ____ to open the box because they knew a new kitten was inside.
questions.why: Eager means wanting very much to do something.

questions.stem: Which word means “to understand”?
questions.why: To comprehend something is to understand it.

questions.stem: True or false: A village that is isolated is far away from other towns and hard to reach.
questions.why: Isolated means set apart or cut off from others.

questions.stem: Match each word (“persistent,” “frustration,” “revelation,” “triumph”) with its meaning.

pairs.right: an upset feeling when you cannot do something
a surprising discovery that makes something clear

questions.why: These words often appear in stories about overcoming challenges.

questions.stem: Does each phrase describe a sensation (something felt by the body) or not?

rows.text: the cold sting of ice on your fingers
the warmth of sunlight on your face
remembering the date of a test
planning what to eat for dinner

questions.why: A sensation is a feeling that comes through the senses.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of “Dots That Speak”?
options: The narrator's teacher wrote special Braille books for each student in class.
The narrator learned that “sea” is the most beautiful word in any language.
The narrator chose to stop reading books for good after losing sight.
With practice, the narrator learned a new way to read after losing sight.
questions.why: The narrative shows the narrator learning Braille and reading again.

questions.stem: How did the narrator of “Dots That Speak” feel when first trying to read Braille?

partA.stem: How did the narrator of “Dots That Speak” feel when first trying to read Braille?

options.label: A
options.text: proud

options.label: B
options.text: sleepy

options.label: C
options.text: delighted

options.label: D
options.text: frustrated

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Each night, I ran my fingertips slowly across the lines, and each night I experienced the same frustration.

options.label: B
options.text: My teacher, Mr. Khalid, patiently introduced me to a book written in Braille.

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Dots That Speak” describes the narrator's turning point?

My teacher, Mr. Khalid, patiently introduced me to a book written in Braille.

questions.why: Reading the first word is the moment everything changes.

questions.stem: Put the events of “Dots That Speak” in order.
sequence: The narrator loses most of their sight.
Mr. Khalid gives the narrator a Braille book.
The narrator reads the word “sea.”
The narrator reads whole chapters alone.
questions.why: Autobiographies usually follow the order of the writer's life.

questions.stem: Which two details from “Dots That Speak” show that the narrator was persistent? Choose two.
options: thinking the pages looked like fog
practicing even harder after reading one word
laughing out loud at the word
questions.why: Persistent people keep practicing even when it is hard.

questions.stem: Find the part of this sentence about the science team's triumph that does not make sense.
questions.why: A triumph is a victory, so it brings pride, not shame.

questions.stem: Living on a tiny island with no bridge, the fishermen felt ____ from the busy world on the mainland.
questions.why: Being cut off by water makes them isolated.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Seeing the stars through the telescope was a revelation; Huda finally understood why her father loved astronomy.” What does “revelation” mean?
options: a slow and very boring wait
questions.why: “Finally understood” is a clue that a revelation is a new understanding.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The persistent woodpecker tapped the tree for hours until it made a hole,” the word “persistent” means the bird kept trying without stopping.
questions.why: Persistent means continuing firmly over time.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “eager”?

rows.text: keen
reluctant
enthusiastic
indifferent

questions.why: Eager means excited and wanting to do something.

questions.stem: What is the author's perspective on the night the radio arrived in “The Voice in the Desert”?

options.label: A
options.text: It was a fun evening, but it did not change the author's life.

options.label: B
options.text: It was a life-changing moment that opened up the world.

options.text: It was the first time the author felt bored in the camp.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I spent my early childhood in a small Bedouin camp in the Empty Quarter.

options.label: B
options.text: The sensation was like a door opening in a wall I had never noticed.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea of “The Voice in the Desert”?
options: The author's uncle became a geography teacher after visiting the city.
Radios were common in desert camps when the author was a young child.
Bedouin camps in the Empty Quarter are a full day apart from one another.
Hearing about the wider world sparked a lifelong love of learning.
questions.why: The radio led the author to school, maps, and a career teaching geography.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “The Voice in the Desert” that show how the radio changed the author's actions.

My uncle helped me find a school in the nearest town, and I memorized maps the way other children memorized songs.
I spent my early childhood in a small Bedouin camp in the Empty Quarter.
That belief changed when I was eight.
A calm voice described snow falling in a faraway country, rivers wider than our valley, and cities with towers that touched the clouds.

questions.why: After the radio, the author wanted to learn and went to school.

questions.stem: Is each statement about the author of “The Voice in the Desert” supported by the autobiography or not supported?

rows.text: The author lived far from other families as a child.
The author's uncle brought a radio from the city.
The author's parents disapproved of the radio.
The author has since visited every country on the radio.

questions.why: Only choose statements that the text actually gives evidence for.

questions.stem: When the author of “The Voice in the Desert” says, “I still remember the night I discovered how isolated we had been,” the word “isolated” tells the reader that the family had been ____.

questions.why: Isolated means separated from other people and places.

questions.stem: Which two sentences use the word “comprehend” correctly? Choose two.
options: Please comprehend the dishes before your guests arrive tonight.
The runner comprehended the finish line in record time.
Even after reading the instructions twice, Nasser could not comprehend how the machine worked.
Young children often cannot comprehend how large the ocean really is.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the word it best illustrates: “frustration,” “revelation,” “sensation,” or “triumph.”

questions.stem: Which word best replaces “persistent” in “The persistent cough kept Sami awake for a whole week”?
questions.why: A persistent cough continues for a long time.

questions.stem: Find the part of this sentence about an eager student that does not make sense.

questions.stem: What is the author's perspective on learning sign language in “The Language of Hands”?

partA.stem: What is the author's perspective on learning sign language in “The Language of Hands”?

options.label: A
options.text: It was a burden that took time from other school subjects.

options.label: B
options.text: It gave the author a full language that had been missing.

options.label: C
options.text: It mattered less to the author than learning to read lips.

options.label: D
options.text: It was a skill the author learned quickly but rarely used.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The hardest challenge came later.

options.label: B
options.text: On the first morning, I watched two teachers talking with their hands, their fingers moving as quickly as birds.

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of “The Language of Hands”?
options: Deaf students in Jeddah always learn sign language faster than children in other cities.
Learning a shared language transformed the author's life and family relationships.
Laughing at jokes is the best way for families to communicate well.
The author's father was too old to learn a new language successfully.
questions.why: Sign language changed school life and, later, the author's bond with the father.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Language of Hands” shows the author's triumph at the end?

segments.text: Two years later, he signed an entire story to me at bedtime.
I wanted my family to learn to sign, but my father insisted he was too old to begin.
We communicated through pointing, facial expressions, and a few homemade gestures.
The hardest challenge came later.

questions.why: The father signing a whole story proves the author's teaching succeeded.

questions.stem: Which three details from “The Language of Hands” support the idea that the author was isolated before school? Choose three.
options: watching teachers' fingers move like birds
no one in the family knowing sign language
enrolling in a school in Jeddah
using only pointing and a few gestures
teaching the father one sign each evening
laughing at jokes without understanding them
questions.why: These details show the author could not fully share in family talk.

questions.stem: Put the stages of the author's life in “The Language of Hands” in order.
sequence: communicating with gestures at home
enrolling in a school for deaf students
teaching the father one sign each evening
watching the father sign a bedtime story
questions.why: The autobiography moves forward through the author's life.

questions.stem: Moving to a new school was hard at first, but Sami learned to ____ to the new schedule.
questions.why: To adapt is to change to fit a new situation.

questions.stem: Which person is most likely homesick?

questions.stem: True or false: A reluctant helper is someone who is eager and happy to help.
questions.why: Reluctant means unwilling or not wanting to do something.

questions.stem: Match each word (“heritage,” “ancestor,” “tradition,” “bewildered”) with its meaning.

a family member who lived long ago
a custom repeated for many years

questions.why: These words help describe family history and new experiences.

a snowy village in Norway
her school's library
a rice farm in Vietnam

questions.why: Unfamiliar means not known or not seen before.

questions.stem: Which word best describes the tone of the first paragraph of “Fog on the Terraces”?

questions.stem: How does Mira change during “Fog on the Terraces”?

partA.stem: How does Mira change during “Fog on the Terraces”?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: She goes from reluctant to comfortable in the village.

options.label: C
options.text: She goes from happy to homesick for her friends.

options.label: D
options.text: She goes from shy to bossy with her grandmother.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Mira was surprised to find herself humming it before she fell asleep.

options.label: B
options.text: All her friends were going to the beach in Jeddah, and she was stuck with a family she barely knew.

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: On the first morning, the fog was so thick that she could not see the end of the winding road.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Fog on the Terraces” uses words that appeal to the sense of smell?

segments.text: The steps were steep, and the air smelled of wet earth and wild herbs.
Her grandmother handed her a basket and pointed toward the terraced fields.
Mira sighed dramatically and followed her reluctantly.

questions.why: Sensory words help readers experience the setting.

questions.stem: Put the events of “Fog on the Terraces” in order.
sequence: Mira arrives unhappily in the village.
Grandmother hands Mira a basket.
Mira learns the names of the goats.
Mira hums the harvest song at bedtime.
questions.why: The events show Mira slowly settling into village life.

questions.stem: Which two phrases from “Fog on the Terraces” show that Mira is reluctant at first? Choose two.
options: knew the names of the goats
humming it before she fell asleep
had not wanted to spend the summer
questions.why: Reluctant characters show unwillingness through words and actions.

questions.stem: Find the part of this sentence about our ancestor that does not make sense.

questions.stem: Faced with a menu written in a language he could not read, Tariq felt completely ____.
questions.why: Bewildered means confused and unsure what to do.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word “heritage” correctly?

My heritage broke when I dropped it on the floor.
questions.why: Heritage means traditions and culture handed down over generations.

questions.why: To adapt is to change in order to fit new conditions.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “unfamiliar”?

well-known
new
common

questions.why: Unfamiliar describes something you do not know well.

questions.stem: How does the tone of “The Blue Gate” change from beginning to end?
options: from curious to bored and tired
from overwhelmed to calm and connected
from cheerful to angry and impatient
from peaceful to frightened and tense
questions.why: Noise and confusion give way to quiet and a sense of belonging.

questions.stem: In “The Blue Gate,” is each phrase an example of a simile or of personification?

The medina of Fez swallowed Adam
a little less like a maze

questions.why: A simile compares with like or as; personification gives human or animal actions to things.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Blue Gate” shows that Adam begins to feel connected to his heritage?

segments.text: He imagined an ancestor he had never met sitting on that same worn bench.
Adam, who had grown up in quiet Toronto, felt bewildered and slightly dizzy.
His grandfather walked ahead calmly, greeting shopkeepers by name.
Adam watched the needle dart in and out of the soft yellow leather.

questions.why: Picturing his ancestor links Adam to his family's past.

questions.stem: In “The Blue Gate,” the verb “dart” makes the old man's stitching seem ____.
questions.why: Dart describes a fast, sharp, sure movement.

questions.stem: Which two sentences use the word “reluctant” correctly? Choose two.
options: The reluctant witness spoke only after the judge asked her three times.
The reluctant puppy raced to the door the moment it heard its name.
Reluctant to leave the warm fire, the travelers waited until sunrise to continue.
Reluctant to swim, Hamad jumped into the pool before anyone else.
questions.why: Reluctant people hold back because they do not want to act.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the word it best illustrates: “homesick,” “adapt,” “tradition,” or “heritage.”

The new student quickly learned the bus routes and school rules.
Every year on the first day of Eid, the family gathers at Grandfather's house.
The old forts and palm groves of Al-Ahsa are protected for future generations.

questions.why: Look for the clue in each sentence that points to the word.

questions.stem: Which word suggests the most confused, uneasy feeling?
questions.why: Bewildered means so confused that you do not know what to do.

questions.stem: Find the word that is used incorrectly in this sentence about Grandmother's move north.
questions.why: Adapt means to adjust; adopt means to take as your own.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Learning the old dances helped Sami honor his ancestors,” the word “ancestors” refers to his younger cousins.
questions.why: Ancestors are relatives who lived long before you.

questions.stem: Which word best describes Dalia's attitude in the first paragraph of “Ninety Years of Dates”?

questions.why: Greeting the trees like friends and honoring the old palm show his love.

questions.stem: Match each word a teacher of a struggling learner might use with its definition: obstinate, discipline, determination, frustration.

anger at being unable to succeed

questions.why: These words describe the feelings and habits of people who face a hard lesson.

questions.stem: Nasser read the model-bridge instructions three times but still could not ____ how the pieces fit together.
questions.why: To comprehend is to understand, which fits someone puzzling over instructions.

questions.stem: True or false: A breakthrough is a sudden, important success that comes after a long period of trying.
questions.why: A breakthrough is the moment when long effort finally pays off.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word persistent correctly?
options: The persistent volunteer knocked on every door until the street signed up.
Laila felt persistent after lunch and quietly fell asleep on the long sofa.
The persistent glass shattered the moment it touched the hard kitchen floor.
The persistent cloud vanished from the sky in less than one short second.
questions.why: Persistent means continuing without giving up, like the volunteer who kept knocking.

questions.stem: Does each reaction to a hard lesson show “frustration” or “determination”?

Huda set her alarm earlier so she could practice before school.

questions.why: Stubborn and headstrong both describe someone who will not change his or her mind.

With discipline, she practiced twenty minutes every evening.

questions.stem: In “The Falcon Lesson,” what is the main purpose of the words in brackets?

to explain the lesson the playwright wants every reader to learn
to tell actors how to move and where the scene takes place

It actually chose me, after everything I said about it.

Forty times is a beginning, not an ending.

questions.stem: In a drama about a stubborn student and a patient tutor, is each event part of the exposition, the rising action, or the climax?

options.label: C
options.text: Shining objects are always worth more than plain ones.

options.label: D

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the letter best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Do not envy the boy with the expensive shoes or the newest electronic gadgets.

options.label: C
options.text: When you make a mistake, admit it immediately and honestly.

options.label: D
options.text: Let me share what seventy years of experience have taught me.

questions.why: A mirage looks real from far away but disappears, just like the value of fancy things.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “A Letter from Grandfather” uses a metaphor to show that honesty guides other people?

segments.text: Honesty is a lantern; people will follow its light long after they have forgotten your name.
When you make a mistake, admit it immediately and honestly.
Your mind is a garden, and every habit you practice is a seed.
Do not envy the boy with the expensive shoes or the newest electronic gadgets.

questions.why: A lantern lights the way, just as an honest person shows others the right path.

questions.stem: In “A Letter from Grandfather,” the advice to ____ habits like seeds in a garden shows that good character must be grown over time.
questions.why: To cultivate is to grow something with care, like a gardener.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about effort and honesty with its type of figurative language.

pairs.left: Hard work is the key that opens every door.
Her promise was as solid as a stone wall.
The lazy afternoon whispered, “Rest a little longer.”
I have told you a million times to be careful!

questions.why: Recognizing figurative language helps readers find a writer's deeper meaning.

questions.stem: What does the metaphor “Integrity is the backbone of a good leader” mean?
options: Good leaders must exercise often to keep their backs healthy.
A leader's honesty is hidden deep inside where nobody sees it.
Leaders with integrity usually stand taller than other people.
Honesty gives a leader strength and keeps him standing firm.
questions.why: A backbone holds the body up, just as integrity supports a leader.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Superficial friendships are paper boats; they sink in the first storm,” the writer suggests that shallow friendships do not last through hard times.
questions.why: Paper boats sink easily, so the metaphor shows that shallow friendships fail under pressure.

questions.stem: Find the part that contradicts the rest of this sentence about a conscientious librarian.
questions.why: A conscientious worker acts carefully, not carelessly.

questions.stem: A father writes, “Do not chase applause; chase the quiet satisfaction of a job done well.” Which two statements express his message? Choose two.
options: Jobs that are noisy and busy are usually the best jobs.
Doing good work matters more than being praised for it.
People should never clap for others at school events.
Pride in honest effort is a better goal than attention.
questions.why: The father contrasts outside praise with the inner reward of good work.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the main message of “A Letter to Lulwa”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the main message of “A Letter to Lulwa”?

options.label: A
options.text: Lulwa should reply to her classmates' messages much more quickly.

options.label: B
options.text: Lulwa should become an architect only because her mother wishes it.

options.label: C
options.text: Lulwa should guard her time so she can work toward her real goals.

options.label: D
options.text: Lulwa should never own a phone, even after she becomes an adult.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the letter best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Yesterday evening you asked me why I refused to buy you the phone that everyone in your class seems to own.

options.label: B
options.text: I was exhausted after a long day at the hospital, and my answer was impatient, so let me reply properly now.

options.label: C
options.text: I want your hours to belong to you, not to a glowing screen that never stops demanding attention.

options.label: D
options.text: I am saying "not yet."

questions.why: The mother wants Lulwa's time spent on her goals rather than lost to a screen.

questions.stem: In “A Letter to Lulwa,” what does the comparison “Time is a quiet thief” suggest?
options: Time is lost slowly and secretly, often without our noticing.
Time can be stolen back if a person locks the door carefully.
Time belongs only to people who own the newest kinds of phones.
Time moves so loudly that people always notice when it passes.
questions.why: A quiet thief takes things without being noticed, just as distractions steal time.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “A Letter to Lulwa” reverses its words to state the mother's message most memorably?

segments.text: When you are older, you will hold the phone, but I simply do not want it to hold you.
You aspire to become an architect, and that ambitious dream deserves to be your priority.
Those habits will carry you further than any number of superficial messages.
Time is a quiet thief.

questions.why: Switching who holds whom makes the warning about control easy to remember.

questions.stem: Which two activities does the mother suggest Lulwa make her priority instead of a phone? Choose two.
options: buying a phone like the ones her classmates own
reflecting on why some rooms feel welcoming
sending short messages to her classmates
questions.why: The mother lists activities that build toward Lulwa's dream of architecture.

questions.stem: In “A Letter to Lulwa,” is each phrase meant literally or figuratively?

rows.text: Time is a quiet thief.
measure the shadows of buildings
it slips away through a thousand small distractions
You aspire to become an architect

questions.why: Figurative phrases compare or exaggerate; literal phrases mean exactly what they say.

questions.stem: A person with ____ tells the truth even when a lie would be easier and no one would ever find out.
questions.why: Integrity means being honest even when no one is watching.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence from a father's advice: “Be the palm tree, not the tumbleweed: put down deep roots, and the wind will not decide where you go.” What is the father's message?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence from a father's advice: “Be the palm tree, not the tumbleweed: put down deep roots, and the wind will not decide where you go.” What is the father's message?

options.label: A
options.text: Windy weather is dangerous, so stay indoors on stormy days.

options.label: B
options.text: Palm trees are more useful than tumbleweeds in desert farming.

options.label: C
options.text: A person should move often so that he can see many new places.

options.label: D
options.text: Strong values keep a person steady when others try to push him.

partB.stem: Part B: Which words from the sentence best support the answer to Part A?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: “the wind”

options.label: C
options.text: “not the tumbleweed”

options.label: D

questions.why: Deep roots stand for firm values that keep a person from being blown around.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a simile to describe a conscientious person?
options: Like a watchman on a city wall, Faten checked every detail of her report.
Faten checked every detail of her long report about a million times.
Faten's report begged her to check every single detail one more time.
Faten was a watchman on a city wall, guarding every detail of her report.
questions.why: A simile uses like or as; the other choices are a metaphor, personification, and hyperbole.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order to build a paragraph that ends with the writer's message about superficial goals.
sequence: Many people aspire to be famous online.
They post photos every hour, hoping for likes.
Yet likes are like sand castles that vanish with the tide.
A goal worth chasing should be something that lasts.
questions.why: The paragraph describes a habit, judges it with a simile, then states the message.

questions.stem: Which part of this advice uses the word “reflect” incorrectly?
segments: and then reflect the goal loudly to everyone.
questions.correction: and then share the goal with your family.
questions.why: Reflect means to think carefully, not to announce something.

questions.stem: Match each word about facing unfair treatment with its meaning: prejudice, restraint, retaliate, adversity.

pairs.right: an unfair opinion formed without knowing the facts
calm control over one's actions or feelings
to strike back at someone who has caused harm

questions.why: These words describe hardships and the ways people respond to them.

questions.stem: The bully tried to ____ Khalid by calling him names, hoping he would lose his temper.
questions.why: To provoke is to try to make someone angry or upset.

questions.stem: True or false: Segregation is the practice of keeping groups of people apart, often through unfair laws.
questions.why: Segregation separates people, usually by race, under unfair rules.

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? “The firefighter's ____ act of running into the smoke saved two children.”
questions.why: Running into danger to save others is a courageous act.

questions.stem: Does each action show “dignity” or a lack of dignity?

rows.text: After losing the final, the captain shook hands with every player on the other team.
Nawaf mocked the referee and threw his shirt on the field.
Even when people laughed at her accent, Mariam answered politely and stood tall.
Fahd shouted insults at the crowd after a missed shot.

questions.why: Dignity means behaving with calm self-respect, even in hard moments.

questions.stem: Which two sentences show restraint? Choose two.
options: Although Ziad was angry, he took a deep breath and walked away from the argument.
Omar shouted back at the player who pushed him and started a fight.
Saja wanted to answer the rude comment, but she stayed silent and kept working.
Rima grabbed the ball from her teammate because she was annoyed.
questions.why: Restraint means holding back an angry reaction.

questions.stem: When rival fans booed him, the runner chose not to ____; instead, he answered with his best race of the season.
questions.why: To retaliate is to strike back, which the runner chose not to do.

questions.stem: Find the part that gives the wrong meaning in this sentence about adversity.
questions.why: Overcoming adversity means continuing through hard times, not quitting.

questions.stem: Which word is a synonym for “prejudice”?
questions.why: Prejudice and bias both mean an unfair judgment made in advance.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order to tell how Bader faced adversity on his new team.
sequence: On his first day, some players made unkind jokes to provoke Bader.
Bader felt angry, but he showed restraint and said nothing.
He trained harder than anyone and scored in the next match.
By the end of the season, his teammates admired his dignity.
questions.why: The events move from the problem to Bader's response to the result.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of “My First Season”?
options: The narrator wins respect by answering cruelty with self-control and effort.
The narrator's father teaches him how to take a powerful left-footed shot.
The narrator decides to leave the academy and return to his mountain village.
The narrator learns that city players are always better than village players.
questions.why: The whole passage shows how calm effort turned mockery into respect.

questions.stem: Part A: What lesson does the narrator learn by the end of “My First Season”?

partA.stem: Part A: What lesson does the narrator learn by the end of “My First Season”?

options.label: A
options.text: Practicing late at night is bad for young players.

options.label: B
options.text: Holding back anger can be a form of strength.

options.label: C
options.text: Fighting back is the fastest way to earn respect.

options.label: D
options.text: New players should avoid speaking to their teammates.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: My boots were old, my accent was strong, and several of the city boys immediately decided that I did not belong.

options.label: B
options.text: I wanted to retaliate more than I had ever wanted anything.

options.label: C
options.text: I realized that restraint is not weakness; it is strength that has learned to wait.

options.label: D
options.text: Gradually, the laughter faded into silence and then into respect.

questions.why: The final sentence directly states the lesson about restraint.

questions.stem: Which two sentences from “My First Season” are the best evidence that the narrator met adversity with hard work? Select two sentences.

segments.text: For weeks, I answered every insult with hard work.
I arrived early, stayed late, and practiced passing until the sun disappeared behind the stadium.
My face burned with humiliation, and I wanted to retaliate more than I had ever wanted anything.

questions.why: Strong evidence names the actual effort the narrator made.

questions.stem: Compare the tall defender at the beginning and at the end of “My First Season.” When does each detail describe him?

rows.text: pushes the narrator to the ground
asks to learn the narrator's left-footed shot
tells the narrator to go back to his goats
treats the narrator as someone with skills worth learning

questions.why: Contrasting the defender's actions shows how the narrator's restraint changed him.

questions.stem: In “My First Season,” the defender's insult was meant to ____ the narrator into a fight.
questions.why: The defender wanted to provoke, or anger, the narrator.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph: “For decades, segregation kept Black players out of the major baseball leagues in the United States. These players formed their own leagues, which produced some of the greatest athletes in the sport's history.” Which sentence best states the main idea?
options: Excluded players built strong leagues of their own despite segregation.
Major league baseball has always welcomed every talented player equally.
The greatest athletes in baseball history all played in the major leagues.
Baseball was not a popular sport in the early part of the twentieth century.
questions.why: The main idea combines the unfair exclusion with the players' strong response.

questions.stem: Match each signal word with what it shows in a compare-and-contrast paragraph about two athletes.

pairs.right: points out how one differs from the other

questions.why: Signal words tell readers whether a writer is comparing or contrasting.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “Like his older brother, Hamza faced prejudice at his new school, but unlike his brother, he reported it to a teacher,” the brothers are compared in one way and contrasted in another.
questions.why: Like shows a similarity, and unlike shows a difference.

questions.stem: A student claims, “Saleh showed dignity after the unfair call.” Which two details are the strongest evidence for this claim? Choose two.
options: Saleh told reporters that he respected the referee's job even though he disagreed.
Saleh had scored two goals earlier in the same match.
Saleh's team was wearing new green uniforms that day.
Saleh calmly shook the referee's hand and returned to his position.
questions.why: Good evidence must connect directly to the claim about dignity.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order to build a paragraph that states a main idea about courage and then supports it.
sequence: Courage is not only found in great battles; it also appears in everyday choices.
For example, a student may speak up when classmates mock someone.
Another student may admit a mistake even though others will laugh.
These quiet acts take courageous hearts, too.
questions.why: A paragraph states the main idea, gives examples, and then sums up.

questions.stem: Part A: In “Two Tournaments,” how is the narrator's response at seventeen different from his response at twelve?

partA.stem: Part A: In “Two Tournaments,” how is the narrator's response at seventeen different from his response at twelve?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: At seventeen he refuses to shake hands, but at twelve he greets everyone kindly.

options.label: C
options.text: At seventeen he faces no unfair looks, but at twelve he faces many of them.

options.label: D

questions.why: This sentence shows how he changed in the way he handled unfair treatment.

questions.stem: Which two things stay the same in both of the narrator's tournaments in “Two Tournaments”? Choose two.
options: The narrator finishes in second place.
The tournaments take place in the same hall.
Some people treat the narrator unfairly.
The narrator loses three games in a row.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of “Two Tournaments”?
options: Unfair treatment at chess tournaments disappears once a player becomes older.
Chess tournaments in Europe are much harder than tournaments at home.
Over time, the narrator learns that his dignity depends on him, not others.
The narrator wins second place because his opponents played carelessly.
questions.why: The passage contrasts two tournaments to show the narrator's inner growth.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Two Tournaments” best explains why the narrator struggled at age twelve?

segments.text: At twelve, I believed that I had to win people's approval before I could win a match.
I remember the enormous hall in Vienna more vividly than any individual game.
Five years later, I returned to the same competition in the same hall.
That year, I finished second overall.

questions.why: Needing others' approval made him easy to shake, which explains his losses.

questions.stem: In “Two Tournaments,” does each detail describe the narrator at twelve or at seventeen?

rows.text: makes careless moves he would never make at home
extends his hand whether or not it is accepted
believes he must win approval before winning a match
finishes second in the tournament

questions.why: Sorting details by age makes the contrast between the two tournaments clear.

questions.stem: Choosing to stay calm instead of fighting back when someone tries to ____ you takes great restraint.
questions.why: Staying calm when someone tries to provoke you shows restraint.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “Although segregation laws kept the two friends in separate schools, they met every Friday to study together by lantern light.” What does the sentence mainly show?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “Although segregation laws kept the two friends in separate schools, they met every Friday to study together by lantern light.” What does the sentence mainly show?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: The friends kept their friendship despite an unfair system.

options.label: C
options.text: The friends' schools taught exactly the same lessons each week.

options.label: D
options.text: The friends were not allowed to meet on any day of the week.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about a reporter does not make sense with the rest?
segments: about the unfair treatment he witnessed.
questions.why: Hiding and refusing to write show fear, not courage.

questions.stem: Which piece of evidence best supports the claim “Adversity can make people stronger”?
options: Asma's family lived near a river that sometimes floods during the rainy season.
Asma enjoys reading books about famous athletes from many different countries.
After losing her home in a flood, Asma started a club that helps families rebuild.
Floods are common in some parts of the world after very heavy rainstorms each year.
questions.why: The best evidence shows someone growing stronger after hardship.

questions.stem: Is each statement about Jackie Robinson's era a fact or an opinion?

rows.text: Jackie Robinson joined the Brooklyn Dodgers in 1947.
Answering insults with silence is the bravest choice anyone can make.
Segregation laws in parts of the United States separated people by race.
Every athlete should be required to learn restraint.

questions.why: Facts can be checked; opinions state beliefs or judgments.

questions.stem: Match each word about learning a new language with its meaning: fluent, bilingual, mimic, isolated.

to copy the way someone speaks or acts

questions.why: These words describe the experience of living with more than one language.

questions.stem: Because Grandmother speaks only Arabic, Yusuf had to ____ the doctor's English instructions for her.
questions.why: To translate is to change words from one language into another.

questions.stem: True or false: A hesitant swimmer jumps eagerly into the deep end without stopping to think.
questions.why: A hesitant person pauses because he or she is unsure.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word anxious correctly?
options: Reem felt anxious the night before her first day at the new school.
Ali was so anxious that he slept peacefully through the entire trip.
The anxious sandwich was delivered warm to the house by six o'clock.
The anxious sofa sat quietly in the corner of the living room all day.
questions.why: Anxious means worried or nervous, which fits a first day at a new school.

questions.stem: Would each situation most likely make a person feel “embarrassed” or “proud”?

rows.text: Sami called his teacher “Mom” in front of the whole class.
Lina won first prize for her poem about the sea.
Majed tripped over his own bag on the stage.
Hessa's grandmother praised the bread Hessa baked.

questions.why: Embarrassment comes from awkward mistakes; pride comes from success.

questions.stem: Which two sentences describe someone who is bilingual? Choose two.
options: Aisha reads newspapers in both Arabic and French every morning.
Daniel speaks Spanish with his parents and English with his friends.
Nora speaks only English, though she enjoys foreign films with subtitles.
Omar is learning his first few words of Japanese from an app.
questions.why: A bilingual person can use two languages well.

questions.stem: Living alone in the tiny island lighthouse, the keeper felt ____ from the rest of the world.
questions.why: Isolated means cut off and alone.

questions.stem: Find the part that contradicts the rest of this sentence about Mark.
segments: a friend to translate for him.
questions.why: A fluent speaker rarely needs someone to translate.

questions.stem: Which word means the opposite of “hesitant”?

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order to tell how Nasser learned English by mimicking his classmates.

questions.stem: Which event is the turning point in “The Market Translator”?

Mama and her daughter walk to the busy market on a Saturday.
The narrator finds Mama studying English words alone at night.
The narrator becomes fluent in English during her very first year.

questions.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses a theme of “The Market Translator”?

options.label: A
options.text: Children should always do the shopping and talking for their families.

options.label: B

options.label: C

Mama asks the narrator to teach her.

questions.stem: Match each part of plot structure with its example from a tale about a shy new student named Kenji.

questions.stem: True or false: “Tamer feels anxious about speaking English, but his sister Hala jokes easily with her new classmates” contrasts two characters.

questions.stem: Which choice states a theme about language rather than a topic?

A boy who learns to speak Spanish at his new school

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentences: “At the family dinner, everyone spoke English except Grandmother. She smiled and nodded, but her eyes kept drifting to the window.” What does the reader learn about Grandmother?

options.label: A
options.text: She feels left out because she cannot follow the talk.

options.label: B
options.text: She is waiting for a guest who has not yet arrived.

options.label: C
options.text: She is bored because the dinner has lasted too long.

options.label: D
options.text: She understands everything but chooses to stay quiet.

partB.stem: Part B: Which detail best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “She smiled and nodded”

options.label: B
options.text: “At the family dinner”

options.label: C
options.text: “her eyes”

options.label: D
options.text: “everyone spoke English except Grandmother”

questions.why: Language leaves Grandmother isolated, even at her own family's table.

questions.stem: Two stories share the theme “Home is found in people, not places.” How might the two stories most likely differ?
options: One might have a theme about home, and the other a theme about sports.
Both must have exactly the same characters, setting, and plot events.
One must be set in a desert, while the other must be set in a big city.
One might show a family moving abroad, and another a boy at a new school.
questions.why: Stories can share a theme while telling very different events.

questions.stem: Put these events of a tale about an embarrassed new student in the order of plot structure: exposition, rising action, climax, resolution.
sequence: Mei Ling joins a class in Dammam and understands little Arabic.
She feels embarrassed when she mispronounces words, so she stops speaking.
During a class play, she must say one line, and she says it perfectly.
Her classmates cheer, and she begins speaking more each day.
questions.why: The plot introduces Mei Ling, builds her problem, reaches a turning point, and resolves it.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the word that best describes the character in it: fluent, hesitant, anxious, isolated.

pairs.left: Rania speaks French so smoothly that people think she grew up in Paris.
Basim stood at the edge of the group, unsure whether to join the game.
Before the exam, Duaa's hands shook and her stomach churned.
The new boy ate lunch alone each day, far from the others.

questions.why: Character details act as context clues for these describing words.
